Cardinals' Trade Deadline Said Everything About Monti Ossenfort's Job Security
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals' trade deadline has officially come and gone. All eyes in the desert were on the Cardinals and what they'd do after falling to 3-6 on the season. Injuries have decimated this year's iteration of Arizona football, and the Cardinals had plenty of talent available to fully establish themselves as sellers.
As fate would have it, despite all the noise, the Cardinals would stay pat and sidestep opportunities to bolster their 2027 stock of draft picks. The decision to retain veteran players while foregoing the chance to add more future ammo for team-building is one that will have ramifications for both present and future.
General manager Monti Ossenfort surprised more than some in the Valley when owner Michael Bidwill brought him back for a fourth season running the show, even in spite of firing head coach Jonathan Gannon.
His work — or lack thereof — spoke volumes today.
NFL general managers operate differently than most positions on an NFL team. Highly drafted rookies and freshly paid stars are often awarded greater lengths of time to succeed due to the capital invested in them. Coaches, meanwhile, are on the opposite end of the spectrum — a bad first season can immediately put their job in serious danger, as the Cardinals are all too aware with Steve Wilks nearly ten years ago.
Yet general managers fall somewhere in the middle of the spectrum of patience. It's hard to truly get a gauge for their impact until a few years down the road. As a GM, their job is to assemble and build talent. Barring a glaringly obvious hit or bust in either the draft/free agency, there's far too many variables to evaluate who is and isn't capable of running an NFL team.
Plenty in Arizona believed three years was more than enough to make a concrete decision on Ossenfort. After completely stripping Arizona's roster down to bare bones in 2023, the following season saw the Cardinals primed for their first playoff appearance since 2021 after entering their bye week at the top of the NFC West.
Yet the Cardinals crumbled, and 2025 brought no better results. Through three seasons, Arizona won just 15 games, and when Gannon was sent packing, many scratched their heads in disbelief as Ossenfort sat in his seat for another year in charge.
The first half of 2026 brought similar results, and for a general manager who very much was thought to be on the hot seat, the trade deadline presented a rare window of opportunity to potentially evaluate how Ossenfort personally viewed his job security.
A general manager offloading top assets for future draft picks just might signal their belief in job security entering the following offseason. Why would Ossenfort assemble loads of draft picks and sacrifice the rest of the Cardinals' 2026 season if he's not going to be the guy orchestrating their draft?
Conversely, you could make the argument that no moves would actually speak volumes for Ossenfort. He clearly had opportunities to continue adding to an impressive 2027 draft haul of six selections in the first four rounds, which includes two second-round picks. A general manager bypassing those opportunities very well could signal a win-now approach in order to save his job.
Many believed prior trades involving Marvin Harrison Jr. and Jacoby Brissett indicated the Cardinals were open for business. The reality sits a bit lower than that — Harrison hired agents for the first time in his NFL career and practically facilitated a way out while Brissett was quickly demoted to QB3/emergency duties.
Case in point, that didn't exactly signal the Cardinals as sellers ahead of the trade deadline — but it did leave the door open, and by Ossenfort shutting it, his silence spoke volumes.
Ossenfort's refusal to make trades does indicate he's a general manager whose job isn't guaranteed past this season. Arizona reportedly had an offer of a second-round pick for star safety Budda Baker while pass rusher Josh Sweat is clearly going to either demand a new contract next offseason or a trade elsewhere. His value won't be close to what it was at the deadline.
By all accounts, this will be a massively important second half of the season for the Cardinals. Perhaps Ossenfort's fate is already decided. Perhaps it all depends on how competitive the team can be. Perhaps injuries, yet again, could play a factor on who Arizona's general manager will be entering 2027.
However you read it, today's moves — or lack thereof — were a pretty big indication that winning is a priority here and now in the desert. The towel isn't being thrown in for anybody, regardless of how much stronger their 2027 draft could have been as a result.
And for a pretty banged-up 3-6 football team being coached by a rookie head coach, that's not good news for the future of its general manager.

title: Winners and Losers From Cardinals' Surprising Trade Deadline
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals didn't cash in on the bountiful number of trade rumors this week, standing still and not pulling the trigger on any moves as the league's trade deadline officially passed this afternoon.
That came as a surprise for most, as massive names such as Budda Baker and Josh Sweat (among others) were available.
The Cardinals failed to move off of both Budda Baker and Josh Sweat — arguably two of Arizona's top players on Nick Rallis' side of the ball. Arizona was facing the potential of selling both and fully hitting the reset button, which would have massively depleted the Cardinals' defensive talent.
Rallis — who was on the hot seat entering 2026 — keeps two established veteran talents, which should only help him down the stretch of the season. There's probably nobody happier than Rallis in the team's facility right now.
Welcome to the NFL, rook! To be clear, the Cardinals were not expected to make any trades to acquire players ahead of the deadline, though the fact still stands that Arizona didn't make any efforts to try and rescue offensive talent for a unit that's pretty gashed across the board in terms of injuries.
Beck will be tasked to prove himself as a potential franchise passer with little around him to work with, and while that was the expectation, it's now official as the Cardinals can't make any trades.
To read our grades for Arizona's trade deadline, you can click here .
This trade deadline was going to tell us a lot about how Cardinals general manager Monti Ossenfort viewed his job security, as it was unlikely he'd offload stars in Baker/Sweat to get top draft capital for picks he didn't believe he'd be making. Why set up another NFL GM for success if you're the one falling on the sword?
By not trading star players to position themselves better for the future, Ossenfort clearly is trying to maximize this season — one that some believe was already on borrowed time. Now, the Cardinals (as much as they could be) are hoping to win as many games as possible, and now Ossenfort hopes his gamble of silence at the deadline pays off to lend himself another season.
Williams found himself in trade rumors after apparently being in Rallis' doghouse, who has played Williams for just nine total snaps in the last two weeks despite being healthy. Williams is effectively benched for Max Melton, Kalen King, Denzel Burke and Kei'Trel Clark, and with his status as a pending free agent, it's unlikely he gets significant playing time for Arizona moving forward barring injury.
A fresh start would have been best for a player once considered to be one of the top slot corners in the game to contribute elsewhere — though that now isn't on the horizon.
Budda Baker is destined for the team's Ring of Honor after he retires. He's been a steady and powerful presence for the Cardinals during some dark times. Quite frankly, he's played his way into deciding what happens with his future. He appeared to be open to a potential trade, but when the Buffalo Bills came calling with a reported strong offer, the Cardinals declined. Who exactly made the call remains unknown, though we're on the fence on how Baker fares here.
On the plus side, he gets to continue his legacy in Arizona while his placement likely means the Cardinals are willing to pay his $20.8 million cap hit. On the downside, Baker clearly won't be competing for a championship soon despite having the door opened for that possibility. His legacy is cemented in Arizona and most here would have cheered him on elsewhere.
Truly mixed feelings for Baker.

title: Trade Deadline: Grading Every Move Cardinals Made — And Didn't
full_text:
ARIZONA — The NFL's trade deadline has officially come and gone.
The Arizona Cardinals opted for a shocking silence following multiple trades in the weeks leading up to today. With so much chatter, a deal for one of their top available players felt more likely than not.
Yet the dust has settled on Arizona's ability to make trades for the rest of the 2026 season, and the Cardinals must live with their decisions for the remainder of the year.
Grading every trade the Cardinals made — and didn't:
Deal : Marvin Harrison Jr. and a 2027 sixth-round pick for a 2027 second-round pick and 2027 seventh-round pick
Why it graded this way : The Cardinals ultimately notched a second-round pick for Harrison amid minor other picks swapped, which was incredible value for a receiver who caught just five passes for Arizona this season before departing. It was obvious Harrison wasn't going to flourish in the desert, and he hasn't done much since joining the Texans. The only thing holding this from being an "A" grade is Arizona's mountain of injuries at the receiver position after Harrison's departure.
Deal : Jacoby Brissett and a 2027 fifth-round pick for 2027 fourth-round pick and 2028 seventh-round pick
Why it graded this way : Listen, getting anything for Brissett after he was demoted to emergency quarterback status is a win. The fact that the Cardinals essentially jumped from a fifth to a fourth-round pick is a major win, especially for an aging veteran on an expiring deal who wasn't going to see the field again. While the bad contract extension still looms from the summer, we're grading the trade here — and Arizona batted well above expectations here for Brissett.
The stakes : Denver Broncos reportedly called on Trey McBride
Why it graded this way : Look, everybody would love to have a Trey McBride. And the fact that the Broncos inquired on McBride probably doesn't go far in the "Cardinals are doing things right!" playbook by not trading him. Still — even engaging in trade discussions for McBride at this point in time would have been pretty demoralizing for a Cardinals fan-base that's already suffered enough. Arizona's a much better team with McBride on the field, and unless a king's ransom was offered, that should have been a quick phone call.
The stakes : Sweat has been heavily tied in trade rumors since the offseason
Why it graded this way : I'd be very intrigued to hear the offers thrown around for Sweat, who clearly hasn't been happy since the Cardinals fired Jonathan Gannon. Quite frankly it's been an odd offseason/regular season for Sweat, who was MIA all summer and hasn't produced close to par based on his 2025 totals. Who knows if things have been smoothed over by now, though Sweat is looking for a restructured contract with more guaranteed money (since there's none remaining in his final two years) and that's not something the Cardinals should do based on their current timeline. It feels like we're pushing inevitable trade discussions to next offseason, but for now, Arizona retains its top pass rusher.
The stakes : The Cardinals reportedly declined a strong offer (Day 2 pick) from the Buffalo Bills for Baker
Why it graded this way : There's a lot to unpack here. The franchise icon wasn't exactly pounding the table for a trade, though he was reportedly open to a move towards a contender. That opportunity came knocking with what was a reported "strong push" by Buffalo with what's believed to be a second-round pick. Baker is a franchise legend and deserves to dictate his future, so if he was the deciding factor — so be it. However, Arizona is not going to get a stronger offer for Baker, who has just one year left on his current contract and will be turning 30. The Cardinals had a rare perfect opportunity to send Baker on a Super Bowl-contending team while getting top value for a non-premium position, and they declined. The love and respect for Baker is admirable, but the failure to stockpile more top draft capital for a loaded 2027 draft is eye-opening given Baker's age, contract and position. This move keeps the fabric of Arizona's defense in the building and continues a legacy of loyalty for Baker, but that's the only positive given how strong Buffalo's offer was.

title: Cardinals Shockingly Quiet as NFL Trade Deadline Passes
full_text:
ARIZONA — The NFL's 2:00 pm MST deadline to submit trades to the league office has officially come and gone — and to the surprise of many, the Arizona Cardinals were silent today.
The Cardinals, 3-6 on the season, had plenty of names available for trade and even more reason to establish themselves as sellers ahead of a massive 2027 offseason.
After trading Jacoby Brissett and Marvin Harrison Jr. earlier this season, the door still appeared to be open for the Cardinals to welcome more change.
Despite the firestorm of rumors, noise and speculation, Arizona stood pat, made no moves at the trade deadline and will continue the rest of the regular season with the current roster.
Baker was one of the top names surrounding the Cardinals, as the perennial Pro Bowl safety made it clear he was open to a move elsewhere if it meant competing in the postseason — though he also wasn't forcing his way out, either. The fan favorite will remain with Arizona with his contract expiring after the 2027 season.
Reports indicate the Cardinals pushed back on dealing Baker despite a "strong" push from the Buffalo Bills today, which was rumored to be a Day 2 selection.
That's an incredibly tough offer to pass up, though it might speak to the Cardinals' insistence on keeping around a fabric of the team.
Sweat was another big-time player with rumors surrounding him, for different reasons than Baker.
While Baker's trade profile was more so rooted in wanting to do right by the longtime safety, Sweat's originates from a previously reported trade request this offseason. Things didn't exactly appear mended between the two sides during the summer and it's hard to gauge if that relationship was patched since the regular season began.
Sweat also is reportedly in search of a new contract that can afford him some guaranteed money on the final two years of his deal, which is probably something the Cardinals aren't eager to do given the current state of things in Arizona.
There were brief rumors of Garrett Williams being available for a trade with his declining snap count share, though the Cardinals opted to keep what's now transformed into a strong depth piece around in the former third-round pick. With his injury history and expiring contract, Arizona may not have gotten much.
The Cardinals, perhaps smartly, didn't emerge as buyers despite a few names that might have made sense for them.
Arizona had plenty of opportunity to ramp up their aggressiveness at the trade deadline. They declined, and now will have to wait until the offseason to see how their silence either helped or hurt their chances.

title: Cardinals Chances of Trading Budda Baker Takes Blow After Bills Move
full_text:
ARIZONA — As the 2026 NFL trade deadline begins to wind down, the Arizona Cardinals and their potential to deal star safety Budda Baker takes a massive blow.
Numerous reports indicate the Buffalo Bills, highly thought to be interested in Baker, made a splash move for Tennessee Titans safety Amani Hooker today. The Titans in return get a second-rounder for Baker but also are giving up a fifth-round pick to facilitate the deal.
The #Titans were clear Amani Hooker wasn't available unless it was significant draft pick compensation. Now, Tennessee gets another 2nd rounder and kicks back a 5. https://t.co/qZQAv61j5O
Hooker, two years younger than Baker, is under contract through the 2028 season (Baker only through 2027 on his current deal) and is making just $13.5 million per season compared to Baker's $18 million.
While it would have been great for the Cardinals to add another second-round pick, Arizona probably held firm on a price and wouldn't budge — which is fine for Buffalo, who gets a younger and cheaper playmaker at safety.
The NFL's trade deadline is 2:00 p.m. MST.
The Cardinals move into the final moments of the trade deadline with the Detroit Lions seemingly being the only feasible contender left for Baker, who reportedly is open to a trade if it means he goes to a playoff-caliber team.
Baker, a franchise legend that will surely see his name in the Ring of Honor, has remained with the organization through some incredibly tough times. With just one year on his contract and his prime not being extended anytime soon, Baker's consistently found himself in trade rumors the last few seasons.
Yet 2026 felt like a different tune, where rather than it just being noise and speculation, there was legitimate talks of Baker being dealt.
Earlier this season, Baker himself addressed trade rumors:
"I'm here. I want to win. I want to be here. And I'm just controlling what I can control, just taking it one week at a time, and hopefully when the deadline ends, I'll still be here. If not, I mean, it's a business. I understand at the end of the day and that's it," he said.
The Cardinals, sitting at 3-6, are clearly not going to make a playoff push this season. 2027's outlook is murky at best as we evaluate things today. Nobody would blame Baker for wanting to have a fresh start, and quite frankly plenty of Cardinals fans would root him on in hopes of him finally hoisting the ever-so-evasive Lombardi trophy.

title: 3 Last-Minute Trade Targets Cardinals Could Pursue Before Deadline
full_text:
ARIZONA — We're creeping toward the end of the NFL's trade deadline , which will officially pass at 2:00 pm MST today. Thus far, the Arizona Cardinals have not made a move besides signing a rookie quarterback to their roster.
The Cardinals, with time ticking, could potentially be looking to make a small move after their roster has been depleted of talent over the last few hours. Likely? Sitting at 3-6, probably not.
Still, general manager Monti Ossenfort has eight total picks in the 2027 draft – six in the first four rounds – and just might be looking to make a small sprinkle at positions of need.
Three last-minute trade candidates the Cardinals could target:
*projected trade values are by Spotrac *
Why the Cardinals could target him : The Cardinals' receiver room has been decimated with injuries this season. On top of Marvin Harrison Jr. being traded, Arizona's now lost all of Michael Wilson , Kendrick Bourne and Jalen Brooks — that's their top four receivers on the depth chart in Week 1. None of them are suiting up on Sunday or moving forward.
Why he might make sense : Downs is on a cheap deal, though the contract is set to expire after this season. Arizona would need to extend him, though his projected trade value is an early Day 3 pick — which could be worth the swing for Arizona. Downs is Indianapolis' leading receiver with 354 yards on 33 receptions through nine weeks.
Projected trade value : 4th-round pick
Why the Cardinals could target him : Arizona, especially if they indeed trade Josh Sweat, will need somebody capable of rushing the passer in their edge room. The Cardinals have a mix of veteran role players and unproven youth — though there's nobody with legitimate upside ahead for the coming years.
Why he might make sense: Stewart, a first-round pick from 2025, would be a swing for the fences in terms of how he'll pan out. The talent is there but the production is not. However, the enticing part here is he'll be paid $6.5 million over the next three years with a fifth-year option available if he pans out.
Projected trade value : 4th to 5th-round pick
Why the Cardinals could target him : Arizona's offensive line depth has taken a massive hit since the preseason, losing numerous starters and depth pieces across majority of spots, which spans inside and out. One constant player, right tackle Elijah Wilkinson, has been less than impressive in 2026. The Cardinals could use competition there.
Why he might make sense : Wylie is a veteran and versatile offensive lineman with starting experience at both tackle and guard. The financial commitment wouldn't be steep, as he'd be paid $4.6 million over the next two seasons — which gives Arizona the ability to potentially plug and play him at one of their spots moving forward.
Projected trade value : 6th to 7th-round pick

title: 5 Questions That Will Decide Cardinals' Final Trade Deadline Moments
full_text:
ARIZONA – We're mere hours away from the NFL's 2026 trade deadline, and more than anything, the Arizona Cardinals are positioned to be sellers.
After trading away Marvin Harrison Jr. and Jacoby Brissett, the organization's 3-6 record entering Tuesday with big names still available has the team hovering around rumors and headlines alike.
The Cardinals can do a variety of different things today ahead of the 2:00 pm MST cutoff — but these five questions need answered first:
This is perhaps the biggest question that needs answered.
While a general manager's job is to always do what's in the best interest of the team, there's a different vibe to decision-makers who might be out of a job at the end of the season, which Ossenfort currently fits as a descriptor this moment.
There's an entirely different sense of operation when you know you quite possibly aren't going to be around to make draft picks that you traded for previously. And if it comes down to acquiring more draft capital for the future or retaining as much talent to win now and stay in his current seat, what will Ossenfort do?
His feeling on job security is the biggest variable the Cardinals will battle today.
Beyond Ossenfort's job status, the Cardinals do have to factor in how competitive they can be for the rest of the season.
It's easy for fans to demand a sell-off of Arizona's biggest stars. In fact, from an outside and logical perspective, the Cardinals should be sellers if they get proper value for some of their biggest names.
Yet there's something to be said on Arizona's mountain of injuries and what it's done for their outlook moving forward into the second half of 2026. While terms like tanking are often thrown around, it would be a disservice to players and coaches with jobs on the line to completely drain more top talent after injuries have reared their ugly head.
Are the Cardinals okay with completely throwing in the towel on 2026?
Rarely does an NFL player have the service, loyalty and respect to make such calls on his career, especially at a trade deadline, though Budda Baker fits that mold.
The respect Baker commands for sticking with the Cardinals through some very dark days, despite being one of the top safeties in the league continually, is what makes this deadline interesting. Baker reportedly is open for a trade but also would be fine with staying in Arizona.
There's some teams that make sense for Baker to land with in terms of a playoff team looking for that one final piece, though that call feels like it's entirely up to the player to dictate his future.
Josh Sweat's value feels like it will never be higher than this moment, as he'll be another year older next offseason and will be in search of guaranteed dollars on the final two seasons (2027-28) of his contract.
With future contract issues and injury concerns on his knee aside, Sweat's asking price/value of a Day 2 pick by Arizona feels pretty set — either a team gets desperate enough to match or the Cardinals feel fine keeping Sweat, who is far and away their top pass rusher.
It's no secret Sweat wanted out earlier this offseason. If that's true or not very much remains up for debate, but if a team does indeed come in with an offer for a second or third-round pick, the Cardinals just might be willing to do business.
The Cardinals move into today's trade deadline with six picks in the first four rounds, leaving plenty of opportunity for Arizona to address some positions of need if they feel so desired.
However, do the Cardinals feel inclined to ditch some of that draft capital with a 3-6 record and little hope for turning things around? Perhaps there's an under the radar player at a position (like receiver) they feel can help both now and in the future.
A weapon like Brian Thomas Jr. is probably off the table. And barring an obviously great trade that appears on their doorstep, the team isn't likely to make any big splashes in terms of buying power.
However, an under-the-radar move might still be on the table if the situation and price is right. Arizona clearly needs more help on their roster at the moment — they just have to weigh opportunity cost.

title: Cardinals Sign New Rookie QB Ahead of Trade Deadline
full_text:
The Arizona Cardinals are set to welcome another fresh face to their quarterback room as their most important position dwindles in numbers.
The Cardinals, just a day after reportedly signing veteran quarterback Josh Johnson, are set to also sign Jacksonville Jaguars practice squad quarterback Joey Aguilar to their active roster.
The Cardinals are signing quarterback Joey Aguilar to the active roster, per source.
Per NFL rules, since the Cardinals signed him off another team's practice squad, Arizona must keep him on their active roster for a minimum of three weeks.
Aguilar went undrafted in the 2026 NFL Draft and signed with the Jacksonville Jaguars before being cut and signed back to their practice squad before the season.
The 25-year-old passer played his final three years of collegiate football at Appalachian State (2023-24) and Tennessee (2025). He led the Volunteers to an 8-5 record with a 67.3% completion rate and 24 touchdowns to ten interceptions.
Aguilar, measuring at 6-3 and 229 lbs, had the following scouting report from NFL.com during this year's draft process:
"Compact, durable quarterback who has climbed levels twice and had success. Aguilar will be a 25-year-old rookie with three seasons of FBS experience. He played in a system heavy on play-action at Tennessee, but his touchdown production and overall consistency dipped after an explosive early stretch in 2025. He dissects zone defenses with adequate processing speed and decisiveness, but tight-window throws are a challenge. Whether on- or off-platform, he makes receivers work too hard for their catches with inconsistent placement and a lack of touch underneath. He’s tough in the pocket and proved he could make plays under pressure. Aguilar’s age shouldn’t work against him, but he must prove he can work through pro progressions and throw with better accuracy to earn a backup job."
That's not exactly a glowing endorsement, though the Cardinals weren't going to trade for a quarterback ahead of today's deadline, especially with Carson Beck firmly in their starting seat.
Arizona recently lost Gardner Minshew to a potential season-ending injury while prior starter Jacoby Brissett was traded last week.
Now, the Cardinals are just 3-6 with a gloomy future entering the second half of their schedule. Their loss against the Seahawks truly swayed the outlook/sentiment of their season, and Michael Wilson's season-ending injury only put the nail in the coffin of Arizona's hopes.
Aguilar has a bit of experience under Jaguars head coach Liam Coen and his offense, who — like Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur - is a disciple of the Sean McVay coaching tree.

title: 3 Brutally Honest Thoughts as Cardinals Begin Carson Beck Era
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Carson Beck era is officially here, whether the Arizona Cardinals like it or not.
After trading Jacoby Brissett and losing Gardner Minshew to a reported UCL injury, the third-round rookie is all but set to enter action for the second half of Arizona's season.
Three honest thoughts as we begin:
Hindsight will forever be 20/20, but after trading Brissett the Cardinals had just two quarterbacks on their roster in Minshew/Beck. Yours truly asked Mike LaFleur if the team would be adding a third quarterback, and a "we'll see" was a response.
As fate would have it, the Cardinals were dwindled down to just Beck for a short time on Monday before reportedly signing Josh Johnson — who is 40 years old.
Arizona probably regrets not bringing in a third quarterback last week, who would have been added to the practice squad and would at least have a week's head start on Johnson in terms of learning LaFleur's playbook.
Kedon Slovis would have been the perfect player to add, though the Ravens signed him early last week to their active roster. Johnson does have some prior connections to LaFleur and current offensive coordinator Nathaniel Hackett, though he doesn't have the first-hand experience Slovis did in Arizona.
The move to sign a third (and emergency) quarterback wouldn't have changed Sunday's outcome or Arizona's trajectory moving forward, though they are indeed less prepared at football's most important position as a result.
The Cardinals' rookie passer has virtually no weapons outside of Trey McBride, a vastly depleted offensive line ahead of him and will face a Rams defense that just saw Myles Garrett return to the tune of three sacks, finally giving Los Angeles the coveted 1-2 punch they've been waiting for with Aaron Donald.
Simply put, Beck is set up for failure against the Los Angeles Rams this week. And to make matters worse, no home cooking will ensure – State Farm Stadium is set to host plenty of Rams fans on Sunday. This will likely be the first time he's ever faced serious crowd noise against him while playing a home game.
Naturally, fans will jump at the first opportunity to overreact from one game. If Beck plays poorly like anticipated — even if not entirely due to his own performance — a good portion of Cardinals fans will be eager to immediately write him off.
Context is key against the Rams' defense, but so is patience. Regardless of how you slice it, this will be Beck's first taste of NFL action since the very first preseason game. He's essentially being asked to win a gun fight with a rubber knife.
Beck's career, outlook and trajectory will not be defined by his first 60 minutes of football, and it's important to remember that.
With the above stated, the Cardinals now enter the Beck era. How long that lasts entirely depends on the second half of the season, and while it will be incredibly hard to judge Beck given the current circumstances around the team, every snap he takes regardless of who is out there will weigh heavily on Arizona's decision to pursue a quarterback in the 2027 offseason.
That's simply the nature of the beast, even an unfortunate one. But the reality is Beck was never going to have ample time or resources available to him to make the best impression as a third-round pick. However, the Cardinals have been gathering information on Beck behind the scenes since the moment he landed in the building.
Fairly or unfairly, everything Beck does from now until the end of the season carries massive weight to decide his — and Arizona's — future.

title: 3 Honest Takeaways as Cardinals Lose Michael Wilson For Season
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals were dealt a massive blow yesterday with news of star wide receiver Michael Wilson being sidelined for the year due to a neck injury suffered in Week 9.
Wilson's injury came as a massive surprise given the Cardinals knew nothing of the severity of the injury. Head coach Mike LaFleur told reporters Wilson suffered it on the fourth play of the game and still played the rest of the matchup against Seattle in its entirety.
Now, the Cardinals are left scrambling.
Three honest takeaways from a brutal break:
Before we dive into x's and o's and what this injury means on the field, this is a legitimate gut-punch for Arizona's locker room. Aside from the talent, Wilson is one of the team's leaders and hardest workers. More so for just the person, Wilson's a gem of an individual who quite frankly didn't deserve this — but he'll bounce back better than ever.
The Cardinals' offense has changed, a lot, within the last few weeks due to unfortunate injuries.
After trading away Marvin Harrison Jr., the Cardinals have lost Jalen Brooks and Kendrick Bourne to injured reserve. Wilson's injury pins Arizona's current receiving corps at... Zay Jones, Simi Fehoko and Reggie Virgil. Maybe Devin Duvernay if you want to get spicy.
Yes, the Cardinals still have Trey McBride. No, Arizona shouldn't just completely throw in the towel on the season. However, Mike LaFleur's offense just got a whole lot worse overnight while defensive gameplans just got a whole lot easier.
Defenses will now be able to stack more boxes, sell out on more runs (against a depleted Cardinals line) and double team McBride — and if one of Arizona's depth receivers can beat them, so be it.
Case in point, it's truly hard to see the light for this Cardinals offense moving forward. It'd be hard for Ted Lasso to find optimism surrounding this team.
Injuries impact every team, every year — but Arizona's attack is officially devoid of established talent outside of McBride. Wilson's injury was the final nail in the coffin.
With the aforementioned section and beliefs, I'm not a fan of the Cardinals pursuing somebody ahead of the NFL's trade deadline.
Had Arizona been in thick competition for a playoff push, I believe it would have been justifiable. Yet due to current circumstances (3-6 record, bottom of the NFC West) and available wide receivers, the bang doesn't quite match the buck in terms of who is available.
The Cardinals, thanks to prior moves with Jacoby Brissett and Harrison, have assembled some strong draft capital for 2027.
Barring an absolute can't-miss deal, that shouldn't change for the Cardinals. A trade for a new receiver isn't some magic elixir that can fix this team, and if the goal is to truly build for the future under LaFleur, that has to remain at the forefront of decision-making.

title: Who Will Be the Falcons' New Starting Center After Ryan Neuzil Trade with Ravens?
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons have agreed to trade center Ryan Neuzil to the Baltimore Ravens in exchange for guard Andrew Vorhees and a 2028 sixth-round draft pick. With Neuzil heading to Baltimore, Atlanta now has an opening at center heading into Sunday's matchup against the Kansas City Chiefs.
Corey Levin is the most likely option to replace Neuzil in the starting lineup. The veteran offensive lineman has been listed as Neuzil's backup throughout the season and now has an opportunity to earn an expanded role.
Although Levin does not have an extensive history as a starting center in the NFL, he brings some experience to the position. He has made seven career starts in the league, giving Atlanta a player who has at least experienced the responsibilities of starting at the professional level.
He was originally selected in the sixth round of the 2017 NFL Draft by the Tennessee Titans. He's played six seasons with the Titans, not counting practice squad duty when he didn't make an NFL appearance, and joined the Falcons as a free agent in March.
The Falcons will need him to get comfortable quickly, particularly with the Chiefs coming to Atlanta this Sunday. Communication along the offensive line will be especially important as Levin takes on responsibility for identifying defensive fronts and helping keep the pocket clean for quarterback Michael Penix Jr.
Atlanta cannot afford to have communication issues up front, especially against a Kansas City defense capable of creating pressure in multiple ways.
Levin's familiarity with the offensive line and his experience serving as Neuzil's backup should help make the transition easier.
While Levin appears positioned to take over as the starter, the Falcons have also made a move to strengthen their depth at the position.
Atlanta signed center Gus Hartwig to its practice squad, giving the organization another option as it adjusts to life without Neuzil.
Hartwig brings considerable college experience, having made 48 starts at Purdue. He also spent time with the Detroit Lions and New York Jets before joining Atlanta.
His addition provides the Falcons with another developmental option at center while giving the coaching staff some insurance behind Levin.
It remains to be seen whether Hartwig will eventually receive an opportunity to compete for a larger role, but his experience at Purdue gives Atlanta another player familiar with the responsibilities of playing center.
Neuzil's departure marks the end of an important chapter for Atlanta's offensive line.
The Falcons originally signed him as an undrafted free agent following the 2021 NFL Draft. He gradually worked his way up the depth chart, appearing in 69 games and making 38 starts during his time in Atlanta.
The trade also reunites Neuzil with former Falcons offensive line coach Dwayne Ledford, who held that position in Atlanta from 2021 through 2025.
In return, Atlanta receives Vorhees, a former seventh-round selection who was considered a potential Day 2 pick before suffering an ACL injury at the 2023 NFL Scouting Combine. Since returning to full health, Vorhees has started 22 of 39 possible games.
The additional draft pick also gives Atlanta another asset as it continues reshaping its roster.
For now, however, the biggest question is whether Levin can provide the stability Atlanta needs in the middle of its offensive line.
With the Chiefs approaching, the Falcons will have little time to adjust. Levin appears to have the inside track to replace Neuzil, and his performance could play an important role in determining how well Atlanta's offense operates moving forward.

title: Falcons Make Shock Trade Deadline Deal with Ravens for Starting Center Ryan Neuzil
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons are making another surprising move ahead of the NFL trade deadline, this time shaking up their offensive line by trading starting center Ryan Neuzil to the Baltimore Ravens. According to a source, Atlanta is sending Neuzil to Baltimore in exchange for offensive lineman Andrew Vorhees and a 2028 sixth-round draft pick.
The move is unexpected considering Neuzil's importance to Atlanta's offensive line over the past two seasons. He has played almost exclusively at center and has been the team's starter since 2025, becoming a familiar presence in the middle of the offensive line.
However, Neuzil is in the final year of his contract, giving Atlanta an opportunity to acquire assets rather than potentially lose him in free agency. He also has ties to Ravens offensive line coach Dwayne Ledford, who recruited him to Appalachian State before the two reunited in Atlanta.
This was the second move the Falcons have made on Tuesday. They also signed Jake Moody from the Ravens practice squad , while releasing Nick Folk in a corresponding move.
Falcons reporter Tori McElhaney also reported that the Falcons released edge rusher Drake Jackson from the practice squad and added former Denver Broncos safety Delarrin Turner-Yell and center Gus Hartwig to the
The trade is another indication of the direction general manager Ian Cunningham wants to take this organization as he continues reshaping the roster.
Atlanta's latest move comes just one day after trading veteran safety Jessie Bates III to the Jacksonville Jaguars in exchange for a 2027 second-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick.
The Falcons are clearly approaching the trade deadline with an emphasis on acquiring future assets rather than sacrificing draft picks to make a playoff push.
Cunningham has been vocal about his philosophy of accumulating draft selections. During his introductory press conference, he made it clear how much he values having additional opportunities to build through the draft.
"I love picks, man," Cunningham said.
He has also described draft selections as currency, explaining that accumulating more picks gives an organization additional opportunities to find impact players.
That philosophy is becoming increasingly evident in Atlanta. Cunningham previously helped oversee Chicago's draft strategy as assistant general manager, and he appears intent on bringing a similar approach to the Falcons.
The organization now has additional draft picks to work with as it looks toward the 2027 offseason.
In return, Atlanta receives Andrew Vorhees, a 27-year-old interior offensive lineman with starting experience.
Baltimore selected Vorhees in the seventh round of the 2023 NFL Draft out of USC. He started all 17 games for the Ravens in 2025 and provides Atlanta with another experienced option along the offensive line.
His arrival gives the Falcons flexibility as they determine who will replace Neuzil at center.
Ultimately, this is another significant roster decision from Cunningham. Between moving Bates and now Neuzil, Atlanta appears increasingly focused on building its future through the draft while adding players who fit its longer-term plans.

title: Falcons Poach Kicker from Ravens, Nick Folk Released, per Report
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons are making a change at kicker, officially releasing veteran Nick Folk and signing Jake Moody off the Baltimore Ravens' practice squad, according to NFL insider Jordan Schultz . Moody will be added to Atlanta's 53-man roster and is expected to take over kicking right away.
The move comes after another disappointing performance from Folk in Sunday's 34-17 loss to the Cincinnati Bengals. The veteran kicker missed a 38-yard field goal in the fourth quarter, adding to a growing list of struggles that ultimately cost him his job in Atlanta.
Moody, meanwhile, is coming off a successful appearance for Baltimore. He connected on a 53-yard field goal against the Jacksonville Jaguars on Thursday, showing the leg strength Atlanta hopes to add to its special teams unit.
Folk entered the season with an impressive track record. He had been the NFL's most accurate kicker in each of the previous three seasons, missing just one field goal in each campaign. However, that consistency did not carry over to Atlanta.
His struggles became increasingly difficult to overlook over the past two weeks.
Against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Week 9, Folk missed a 53-yard field goal in Atlanta's 16-0 shutout loss. He followed that performance by missing a 38-yard attempt against Cincinnati, his first missed field goal from inside 40 yards in a regular-season game since 2017.
The miss against the Bengals snapped a streak of 107 consecutive successful field goals from that distance.
Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski addressed Folk's struggles following Sunday's loss and offered a noticeably different response than he had in previous weeks.
"I'm very focused on this game," Stefanski said. "Obviously, I expect Nick to make his kicks. Nick expects to make his kicks, but really just focused on this game."
When asked whether he was concerned about Folk's performance, Stefanski added:
"He knows we're counting on him, and that's the nature of being a guy that you're counting on. But he's a pro."
Those comments represented a shift from the confidence Stefanski previously expressed in his veteran kicker. After Folk's missed 53-yarder against Tampa Bay, Stefanski said he was very confident in his abilities and would not think twice about putting him on the field.
That confidence ultimately did not prevent Atlanta from exploring other options. The Falcons have now decided to move on from Folk entirely.
Moody gives the Falcons a younger option with starting experience and the ability to connect on longer field goals.
The 26-year-old was originally selected by the San Francisco 49ers in the third round of the 2023 NFL Draft. He spent time with San Francisco and Washington before joining Baltimore's practice squad.
Moody most recently appeared for the Ravens against the Jacksonville Jaguars on November 5. He connected on his lone field-goal attempt, a 53-yarder, and converted his only extra-point attempt.
For his NFL career, Moody has converted 65 of 83 field-goal attempts, a 78.3 percent success rate. He also has experience making kicks from beyond 50 yards, including a career-long 57-yard field goal.
The Falcons are hoping Moody can provide more consistency at a position that has become an unexpected problem this season.
Atlanta has dealt with several issues throughout its disappointing campaign, and missed kicks have only added to the frustration. With Folk unable to deliver the reliability the organization expected, the Falcons have decided it is time for a different direction.
Moody now gets an opportunity to establish himself as Atlanta's kicker moving forward, while Folk will look for his next opportunity after his release.

title: Falcons Earn High Marks for Jessie Bates III Trade with Jaguars
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons made headlines yesterday when they traded All-Pro safety Jessie Bates III to the Jacksonville Jaguars for a second-round pick in April's NFL Draft and a fifth-round pick in 2028.
The Falcons were busy in the offseason with multi-year contract extensions for their young nucleus of players , but Bates was left without a new deal. Bates turns 30 in February, and his not getting a new contract was a harbinger of things to come by Tuesday's trade deadline.
From the Falcons' point of view, they are 3-6, paying a significant salary to a non-premium position to an aging player who is on the final eight games of his contract.
Despite denials from Kevin Stefanski on Monday , it's definitely a signal that the Falcons are focused on 2027, loading up on draft picks and sitting on the most available salary cap in the NFL.
To Falcons fans, it's a sign of another lost season from a franchise that has had eight-straight losing seasons.
But what did the national media think about the deal? Looking from the outside in, ESPN's Seth Walder, who hated pretty much every move the Falcons made over the last five seasons, loved the move, giving the Falcons a B+ on their return.
Walder rightly points out that keeping Bates and trying to get a comp pick for him wasn't going to work in Atlanta. They have $150 million in available salary cap space, and it's likely they'll sign multiple free agents who would cancel out the Bates loss in the formula.
"If the Falcons were not going to be contenders this season, then they almost had to deal Bates for the most they could get for him," Walder wrote on ESPN . "And while the 3-6 Falcons are still in the race in the lowly NFC South, they had to ask themselves: Is this team really going to make a run in 2026? It seems they answered that question honestly."
The Jaguars may have overpaid on the surface, but if they let Bates walk at the end of the season, they could get up to a third-round draft pick in return via the comp formula. The Jaguars are sitting $20 million over next year's cap already and aren't expected to be players in free agency.
After the trade, the Falcons are sitting on picks No. 10, No. 41, No. 60, and No. 72 in next year's draft. They can address a plethora of needs with those picks , including offensive tackle, wide receiver, and cornerback, among others.
It also gives them another pick to add to a package should they decide to trade up into the top five for a quarterback if they deem that's the move to make.
From all of the one year contracts to the salary cap hoarding, the Falcons indicated they were pointing towards 2027 as a re-tooling year for the franchise.
An excellent return on the Bates trade further indicated their intentions.

title: Falcons QB Michael Penix Jr. Flashes Rarely Seen Skill Amid Performance Drop-Off
full_text:
Michael Penix Jr. isn’t a scrambling quarterback by any means.
Entering this season, he had just 81 career rushing yards.
“I get that a lot about me not really scrambling much,” Penix said.
The third-year Atlanta Falcons quarterback is a pocket passer relying on processing defenses and a strong arm.
But that doesn’t mean the 6-foot-3, 220-pounder doesn’t possess the athleticism and wheels to elude opposing defenses if a play breaks down.
“That’s definitely part of Mike’s game,” Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski told reporters Monday. “He’s plenty big and fast enough, and I thought those were excellent moments where he could move forward and make plays with his legs.”
In Atlanta’s NFL Madrid game debacle that was a prelude to a roster shakeup , Penix rushed for a career-high 50 yards on three carries in the 34-17 Week 9 loss to the Cincinnati Bengals at Santiago Bernabéu Stadium. He had 15 yards on the ground before the breakout performance.
His top rush was for 23 yards in the first quarter. Look too fast, and you’d think it was another left-handed Falcons quarterback named “Michael”.
The run put Atlanta in position to take a 10-7 lead on a 31-yard Nick Folk field goal.
“I felt good out there,” Penix said, discussing his mobility at Sunday’s postgame press conference. “I was able to scramble – get a couple of first downs. That’s what I felt we needed in those situations, so I took advantage of it.”
Penix finished the game with 20-for-31 passing for 162 yards, a touchdown, an interception, and 50 yards on the ground, second on the team behind running back Bijan Robinson’s 100 .
Penix’s running was a silver lining as his performance has dwindled the last two games, with one being a four-interception outing , after back-to-back three-touchdown pass games and an NFC Offensive Player of the Week award .
It could potentially introduce a new layer to offensive coordinator Tommy Rees’ scheme.
Knowing Penix can willingly pull the football and make a run for it can keep defenses honest as they’ve begun stacking the box on Atlanta to stop Robinson and the Falcons’ rushing attack .
“That adds a different dimension to your offense when your quarterback is getting out of there,” Stefanski said. “Those happen when you have really good pocket movement, when you have good decisions, when you’re listening to your feet.”
After losing four of their last five, the Falcons’ (3-6) upcoming schedule is unrelenting.
Up next is a Week 10 home game as Atlanta hosts the Kansas City Chiefs (6-2) and their three-time MVP and Super Bowl champion quarterback Patrick Mahomes.
Kansas City hosted and defeated the New York Jets 35-12 in Week 9 behind standout performances from Mahomes and running back and reigning Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker III, formerly of the Seattle Seahawks.
Kickoff is at 1 p.m. from Mercedes-Benz Stadium on CBS.

title: Kevin Stefanski Sends Message to Falcons Fans After Jessie Bates Trade
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons are insisting they are not giving up on the 2026 season, despite making a significant move that suggests the organization is also looking toward the future.
Atlanta traded veteran safety Jessie Bates III to the Jacksonville Jaguars on Monday, a move that could be interpreted as a sign that the Falcons are shifting their focus toward 2027 rather than making a push for the playoffs this season. However, head coach Kevin Stefanski pushed back against that notion during his Monday press conference.
Stefanski acknowledged the difficulty of moving on from Bates.
“You guys know how I feel about Jessie, the person, Jessie, the player,” Stefanski told reporters. “But at the same time, this is football, where sometimes you have one foot in the short term, one foot in the long term. There's things like this that make your team better in the long run. Draft picks are the lifeblood of an organization. That's something we believe in.”
The decision to trade Bates is significant considering his importance to Atlanta's defense. He has been one of the team's most recognizable leaders and an important piece of the secondary. Losing him creates another challenge for a Falcons team that has struggled to find consistency this season.
Still, Stefanski wants fans to understand that the trade does not mean Atlanta is abandoning its postseason aspirations.
When asked whether the organization was essentially punting on the season, Stefanski made his position clear.
“Our fans are smart enough to know that in no way, shape, or form would we punt on this season. We have three wins, just like the rest of our division. Obviously not where we want to be, we want to play better, but we're very much in the thick of this thing and we trust in the guys that we have,” Stefanski said.
There is some truth to Stefanski's argument. The NFC South remains wide open, and Atlanta is still within reach of the division title despite sitting at 3-6. The Falcons have an opportunity to make up ground if they can turn things around over the second half of the season.
However, there is a difference between remaining mathematically competitive and making moves that suggest an organization believes it can contend right now.
Trading Bates sends a complicated message. Atlanta is collecting valuable draft picks for the future while simultaneously asking its current roster to find a way to compete without one of its most important defensive players.
Stefanski also emphasized that replacing Bates will require a collective effort.
“It's not just one person that has to step up. It's all of us that have to step up,” Stefanski said.
The Falcons can insist they are not giving up on 2026, and technically, they remain in the NFC South race. But Monday's trade raises legitimate questions about the organization's priorities.
Atlanta may still have a chance to win one of the weakest divisions in football, but trading away a player of Bates' caliber is not necessarily the move expected from a team that believes it is positioned to make a serious postseason run.
Stefanski can say the Falcons are not punting on the season. Now, the team will have to prove it on the field.

title: Falcons Move Jessie Bates, But Who Could be Next?
full_text:
With Monday morning’s announcement that Jessie Bates III would be moved to Jacksonville , the Atlanta Falcons are officially trade-deadline sellers. The All-Pro safety was entering the final year of his contract, and Ian Cunningham nets a solid return for the takeaway machine, landing a 2027 second-rounder and a 2028 fifth-rounder.
Now the question is who is next?
In a bad division, Atlanta could earn a playoff spot, but the team's current construction isn't set up for a run. At 3-6 and staring down the barrel of another losing season, the Falcons could be open for business. Falcons OnSI highlighted some potential targets and outlined why they will (or won’t) be involved in any discussions.
The first person who comes to mind is the Falcons’ tight end. After signing an expensive offseason deal, Pitts has not emerged as a consistent contributor for the Falcons this season. He has been an outstanding red-zone threat, scoring four touchdowns so far, but he has accounted for a pedestrian 25 receptions for 220 yards.
He has flashed some of the playmaking ability that helped him post a career year in 2025, but for whatever reason, the Falcons haven't consistently gotten him involved.
Moving Pitts would make sense on the surface, but the money makes any deal extremely unlikely. The Falcons just signed him to a new deal, and he carries a $36 million dead cap hit this season and a $31.4 million dead cap hit in 2027.
In reality, this star tight end is not going anywhere.
C.J. Henderson has turned his career around in Atlanta, emerging as a starting-caliber player this season. The former first-round pick has started more games than he has since 2022 and has been a solid second cornerback behind A.J. Terrell Jr.
With Avieon Terrell emerging as a viable outside option, the Falcons could look to move Henderson to give the rookie more snaps. He wouldn’t fetch a lucrative return, but he would be a good depth piece for a contender.
On the other hand, Henderson is still only 28, and he is the prototype of a starting corner in this league. The Falcons need secondary depth, and retaining a player of his caliber would be smart. But if they aren’t going to re-sign him this spring, then a trade could be on the table.
The Falcons’ late-summer add has more than paid off this season. The veteran pass rusher has 4.5 sacks and would be an ideal rotational piece for a contending team.
In Atlanta, James Pearce Jr. returned to the mix in Madrid, but they also lost Samson Ebukam to a hamstring injury. Smith is still needed, and at 34 on a one-year deal, there wouldn’t be much return in a trade. But if the Falcons are only interested in picking up assets, it could be worth considering.
Like Za’Darius Smith, the Falcons could also look to move Cameron Thomas. The veteran is on a team-friendly deal, and he has been an outstanding member of the rotation. He is an effective run defender and has a high motor in the pass rush, both of which would be attractive to a contending team looking for a rotational piece.
If Cunningham makes another move, expect it to be a veteran on an expiring deal, not a core piece. Pitts is extremely unlikely, and Henderson is more valuable as depth than as a return.
In August, the Falcons said they were competing for a playoff spot. The next 48 hours will show whether Bates was a one-off or a new direction.
Garrett Chapman is a sports broadcaster, writer, and content creator based in Atlanta. He has several years of experience covering the Atlanta sports scene, college football, Georgia high school football, recruiting for 24/7 Sports, and the NFL. You can also hear him on Sports Radio 92.9 The Game.

title: Who Replaces Jessie Bates III after Atlanta Falcons Trade with Jacksonville Jaguars?
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons have a significant hole to fill in their secondary following the reported trade of Jessie Bates III to the Jacksonville Jaguars . While replacing a player of Bates' caliber will not be easy, Atlanta has several options already on its roster, with Sydney Brown potentially getting the first opportunity.
Brown is an intriguing candidate to take over Bates' role, especially considering how the Falcons have utilized him throughout the 2026 season. The former Philadelphia Eagles safety has spent considerable time playing nickel, rotating in and out of the lineup while giving Atlanta another option closer to the line of scrimmage.
With Bates now out of the picture, the Falcons could move Brown back to his more natural safety position alongside Xavier Watts.
Through nine games this season, Brown has recorded 32 total tackles, 19 solo tackles, 13 assisted tackles, one pass defended and one forced fumble. He has appeared in all nine games while making four starts. He has also played 35% of Atlanta's defensive snaps, giving an indication of the rotational role he has occupied.
Brown's versatility is something Atlanta has valued since acquiring him from Philadelphia in March. Defensive coordinator Jeff Ulbrich previously praised the number of options available in the secondary, saying the team had "millionaire problems" when discussing how to utilize all its defensive backs.
That depth is particularly important considering Atlanta elected to keep 14 defensive backs on its initial 53-man roster, carrying nine cornerbacks and five safeties. This reflects the organization's desire to have multiple options capable of handling different responsibilities across the secondary.
Ulbrich has also explained why having that flexibility matters. When discussing Brown's workload at nickel, he pointed out how demanding the position can be.
"For Sydney to have to play that every single down, that can get taxing for a guy because what we ask that position to do is so difficult," Ulbrich said.
Next in line would be fourth-year veteran DeMarcco Hellams. Hellams has been a special teams stalwart for the Falcons this season, but he's also seen 24 snaps on defense, including a season-high 13 in a blowout win over the Saints.
Hellams is a big hitter who would be best used as a box safety in run support as opposed to coverage.
Moving Brown from nickel would mean more snaps for someone else as the Falcons have had trouble keeping Billy Bowman Jr. and Avieon Terrell healthy.
That is where Mike Hughes could become important.
Hughes has experience playing both outside cornerback and nickel. The veteran stepped inside against San Francisco when Atlanta needed additional help at the position, playing 17 defensive snaps at nickel and allowing just one reception for 11 yards while recording a pass breakup.
Ulbrich praised Hughes for embracing the adjustment, calling him a valuable asset and highlighting his willingness to do whatever the team needed.
Ultimately, Brown appears to be the most logical candidate to receive an expanded opportunity at safety. His experience at the position, combined with Atlanta's depth at cornerback, gives the Falcons a potential solution without needing to make an immediate outside addition.
Replacing Bates' production and leadership will be difficult, but Atlanta's decision to maintain significant depth in its secondary could help soften the blow.

title: Atlanta Falcons and Jacksonville Jaguars Execute Big Trade for All-Pro Jessie Bates III
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons are moving on from one of the most important players in their secondary, trading Pro Bowl safety Jessie Bates III to the Jacksonville Jaguars in exchange for a 2027 second-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick, according to ESPN's Adam Schefter .
The move marks a significant change for Atlanta's defense as the organization parts ways with one of its most experienced defensive playmakers. Bates was also in the final year of his contract, making the decision to move him now an opportunity for the Falcons to receive draft compensation rather than risk losing him without anything in return during the offseason.
Bates joined the Falcons in 2023 after spending the first five seasons of his NFL career with the Cincinnati Bengals. He quickly became a leader in Atlanta's secondary and one of the team's most consistent defensive contributors.
The 29-year-old was brought to Atlanta to provide stability, playmaking ability and veteran leadership. He delivered on those expectations, establishing himself as one of the better safeties in the league during his time with the organization.
Bates earned Pro Bowl recognition and second-team All-Pro honors during his career, making him one of the most accomplished defensive players on Atlanta's roster.
Through eight games this season, Bates has recorded 46 total tackles, one interception and three forced fumbles. His production has continued to demonstrate his ability to impact games in multiple ways.
Since arriving in Atlanta, Bates has also been a consistent presence around the football, recording 14 interceptions during his Falcons tenure.
For Jacksonville, acquiring Bates provides an experienced defensive back who can immediately strengthen the back end of its defense. His experience and leadership should give the Jaguars another proven playmaker as they look to compete in the AFC.
Meanwhile, Atlanta receives a valuable return for a veteran player who was approaching the end of his contract. The second-round selection in 2027 and the fifth-round pick in 2028 give the Falcons additional flexibility as they evaluate the direction of their roster moving forward.
Losing Bates is not a minor departure for Atlanta. Replacing his production, communication, and leadership will be a challenge for a secondary that has relied on his presence.
Ultimately, the Falcons turn a potentially expiring contract into two future draft selections while giving Bates an opportunity to continue his career in Jacksonville. The focus now shifts to how Atlanta plans to replace one of its biggest defensive playmakers.

title: 'Unacceptable' Falcons Penalties Prove Costly in Loss to Bengals
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons had plenty of opportunities to keep Sunday’s matchup against the Cincinnati Bengals competitive, but a series of costly penalties made an already difficult afternoon even tougher.
Atlanta committed 12 penalties for 88 yards in its 34-17 loss to Cincinnati in Madrid, Spain. The season-high in penalties proved particularly damaging, as the Falcons repeatedly put themselves behind the chains and erased opportunities to generate points against one of the NFL’s most explosive offenses.
Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski was understandably frustrated with the lack of discipline, especially considering how much emphasis the coaching staff places on avoiding penalties throughout the week.
“We had too many self-inflicted things today that will make it really hard to win versus any opponent, and in this case, a very good football team,” Stefanski said after the game.
The penalties were especially damaging in critical situations. One of the biggest examples came during Atlanta’s second offensive possession.
Michael Penix Jr. scrambled for a six yard gain that brought the Falcons to the one-yard line, putting them in an excellent position to score a touchdown. However, a holding penalty on left guard Matthew Bergeron wiped away the play and pushed Atlanta back to the 17-yard line.
After another penalty further complicated the drive, the Falcons were unable to reach the end zone and settled for a field goal.
Against a Cincinnati offense led by Joe Burrow, those missed opportunities were difficult to overcome.
The Falcons had another costly sequence in the fourth quarter. Facing third and two at the Bengals’ 10-yard line, Atlanta committed multiple penalties on the same play. Cincinnati accepted a holding penalty against Kyle Pitts, and the Falcons ultimately failed to convert the first down. Nick Folk subsequently missed a 38-yard field goal attempt.
Stefanski specifically pointed to the pre snap penalties as an area that simply cannot continue happening.
The Falcons' head coach called those mistakes “inexcusable,” emphasizing the importance of translating what the team accomplishes during practice into its performance on game day.
Penix also acknowledged the frustration, explaining that penalties have been a major point of emphasis during team meetings.
“Usually it’s less than one or two penalties each day,” Penix said, referencing the numbers Stefanski typically reviews with the team. “We’ve had some clean days as well.”
However, Sunday’s performance was a different story.
“Whenever we come out here and, you know, have 12 penalties between all three units, it’s tough to win like that,” Penix said.
The quarterback also recognized how damaging the holding penalty was after his scramble brought the Falcons within inches of the goal line.
“Whenever we do have a penalty like that bringing us from the one to the 15, or whatever it was, that’s crushing,” Penix said. “And we can’t do that. Great football teams can’t do that, and we can’t beat ourselves. We have to go out there and beat the other team.”
Ultimately, the penalties were only part of Atlanta’s problems. The defense struggled to contain Burrow, who completed 24 of 29 passes for 271 yards and three touchdowns. Ja’Marr Chase added 155 receiving yards, while Tee Higgins caught two touchdowns.
Still, the Falcons made their afternoon considerably more difficult with mistakes they could have avoided.
Stefanski knows his team cannot afford to continue making those mistakes, particularly with another difficult matchup against the Kansas City Chiefs approaching.
“When you’re playing good football teams you have to be at your best, and we were not at our best today,” Stefanski said.
Atlanta falls to 3-6 with its second consecutive loss. If the Falcons want to turn their season around, improving their discipline and eliminating self-inflicted mistakes will have to be part of the solution.
