title: Lions Trade for Jets Safety: What We Know
full_text:
The Detroit Lions have made a trade ahead of Tuesday's deadline.
After defeating the Miami Dolphins to earn their fourth straight win and advance to 6-2 on the season, the Lions have made an effort to bolster their roster ahead of a postseason push.
On Monday, the Lions made a trade to acquire New York Jets safety Andre Cisco. In exchange, the Lions sent the Jets a 2028 sixth-round pick. Cisco has appeared in nine games with four starts for the Jets this season. He has 23 combined tackles, one pass defensed and one sack.
A third-round pick of the Jacksonville Jaguars in 2021, Cisco played four years in Jacksonville before signing with the Jets last year. He is currently on an expiring contract.
The Lions add Cisco to a safety room that features Brian Branch and Chuck Clark. Kerby Joseph, an All-Pro in 2024, is also returning from an injury and could be due to return in the coming two weeks.

Detroit's defense was viewed as a weakness throughout the start of the season, as the unit struggled to keep opposing offenses in check. They were exposed in early season losses to Buffalo and Carolina, and gave up 127 points in that stretch.
However, over the last four games the Lions' defense has improved. By adding another player to the mix, coordinator Kelvin Sheppard's group could have even more success. They're coming off a win over the Dolphins in which they did not allow a touchdown and forced field goals on all three of Miami's trips inside the 20-yard line.
Making this move helps the Lions stay in the mix amidst their NFC counterparts who have also made trades. Two of their divisional rivals have already made trades during the regular season.
The Minnesota Vikings dealt quarterback J.J. McCarthy to the Giants for a draft pick while the Chicago Bears took a big swing by dealing multiple picks for Tennessee Titans defensive lineman Jeffrey Simmons.
The Lions have been active in previous deadlines under Holmes. They did not make a move last year, but the year prior they added veteran defensive end Za'Darius Smith after Aidan Hutchinson suffered a season-ending leg injury.
In 2023, the Lions traded for wide receiver Donovan Peoples-Jones. and the year before that they were sellers as they dealt tight end T.J. Hockenson to the Minnesota Vikings.

title: Winners and Losers as Packers’ Long NFL Trade Deadline Streak Continues
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The streak goes on.
The Green Bay Packers haven’t been buyers at the trade deadline since the Super Bowl season of 2010. While there were reasons to believe it might be different this year, general manager Brian Gutekunst once again saw a good team and believed it was good enough.
Here are the winners and losers from a trade deadline (presumably) filled with talk but, once again, no action.
There was one good reason for general manager Brian Gutekunst to not make a trade. The team is tight against the salary cap, with the outlook not being especially better next season. Good teams are filled with good players; good players make a lot of money (or will make a lot of money).
So, that Gutekunst didn’t try to shoehorn a high-priced veteran onto the roster was probably good news for Russ Ball, who would have had to tie himself into about a dozen pretzels to make it fit for the rest of 2026 and beyond.
Green Bay Packers Salary Cap Update: 11/08/2026 🚨Trade Deadline Edition!!🚨 Salary Cap: 💰Current: $6.03m 💵Effective: $4.31m Roster: 83 🏈Active: 53/53 📋Practice: 16/17 🩹Injured: 12 🩼PUP: 2 Meaningful Restructures Available: 🔄Jordan Love: $3.44m -end of list- pic.twitter.com/jQAsawPqXL
Aaron Rodgers can probably feel Jordan Love’s pain.
For more than a decade after winning the Super Bowl, Rodgers slipped on Superman’s cape and did everything humanly possible to lead the team into a good spot in the playoff race at the trade deadline, only for the general manager – either Ted Thompson or Brian Gutekunst – to not make that one final move to perhaps push the Packers over the top.
The Packers are 6-3 through nine games due in large part to the superhuman play of Love. No Micah Parsons? Too many dropped passes? No running game? A leaky offensive line? Too many penalties?
Now, he’ll have to overcome a general manager who didn’t follow in the footsteps of the men in charge of the Seahawks, Bears, 49ers and Vikings.
Adding a player in a trade would have meant a player losing his spot on the roster.
So, the Packers didn’t trade for a defensive tackle. That’s good news for Anthony Campbell or Jonathan Ford. The Packers didn’t add a running back. That’s good news for Kaleb Johnson or Pierre Strong. The Packers didn’t add a receiver. That’s good news for J. Michael Sturdivant. Even with a wave of injuries, the Packers didn’t add a linebacker. That’s good news for Kristian Welch. Ditto for tight end and the offensive line.
This one has nothing to do with the lack of roster moves made by Brian Gutekunst. Instead, the Vikings traded a third-round pick to the Raiders to acquire Kirk Cousins.
Defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon no doubt would have loved to face Carson Wentz or Max Brosmer, the two quarterbacks who were showered with boos as the Vikings were demolished by the Bills on Monday night. Instead, he’ll almost certainly have to face Cousins, who is on pace to throw for 4,420 yards and 38 touchdowns after a productive half-season with the Raiders.
“You need to have a plan ready to go for anybody that they put out there,” Gannon said before the trade was made public.
Kaleb Johnson had a breakout performance last week against the Patriots. With Josh Jacobs out after suffering a broken finger, Johnson carried the ball 14 times for 68 yards. The Packers were averaging less than 61 rushing yards per game entering the game.
“I was excited about him coming into the game,” offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich said on Tuesday. “He had some really nice practices leading up to the game and he ran hard. That was the good thing about it. That's what we've been challenging him, is he's a big, physical, fast guy. Just run hard. Run angry. And I thought he did a nice job with that, for sure.”
The Colts did not trade Jonathan Taylor and the Titans did not trade Tony Pollard. Had the Packers acquired either, Johnson almost certainly would have been one of the odd men out in the backfield. Instead, with Jacobs out for at least a couple games, Johnson will have a chance to be the top back for the short term and perhaps earn a key role for the stretch run.
The Seahawks traded for receiver/returner Rashid Shaheen at the trade deadline last year, and he became a key player in their run to a Super Bowl championship.
Before this year’s trade deadline, the Seahawks traded for All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson. The 49ers traded for veteran defensive tackle DeForest Buckner. The Bears traded for All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons. The 49ers doubled down with aging receiver Keenan Allen. The Vikings made their big move at quarterback with Kirk Cousins.
Well, they did nothing. No starters were added. No depth pieces were acquired. Nothing. Now as always, help is not on the way.
The Packers don’t have a first-round pick due to the Micah Parsons trade. Because they didn’t make a trade, they’ll at least have their second- and third-round picks, plus their projected four compensatory picks as well as the fourth-round pick from the Rashan Gary trade.
(As an aside, OverTheCap.com is projecting the Packers will go from a third-round pick for quarterback Malik Willis and a fourth-round pick for receiver Romeo Doubs to a fourth-round pick for Willis and a fifth-round pick for Doubs because they are on injured reserve. Compensatory picks are awarded based mostly on salary but also on playing time.)
The 2027 draft class is supposed to be loaded. Gutekunst will have his full arsenal of picks (other than the first round) to add some young, cheap talent to a top-heavy roster.
There’s no word to describe what last year’s trade for Micah Parsons meant to the locker room. Excited, fired up – none of that fits the jolt that trade provided to the rest of the players on the roster.
No trade made on Tuesday would have had that visceral impact. And it’s not as if the players are pouting that no trades were made at the deadline.
Still, Green Bay’s players – especially the veteran players – understand what happened over the last week. The Seahawks added a Hall of Fame lineman. The Bears added a potential Hall of Fame defensive lineman. The 49ers made two trades. The Vikings did what they had to at quarterback.
And their boss did nothing. Getting to and winning the Super Bowl is incredibly hard. Seahawks general manager John Schneider was aggressive, as always, in his quest to go back-to-back. Bears general manager Ryan Poles had built the best roster in the NFC North, then added a true game-wrecker. 49ers general manager John Lynch’s team had the best record in the NFC, then added two useful veterans.
If you’re a member of the Packers, it would be hard not to reflect on what happened this week and not think the Lombardi Trophy got just a bit further out of reach.

title: Packers Sign Defensive Tackle-Turned-Tight End to Practice Squad
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers filled an opening on their practice squad on Tuesday by signing rookie tight end Kenny Fletcher Jr.
Fletcher was part of a Tuesday workout that included four tight ends and two quarterbacks. One of the tight ends was Zack Kuntz, who was drafted by the Jets in 2023. One of the quarterbacks was rifle-armed Jalen Morton.
The Packers opted to go with Fletcher, who went undrafted this year out of Rutgers. He spent the offseason and training camp with the Buccaneers but didn’t catch any passes in the preseason and failed to make their 53-man roster. He spent the start of the season on the Colts’ practice squad.
Fletcher caught 46 passes for 373 yards and two touchdowns in 2024, a season cut short by an injured wrist, and 2025. He spent the 2022 and 2023 seasons at defensive end, where he had 2.5 sacks among 10 tackles.
“Believe it or not, Kenny came in, he was frustrated, he wasn't getting enough playing time at defensive end,” then-coach Greg Schiano said . “We were discussing maybe a transfer and I said, ‘Kenny, I don't want you to transfer. You belong here.’
“I said, ‘Look, you played wideout in high school. Why don't you give tight end a try? I got a funny feeling you're going to be pretty good at this.’ And in whatever it was, 15 practices, he got himself ready. I think literally we've just scratched the surface with Kenny as a tight end. And he's another guy that I expect to see in that league and he's talented enough to do it for a while.”
Fletcher embraced Schiano’s idea.
“As soon as he told me that [moving to tight end was in the best interests of he and the team], I was ready for the change. I played wide receiver in high school, so that was cool. As soon as he brought up tight end, I knew I could do the job. It really wasn’t hard for me after he told me that was our best chance of winning. After he told me that, it was great.”
Fletcher made an instant impact. He caught four passes in his first game at the position and touchdowns in each of his first two games. He added seven catches against Virginia Tech. He had 19 catches in the first six games before the injury against Wisconsin.
The ability to catch the ball was easy because he played receiver in high school. How about as a blocker?
“I love blocking because of the violence in it,” Fletcher said in 2024 . “You can use some of your defensive violence and techniques and transfer it to tight end.”
“Blocking, I feel like I’m a violent football player,” Fletcher added . “So blocking, the violence in me helps me block. It’s second nature, again.”
Fletcher measured 6-foot-2 7/8 and 250 pounds at this year’s pro day. He ran a 4.71 in the 40 but put up some strong numbers in other tests for a Relative Athletic Score of 8.26 .
The Packers have four tight ends on their 53-man roster with Tucker Kraft, Jonnu Smith, Mark Redman and Josh Whyle. With Whyle out with a concussion, they promoted their practice squad tight end, Drake Dabney, to the gameday roster for the win at New England.
Luke Musgrave remains on the physically unable to perform list with a neck injury.
Fletcher will embrace the opportunity.
“It means the world,” Fletcher said while at Rutgers. “It’s my dream playing football. Whatever comes with it, I’m going to take it and roll with it.”
The Packers have a full practice squad.
Offense: CB Cam Miller, G Dillon Wade, T Dalton Cooper, TE Drake Dabney, TE Kenny Fletcher, WR Isaiah Neyor and WR Quincy Skinner.
Defense: DT Mazi Smith, DT David Blay Jr., edge Nyjalik Kelly, edge Arron Mosby, edge D.J. Johnson, LB Jack Dingle, CB Domani Jackson, CB Elijah Culp, S John Saunders Jr.
International: K Lenny Krieg.
Wade, Cooper, Dabney, Neyor, Kelly, Mosby and Jackson spent training camp with the Packers.
“You’ve got to try to get this guy up to speed in regards to our offense and all that as soon as possible, which is always a little bit more of a challenge in-season,” coach Matt LaFleur said of Miller last week. “So, he’s going to have to learn a lot on his own and pay attention and we’re going to have to find time to devote to him, as well.”

title: Packers-Vikings Matchups: Who Has Advantage in Love-Flores Showdown?
full_text:
It’s redemption weekend in Green Bay, Wisconsin.
The Green Bay Packers are about to play what is, to date, their biggest game of the season. Kick-started by their Week 1 win over the Packers, the Minnesota Vikings started the season 6-0. They looked poised to run and hide from the Packers, who lost two of their first three games.
On Sunday at Lambeau Field, the Packers have a chance to avenge their season-opening loss while tying the Vikings in the standings.
Can they? Here are our weekly matchups.
Justin Jefferson is awesome. The analysis on him as a player can start and stop there.
But who is going to be throwing him the ball?
Minnesota opened training camp with four quarterbacks. Kyler Murray was signed to be the starter but is on the sideline with a strained hamstring. With the addition of Murray, former first-round pick J.J. McCarthy was traded to the Giants in late September. The backup, Carson Wentz, started in place of Murray on Monday night but looked lifeless in the process of losing to the Bills. Max Brosmer got some time last year when injuries struck the position, but he’s not a sound solution.
So, the Vikings were forced to make a move at quarterback. At Tuesday’s trade deadline, they sent a third-round pick to the Raiders to reacquire Kirk Cousins. Cousins is a four-time Pro Bowler, including three selections during his time in Minnesota. He starred under Kevin O’Connell from 2022 until he suffered a torn Achilles at Lambeau Field in 2023.
With experience in the offense, Cousins is the odds-on favorite to start against Green Bay.
Meanwhile, the Packers’ defense is coming off one of its best games of the season. It picked off Drake Maye three times, sacked him four times and pressured him on 18 of his 38 dropbacks.
Outside of a game at Ford Field in Detroit, the Packers’ defense has mostly been excellent since the calendar turned to October.
The Packers’ defense, until further notice, is good. Minnesota’s offense is a mess.
Bijan Robinson ran wild on the Packers in Week 3. Outside of that, the Packers have done a good job of keeping opposing ground games under control. Jahmyr Gibbs ran for more than 100 yards against them, but it took him 29 carries to get to his 116 yards.
The Packers are familiar with the backfield that the Vikings will bring with them this weekend. Aaron Jones and Jordan Mason spearhead this attack. Jones leads the Vikings with 474 rushing yards and is averaging 4.1 yards per carry. He’s not the same player he was during his prime seasons with the Packers, but he is still good.
The Packers’ defense, however, is rolling.
Here’s the matchup of the game. The last time these teams played, Jordan Love threw for 387 yards on 21 completions. He was sacked four times and threw one interception and lost two fumbles.
He was under siege essentially from the beginning of the game to the end, when the game got out of hand. The Packers’ offensive line that day was Jordan Morgan at left tackle, Donovan Jennings at left guard, Sean Rhyan at center, Jacob Monk at right guard and Zach Bako-Bewele at right tackle.
This week, the Packers will have a new starting five with the interior certain to be three new players and Anthony Belton playing at right tackle. The offensive line has gotten better from the first game of the season but is still prone to blown blocks and missed assignments.
Minnesota’s blitz-happy defense sacked Buffalo’s Josh Allen four times on Monday and has brought pressure all season.
The difference this time around is that Love is playing as well as he ever has in his career.
Is he ready for the No. 1 defense in the NFL? Minnesota is allowing just 14.5 points and 161 passing yards per game. It’s suffocated everyone all season.
So, why does the edge go to Green Bay?
Jordan Love is on a heater. His performance against New England may have been the best of his career. He was excellent for three quarters against Carolina before one bad interception started to turn the tide.
He has been very good against almost any defense he has faced this season. That includes Flores’ group in Week 1 before he got snowed under by a defense that smelled blood.
The Packers’ defense should be better prepared for Minnesota’s quarterback situation this week. They’re also at home, which means their offensive line won’t be behind the gun of having to deal with Minnesota’s crowd noise.
Great quarterbacks can overcome almost anything. Love has been great the last few weeks, and that gives him the nod against a great defense.
Does Green Bay have a run game now? OK, that’s probably a step too far. However, the ground attack had by far its best performance on Sunday against the Patriots.
Josh Jacobs dropped out of the game with a fractured finger that will require surgery and won’t play on Sunday, but perhaps they found something with Kaleb Johnson. Johnson ran for a season-high 68 yards. That’s a season high for the Packers, not just Johnson.
Will Johnson get more run this week with the team they are playing? That remains to be seen. Chris Brooks and Pierre Strong are better in pass protection and that could play a big role against Brian Flores’ nasty defense.
Despite the improvement last week, the Packers are a bad run offense until further notice.
One thing to keep an eye on as the game gets into the fourth quarter: The Vikings’ defense was on the field for more than 40 minutes against Buffalo and will be playing on a short week. Will they wear down late?
Green Bay’s special teams is coming off what was perhaps its best game of the season.
Trey Smack, the embattled kicker, was asked to put the ball through the uprights seven times on Sunday. He booted all seven right down the middle, looking as confident as he has all season. Bo Melton returned a kickoff to the midfield, and the kick coverage was solid.
Can the Packers repeat that performance this week in a bigger game?
On Minnesota’s side, kicker Will Reichard is a legitimate weapon. He made 11 kicks of more than 50 yards a season ago, including a 62-yard bomb. He has missed just two field goal attempts this season, and both came from more than 50 yards.
Myles Price will handle return duties. He is averaging 29.9 yards per kickoff return. He almost took two kickoffs back for touchdowns against Green Bay, including a 68-yarder. He is averaging 17.5 yards per punt return, as well, with an 86-yard touchdown against Tampa Bay.
The Packers’ special teams has had its moments but is too up-and-down to be trusted in this spot.

title: Week 10 Consensus NFL Power Rankings: How Far Did Packers Move Up After Blowout?
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The dominance of the Green Bay Packers in their victory over the Patriots is evident in our new Packers On SI Consensus NFL Power Rankings.
So is the overall dominance of the NFC North.
Our Consensus Power Rankings take eight sets of national power rankings to build one elite power ranking, with one point for first place, two for second place and so on. The Packers moved up from 13th last week to ninth this week.
How loaded is the NFC North? The Bears are fourth, the Lions are eighth and the Vikings – the Packers’ opponent on Sunday – are 10th.
Here is where you’ll find the Packers in each of the individual rankings, with more information available at the links.
The Packers move up three spots in Conor Orr’s rankings.
“Here’s why I love what I do (honestly): I spent all offseason studying the run game, heavier personnel packages and the increased usage of 21 personnel. Jordan Love is going to come out and throw for 5,000 yards (seriously) with no running game to speak of whatsoever and the Packers are one of the best teams in the NFL.”
The Packers zoomed up six spots from 14th in Frank Schwab’s rankings. Why?
“The offense looked great again against the Patriots on Sunday, and Micah Parsons' return is looming for the defense. It is very easy to forget that when Parsons tore his ACL last season the Packers were 9-3-1 and leading in the second half at Denver. And Green Bay has been playing much better on defense the past six games.”
Josh Jacobs’ broken finger is a setback, though.
The Packers shot up five spots from 13th in Nick Shook’s rankings.
Looking beyond Jordan Love’s “hot streak,” Shook zeroed in on the “secret sauce” that is their defense.
“Jonathan Gannon has evolved this group into an aggressive, opportunistic bunch that relies on its safeties, forces turnovers and hands Love additional possessions. It’s a unit that caused major issues for Drake Maye and will only get better with Micah Parsons’ impending return, making for a largely complete team (save for the general absence of a rushing attack) that is looking stronger with each week.”
The Packers moved up from No. 14 in the rankings selected by Chad Graff and Josh Kendall.
This week’s theme is midseason grade, and they gave the Packers an A-minus.
“The Packers’ pass defense has quietly been among the best in the league, and they soon get to welcome back arguably the sport’s best pass rusher in Micah Parsons. It’s still fair to wonder if their lack of a running game will haunt them, but Jordan Love is playing like an MVP, and Matthew Golden and Christian Watson are a heck of a receiving duo.”
The Packers shot up six spots from No. 15 in Ralph Vacchiano’s rankings. It’s a “big jump,” he said, but warranted after blowing out the Patriots.
“More than that, they are playing outstanding on defense, and they are showing off a passing game that might just be the best in the league (or at least outside of Cincinnati). It’s hard to find a quarterback playing better than Jordan Love, and it’s impossible to find a receiving tandem better than Christian Watson and Matthew Golden at the moment.”
Pete Prisco inched the Packers up two spots in his rankings.
“Jordan Love and the passing game get a lot of the attention, but that defense has really impressed. When they get Micah Parsons back, look out.”
The Packers gained three spots in the rankings put together by ESPN’s team of beat writers.
This week’s theme is the most important game during the second half of the season. Rob Demovsky picked the Week 12 game at the Rams, which might mark the debut of Micah Parsons.
“How can it not be one of the remaining NFC North games, you ask? Yes, next Sunday against the Vikings is huge. So is Week 16 at the Bears. So is Week 18 against the Lions. But given the likelihood that one of those other teams will win the NFC North, the Packers might need to make sure the Rams don't catch them for an NFC wild-card spot. As damaging as a loss to a division team would be, so would a loss to another NFC team they might need the head-to-head tiebreaker against.”
The Packers moved up three spots in Mike Florio’s rankings. “When Micah Parsons returns, they could make a major move.”
The Vikings will play at the Packers at noon Sunday at Lambeau Field. They are 10th in the Consensus Rankings, ranging from seventh to 13th. The Vikings are 11th at Yahoo. As Schwab explained as part of a longer note:
“It's hard to remember the last time a team that was 6-2 with one of the top two defenses in the NFL felt this hopeless. Monday night's performance was absolutely deflating for the Vikings. Carson Wentz took over for an injured Kyler Murray, who had been struggling so much that everyone wondered if him sitting out Monday was a ‘soft benching.’ Then Wentz went 8 of 25 for 81 yards, two interceptions and an 8.9 passer rating. It was one of the worst quarterback performances in recent memory.
“For the second straight season, the Vikings cannot find one quarterback to get Justin Jefferson the ball.”
We don’t use sportsbook odds in our rankings, but they do provide an additional perspective. In Packers-related odds at FanDuel Sportsbook :
The Packers, who were +2000 to win the Super Bowl before Week 1, plunged to as low as +6000 following their slow start to the season but finally are back to where they started. That is tied for 11th on the board.
Among NFC North teams, the Bears have separated themselves at +850. The Lions are +1600 and the Vikings crashed all the way to +3000 following their punchless loss to the Bills.
Green Bay opened the season ranked seventh in the NFC playoff odds at FanDuel at -112 but fell to as low as 12th at +250 after the win at Tampa Bay. Now, even though they are in seventh place in the NFC standings, they are fourth in the odds. The 49ers are -4500, and the four NFC North teams are next – the Bears at -1000, the Lions at -400, the Packers at -230 and the Vikings at -184.
Quarterback Jordan Love’s huge game at New England gave him a huge surge in the MVP race. Love, who opened at +2200 and fell to as far as +10000, went from +4000 last week to +700 now. That trails Joe Burrow (+200), Josh Allen (+300), Brock Purdy (+400) and Trevor Lawrence (+600) in what is a five-man race .
The Packers remain last in the NFC North standings and remain well off the pace in the division odds at DraftKings. Chicago is first at +144, followed by Detroit at +245, Minnesota at +330 and Green Bay at +510. The Bears and Vikings flip-flopped positions this week. The Packers were as low as +1125 after losing to the Lions.
Here are our top 15 teams this week. Every team can be found in the top 17 in all eight of the individual rankings, signifying a real divide between the great teams, the good teams and everyone else.
1, Buffalo Bills (13 points; five first place); 2, San Francisco 49ers (19 points; one first place); 3, Jacksonville Jaguars (24 points; two first place); 4, Chicago Bears (34); 5, Denver Broncos (40); 6, Kansas City Chiefs (51) 7, Cincinnati Bengals (54); 8, Detroit Lions (69); 9, Green Bay Packers (71); 10, Minnesota Vikings (83); 11, Seattle Seahawks (85); 12, Pittsburgh Steelers (93); 13, Los Angeles Rams (104); T-14, New England Patriots (112); T-14, New York Giants (112).

title: Pros, Cons of Six Trade Deadline Options Who Would Fit Packers’ Limited Budget
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The clock is ticking. The NFL trade deadline is approaching, and there are opportunities for the Green Bay Packers to add to a roster that was good enough to crush the Patriots but also has some notable holes.
Here are six possibilities worth considering.
If Jonathan Taylor is too rich in terms of the finances and the trade capital to acquire him, Tony Pollard would be an excellent Plan B.
The reason to do it: Pollard is a legit starter and would give the Packers quite the one-two punch in the backfield. He is coming off four consecutive seasons of 1,000 rushing yards and is on track to do it again. He’s also on a streak of five consecutive seasons with 33-plus receptions. The Titans are a bad team but he’s still averaging 4.5 yards per carry.
Pollard, 29, would add $3.61 million to the cap. He’s not under contract for 2027, so he could be a half-year rental with the cost of a trade at least partially offset by a future compensatory pick.
The problem: It’s not really a problem, per se, but the Packers have a full-house backfield. If all goes well with Josh Jacobs’ surgery, he might only miss a couple games, which means he wouldn’t have to go on injured reserve.
Chris Brooks should be back from injured reserve this week. Kaleb Johnson showed his talent with a strong performance against the Patriots. MarShawn Lloyd’s knee injury held him out of Sunday’s game but isn’t serious enough for injured reserve.
Pierre Strong could be released and re-signed to the practice squad, but a backfield of Jacobs, Pollard, Brooks, Johnson and Lloyd would be bursting at the seams.
The reason to do it: A first-round pick in 2024, Brian Thomas had a blockbuster rookie season with 87 catches for 1,282 yards and 10 touchdowns. He’s big and fast, so would be a great fit for Green Bay’s offense.
With one more year on his rookie contract, Thomas could be a low-cost, high-reward addition for an offense that might be up Bleep Creek if Christian Watson or Matthew Golden were to miss significant time.
The problem: Thomas is big and fast and talented but has only 10 catches for 117 yards in eight games this season.
The reason to do it: Jayden Reed’s season-ending injury was a significant blow to the offense. Reed was a dynamic threat in the slot and irreplaceable from that perspective. A third-round pick in 2023, Tre Tucker caught 57 passes for 696 yards and five touchdowns last season and is on pace to crush those numbers with 33 catches for 529 yards and four touchdowns this season.
He’d add only $1.84 million to Green Bay’s cap. He’ll be a free agent at the end of the season, so the Packers could recoup some of the cost with a future compensatory pick.
The problem: The Raiders need to figure out Tucker’s future, first . He’s also short – the Packers don’t like short receivers but maybe they could overlook it for what he could bring in the slot for a half-season.
Tre Tucker is a WR prospect in the 2023 draft class. He scored a 7.07 RAS out of a possible 10.00. This ranked 848 out of 2895 WR from 1987 to 2023. https://t.co/Hbu81k8xFH #RAS pic.twitter.com/K6RyyBBn61
The reason to do it: This would be a forward-thinking trade. A second-round pick by the Raiders in 2024, Jackson Powers-Johnson started 14 games as a rookie but only four games this season. He’d count $796,000 against this year’s cap and $1.99 million in 2027, so would be worth a flier.
The problem: Powers-Johnson probably wouldn’t do anything to help the offensive line this year.
The Packers are in an odd position of having a bad offensive line but a glut of decent linemen. They have Aaron Banks, Laken Tomlinson and Kevin Zeitler to play the guard positions, and Sean Rhyan should be back soon at center. Banks and Rhyan are among the highest-paid players at their positions.
At tackle, they used their first-round pick on left tackle Jordan Morgan and a second-round pick on Anthony Belton, who replaced high-paid standout Zach Bako-Bewele following his season-ending injury.
What about offensive tackle? The Packers could use depth, obviously, given the lack of it behind Morgan and Belton, but so could every team and there might not be a good one available.
Overall, the Packers have made a lot of investment on the offensive line. The Packers don’t need to add another decent lineman. They need their linemen to play better.
The reason to do it: A passing-game threat is a passing-game threat, no matter the position.
Ja’Tavion Sanders was a fourth-round pick in 2024. He caught 62-of-77 targets for 532 yards and two touchdowns during his first two seasons but has played in only one game this year. He’s played a lot as a big slot, so would be a different way to replace Jayden Reed. Jonnu Smith hasn’t done much to help the offense, so maybe it would be worth taking a shot on a younger player.
The problem: Sanders can’t get on the field for the below-average Saints and he averaged only 6.6 yards per catch last year.
The reason to do it: Dalvin Tomlinson is 32 and in his 10th season. He has started 148 games in his career. He’s been a durable, run-stopping defensive tackle throughout his career, including this year with the Chargers, for whom he’s started all six appearances.
The Packers have been plagued by injuries at defensive tackle, though Jonathan Ford should be back from injured reserve soon. Tomlinson would provide solid depth at a reasonable price, with just $1.89 million added to the cap.
The problem: Tomlinson wouldn’t help the pass rush in the same way that the Patriots’ Christian Barmore is capable of doing. He’s up to 4.5 sacks after getting one against the Packers on Sunday.
Barmore, however, would add $6.6 million to the Packers’ tight salary cap. He’s got cap charges of $20 million in 2027 and $21 million in 2028, though those could be handled via kicking-the-can-down-the-road restructures.
The Packers just don’t have the financial wherewithal to get much done at the trade deadline. Here’s the salary-cap outlook from Ken Ingalls.
Green Bay Packers Salary Cap Update: 11/08/2026 🚨Trade Deadline Edition!!🚨 Salary Cap: 💰Current: $6.03m 💵Effective: $4.31m Roster: 83 🏈Active: 53/53 📋Practice: 16/17 🩹Injured: 12 🩼PUP: 2 Meaningful Restructures Available: 🔄Jordan Love: $3.44m -end of list- pic.twitter.com/jQAsawPqXL
Ingalls went into greater depth:
The Packers have more than enough current salary cap reserves to navigate the rest of the 2026 season to cover small maintenance signings and practice squad elevations covering for injuries.
On paper, the Packers have $6.03 million in cap space. This figure is important as it represents how much space they have right now in order for the league to allow a trade or signing to go through. For example, if the Packers were to attempt to trade for a player with $10 million remaining in base salary, the trade would be denied since they don’t have that much cap space.
In order to trade for running back Jonathan Taylor, for instance, the acquiring team would need about $4.6 million in cap space, according to Spotrac. The Packers have this covered.
While the Packers do have $6.03 million of cap space, I estimate they have closer to $4.31 million in “effective cap space” considering their likely future costs, such as filling out the practice squad, practice-squad elevations and per-game roster bonuses.
There are still levers the Packers can pull to free up more cap space for this season.
While the Packers would likely try to avoid backloading Jordan Love’s contract even more than it already has, they could convert his remaining base salary into a signing bonus to free up $3.44 million this season, adding cost to future years instead.

title: The Trade Deadline Is Here, And Packers’ Mission Is Clear After Statement Win
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers entered Sunday’s game at the New England Patriots at a bit of a crossroads in terms of their season and the direction they should take at the NFL trade deadline.
They were 5-3 but hadn’t really beaten anyone. During their early-season struggles, the wins came against the Jets, who are among the worst teams in the league, and the Buccaneers, who had an undrafted rookie quarterback making his first start.
They followed the win at Tampa Bay with a blowout victory over the rival Bears, who were without star quarterback Caleb Williams, and a win over the Cowboys, the chronic underachievers who haven’t beaten anyone of note this season.
Their three-game winning streak died at Detroit, where they were guilty of too many self-inflicted mistakes, but they rebounded to beat the Panthers, the worst first-place team in the history of mankind.
That set the stage for the game against the Patriots. The defending AFC champions had won four of their last five games and were undefeated at home. They are a very good team with a very good quarterback and a very good coach.
Because of the overwhelming power of the NFC North, the Packers’ season could have tipped in either direction. Nevermind the standings, though. They needed to beat a good team to prove that they are a good team and not just one of the mediocre teams lingering on the fringe of the playoff race.
Mission accomplished. The Packers destroyed the Patriots 45-27. It really wasn’t even that close. Jordan Love played like an MVP-level quarterback. The defense dominated. The special teams held their own.
So, the Packers left Foxborough with more than their sixth win of the season. They left having proven they are legitimate Super Bowl contenders.
Now, it’s general manager Brian Gutekunst’s turn.
The team he built has some obvious flaws. It also had just pummeled one of the top teams in the NFL. A year after going 0-5 down the stretch without Micah Parsons, they improved to 6-3 with Parsons only having just returned to practice.
When Gutekunst takes the 10,000-foot view of everything, he’ll see that his team has some warts. But then he’ll look at the other teams and also see warts. Here’s the lay of the land in the NFC.
1. San Francisco 49ers, 7-1. The 49ers are relying on the oldest roster in the league. Brock Purdy is playing at an MVP level and the defense is really good, but they’ve also fattened up on one of the softest schedules in the league.
2. Chicago Bears, 7-2. The Bears are really good, with back-to-back wins over last year’s Super Bowl teams before surviving a mistake-plagued game against the Buccaneers on Sunday.
3. New York Giants, 5-2-1. It’s hard to take any team led by quarterback J.J. McCarthy seriously. They’ve played by far the easiest of any team in the league.
4. Carolina Panthers, 3-5. It’s impossible to take the Panthers seriously. They’ve lost three consecutive games but are still in first place in the NFC South.
5. Detroit Lions, 6-2. The Lions have won four in a row, with narrow wins over the Packers and Vikings at home and an ugly win at Miami on Sunday. Their high-powered offense isn’t nearly as good away from Ford Field.
6. Minnesota Vikings, 6-2. The Vikings might have the best defense in the NFL; they also might have the worst offense. It will be interesting to see if they can find a season-saving quarterback at the trade deadline.
7. Green Bay Packers, 6-3. The Packers had to tread water until the return of Micah Parsons. With six wins, they’ve done much more than that. Whatever happens at the trade deadline, no team will acquire a player with as much game-wrecking potential as Parsons.
8. Seattle Seahawks, 5-4. The Seahawks aren’t quite in the same boat as the Vikings, but the defending Super Bowl champions’ one-man offense is on a four-game streak of scoring 20 or fewer points.
9. Los Angeles Rams, 5-4. The Rams were the obvious pick to win the Super Bowl after a huge offseason. After a slow start, they’ve won three in a row, but Matthew Stafford is 18th in passer rating.
So, why not Green Bay? The Packers are good enough to beat all of those teams. They’re also capable of losing to all those teams. That’s the way it is in the wide-open NFC, where every team should see an opportunity to do something big.
Making a move at the trade deadline isn’t the Green Bay way. The Packers haven’t acquired a player at the deadline since 2010, an irrelevant trade for safety Anthony Smith.
There’s reason to believe this year could be different. General manager Brian Gutekunst pulled off the blockbuster trade for Micah Parsons, so he’s shown a willingness to do the big, bold moves needed to accomplish big things. The Packers, usually the youngest team in the NFL, have quickly advanced to middle age. With a five-alarm fire on the offensive line, he did the unthinkable by acquiring not one, not two but three veterans. Sure, the line is still a weakness, but signing 36- and 34-year-old guards is out of character for a draft-and-develop team.
Gutekunst has the draft capital to get something done. While they don’t have a first-round pick, there is the potential of having two third-round picks and three fourth-round picks.
The finances might be the biggest challenge. The Packers don’t have the salary-cap space to acquire a star player with a big salary.
Green Bay Packers Salary Cap Update: 11/08/2026 🚨Trade Deadline Edition!!🚨 Salary Cap: 💰Current: $6.03m 💵Effective: $4.31m Roster: 83 🏈Active: 53/53 📋Practice: 16/17 🩹Injured: 12 🩼PUP: 2 Meaningful Restructures Available: 🔄Jordan Love: $3.44m -end of list- pic.twitter.com/jQAsawPqXL
That doesn’t mean a trade can’t be made. Or shouldn’t be made.
For years, Aaron Rodgers dragged the team into championship contention, only for the general manager – Ted Thompson or Gutekunst – to basically say, “You’re on your own, buddy.” This year, Love is playing at an elite level. What’s got to be encouraging for Gutekunst is how the team’s young veterans have taken the next step.
Christian Watson, Matthew Golden and Evan Williams are young stars. The draft class, led by cornerback Brandon Cisse, has provided sudden impact and is getting better every week.
After the blowout win at New England, SI.com’s Albert Breer said the Packers are “ starting to have the look the Seahawks did a year ago.” That team’s young players became “among the very best at their positions.” The same thing is happening for the Packers.
The Seahawks have been active at past trade deadlines with defensive tackle Leonard Williams in 2023 and receiver/returner Rashid Shaheen in 2025. They were key players in their run to the Super Bowl championship last year.
The Seahawks struck again this year with guard Quenton Nelson. The 49ers responded with defensive tackle DeForest Buckner and the Bears made a blockbuster trade for defensive tackle Jeffrey Simmons. The NFC arms race started early.
The Packers can’t be left in the dust.
The Packers proved they are a good team by routing the Patriots, but they’re probably not good enough to make a Super Bowl run without adding a difference-making player at the deadline.
The Packers haven’t gotten to the Super Bowl since 2010. They’ve been routinely good but never good enough due in part to their do-nothing approaches at the trade deadline.
It’s time for a new approach. This year’s team has an opportunity to do something big. Now, whether it’s addressing the trenches or giving the offense one more playmaker, it’s time for Gutekunst to give his team one final push to greatness.

title: How Long Will Josh Jacobs Be Out After Surgery And How Will Packers Pivot?
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs’ broken finger will require surgery that will keep him out of the lineup for the next couple games, a source told Packers On SI.
Jacobs was injured while stiff-arming Patriots safety Craig Woodson on his fourth carry of the game. His right ring finger got caught in the defender’s facemask.
Josh Jacobs got his right hand caught in the defenders face mask. I’m curious if it’s his hand or his fingers. It almost looks like one of his fingers snaps. pic.twitter.com/hngCa0PdG6
“It looked nasty,” Jacobs told reporters after Green Bay’s 45-27 victory. “It look a lot better now than what it did, but we’ll see. We’ll see how it goes.”
Jacobs and the team opted for surgery rather than trying to have him play with a splint or some other protective appliance, which would hinder him in warding off defenders and for ball security.
Jacobs tried to play through the injury.
“That’s what we was trying to do during the game,” he said. “We was just trying to figure out a way if I can still go, and the biggest thing is just being able to grip the ball. Catching is obviously going to be tough, but just being able to grip the ball, but we’re going to see. I know it’s broke, but I don’t know the extent.”
The Packers will host the Vikings in a big rivalry rematch on Sunday. Then comes an unusual schedule, with what’s essentially back-to-back mini-byes rather than a traditional bye week. There will be an extended break before the Thanksgiving Eve game at the Rams and then another extended break before the Dec. 6 game at the Saints.
It’s possible Jacobs could be back for the game against New Orleans, according to a source. If not, the Packers will host the Bills on Dec. 13.
The Packers’ running game sputtered during Jacobs’ six games on the exempt list, and it wasn’t much better during his two games back in the lineup. He carried four times for 5 yards before the injury.
Against New England, Jacobs, Kaleb Johnson and Pierre Strong were the running backs with MarShawn Lloyd (knee) inactive and Chris Brooks (ankle) not activated from injured reserve.
With Jacobs set to miss at least the next couple games, the Packers will have to shuffle the deck at running back.
After spending four games in the doghouse due to a fumble at Tampa Bay in Week 4, Johnson had a big-time game against the Patriots. His 68 rushing yards eclipsed the team’s meager season average of about 61 yards entering the game. He presumably will have a key role the next couple weeks.
“He played really good. He played really good,” Jacobs said. “I was trying to tell him just on the sideline, just keep doing what he’s always done his whole life. Trust his eyes, trust his reads and just keep making plays and don’t try to overpress, and just get it when it’s there and he did a really good job at that today. So, I’m happy for him because I know that was big for him.”
Brooks returned to practice last week but was not activated from injured reserve. That presumably will happen this week. He figures to immediately reclaim the third-down role.
Lloyd was added to the injury report on Thursday, and while he practiced on Friday, he was inactive for the game. He’s averaging only 2.6 yards per carry.
Strong was promoted from the practice squad for the Week 5 game against Chicago. In his five games on the roster, he played 25 snaps vs. the Bears, 41 vs. the Cowboys, a combined 17 vs. the Lions and Panthers, and 30 vs. the Patriots. He’s averaging only 2.4 yards per carry.
There will be a logjam at running back from a roster perspective with Jacobs, Brooks, Lloyd, Johnson and Strong. If Jacobs is only going to be out a few games, injured reserve will not be an option to create a spot on the roster.
Johnson was a third-round pick by the Steelers last year but quickly fell out of favor. The Packers acquired him at the end of training camp for a 2028 sixth-round pick.
After the fumble at Tampa Bay, Johnson played a combined 13 snaps against Chicago and Dallas and was inactive against Detroit and Carolina. Now, just in the nick of time, he should be back in the coaches’ good graces. He had a 2-yard touchdown in the first half and runs of 34 and 10 yards in the second half.
“It felt great. I feel like I’m getting back to me, getting back comfortable with the system and running the ball,” Johnson said.
The Packers hadn’t rushed for more than 86 yards in a game this season. Over the previous four games, which included two games with Jacobs, they averaged 2.6 yards per carry. Against the Patriots, they rushed for 129 yards and averaged 4.0 yards per carry.
“I just think that everybody coming together as a team and knowing what we’ve got to do each and every day on and off the field – especially in practice – and everybody just coming together and just executing and all being one unit,” he said. “When everyone does that, it’s unstoppable.”
We’ll see about unstoppable, but at least the Packers had an effective run game against the Patriots.
“I thought it was big time,” coach Matt LaFleur said after the game. “I thought all those guys going in … especially losing Josh, I mean, that’s a tough loss right there. For Pierre and Kaleb to step up and go in there, and Kaleb ripped off a couple explosive plays, he scored his first touchdown. That was huge.”

title: Three Words Perfectly Summarize Packers’ WRs Christian Watson, Matthew Golden
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Josh Jacobs said it perfectly when asked about Green Bay Packers receivers Christian Watson and Matthew Golden after Sunday’s blowout win over the Patriots.
During the Packers’ destruction of the Patriots on Sunday:
Watson caught 7-of-8 targets for 171 yards and one touchdown. It was the seventh-most receiving yards by a player this season.
Entering Monday’s game, there have been 197 instances of a receiver being targeted at least eight times in a game this season. Watson’s 21.4 yards per target against New England was the highest figure of the year. Watson now holds four of the top five spots this season.
Golden caught all 10 targets for 164 yards and one touchdown. It was the ninth-most receiving yards by a player this season.
Among receivers who have been targeted at least 10 times in a game this season, Golden is the only player with a 100 percent catch rate. He finished with the most receiving yards by a player who caught all 10-plus targets in a game since the Steelers’ Antonio Brown in 2017. Over the past 40 years, Golden is just the third receiver with a 100 percent catch rate, 10-plus targets and 16 yards per target.
Combined, they caught 17-of-18 targets for 335 yards and two touchdowns.
“It’s crazy. The plays, I mean, it’s elite. That’s the only way you can really describe it,” Jacobs said.
According to the league, they became the fifth pair of teammates in NFL history with at least seven receptions for 160 yards and a touchdown apiece in the same game. The last were the Dolphins’ Tyreek Hill and Jaylen Waddle in 2022.
It was one of the most dominant dynamic-duo performances in Packers history.
Christian Watson and Matthew Golden are the first Packers teammates with 150+ receiving yards and 1+ receiving TD since Don Hutson and Andy Uram in 1942. #GoPackGo | @packers
And they did it with coach Matt LaFleur not calling a passing play during the fourth quarter.
The 335 combined receiving yards between Christian Watson and Matthew Golden are the most by a Packer duo since Nov. 1, 1942, when Don Hutson (207 yds) and Andy Uram (174 yds) totaled 381 yards in a 55-24 rout of the Chicago Cardinals.
“We talk about it all the time. We feed off each other,” Golden said. “Whenever he gets going, I get going. It goes back and forth. I think when we’re on the same side of the ball, it makes it even better. You got to pick one. I know me and him, we talked about it all offseason – we were going to come in, do this thing and take off with it. It’s just about continuing to keep going and keep winning games.”
Watson and Golden are the only duo to have a combined 300 receiving yards in a game this season. Moreover, there have been only 19 games this season in which a quarterback threw for at least 335 yards in a game, let alone all those yards going to two players.
“Not to sound cocky or anything, but I think we did what we expected us to do,” Watson said. “And I say it every week, we’ve got one of the best receiving corps in the league just because of the playmakers that we got. Obviously, me and MG doing our thing, Tuck and the tight end room, I mean we’ve got it all.
“Our goal every single game is to make plays when our number is called, and we did just that.”
Watson and Golden have combined for 1,662 receiving yards in nine games. That’s more than 200 yards ahead of the next pairing, Dallas’ CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens.
Watson and Golden are on pace for 3,139 receiving yards. Only four receiver duos in NFL history have reached 3,000 yards, with Detroit’s Herman Moore and Brett Perriman holding the record of 3,174 yards. That is within reach, though Moore and Perriman did it over the course of a 16-game season.
Regardless, what they are doing together is staggering. Every defense knows the Packers are going to throw the football with Jordan Love. Every defense knows Love’s two preferred targets.
On Sunday against New England – one of the best defenses in the NFL with one of the best cornerback tandems in the league – they were unstoppable. They combined for 90.1 percent of Love’s passing yards.
For the season, they are up to 63.5 percent of the team’s passing yards and more than half of the team’s total yards.
What Matthew Golden and Christian Watson are doing right now has not been done over a full season in the past two decades 🧀 pic.twitter.com/D0tD6D9F3X
“It just speaks about the confidence the coaches got in us, especially with Jordan,” Golden said. “It wasn’t just built now. It happened over time. We had to put the work in to get where we are now. If we continue to do that, it’s going to keep happening.”
The Packers haven’t had a 1,000-yard receiver since Davante Adams. Well, Watson and Golden might get to 1,500 yards this season.
Watson is third in the NFL with 879 yards. He’s on pace for 1,660 receiving yards and 13 touchdowns. In NFL history, there have been only 10 seasons of at least 1,600 receiving yards and 13 touchdowns.
Golden is fourth in the NFL with 783 receiving yards. He’s on pace for 1,479 receiving yards and nine touchdowns.
“We’ve got to keep building,” Love said. “There’s still more out there for us. I talk about this all the time, but just the connection we’ve been having and making plays downfield, and I think tonight was just kind of the epitome of everything we’ve been putting work in for. But I think there’s still more out there . But these guys, those two, they’re just making play after play. So, it really makes it easy for me. Just keep going to them.”

title: Packers Overreactions: NFL Should Be Terrified of What Jordan Love Said
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers blew out the New England Patriots on Sunday. It was a statement victory against the defending AFC champions.
With Jordan Love, Christian Watson, Matthew Golden and some big plays on defense, the Packers are good enough to beat any team on any given Sunday.
Maybe even the second Sunday of February.
Here are this week’s Packers Overreactions
Jordan Love threw 18 passes to Christian Watson and Matthew Golden. They turned those into 17 completions for 335 yards and two touchdowns. To say that trio single-handedly led the Packers to victory would be exaggeration, obviously, but they powered an emphatic win over one of the top teams in the NFL.
Asked about Watson and Golden after the game, Love had this to say:
“I think that’s something that we’ve been building on. You know, me and Christian have been together for a while now, and MG going in Year 2. I think more opportunities for those guys, and to really just settle in and get as many reps as possible throughout OTAs, training camp, and we made the most of it.
“So, we’ve got to keep building. There’s still more out there for us. I talk about this all the time, but just the connection we’ve been having and making plays downfield, and I think tonight was just kind of the epitome of everything we’ve been putting work in for. But I think there’s still more out there. But these guys, those two, they’re just making play after play. So, it really makes it easy for me. Just keep going to them.”
The three big words there?
More? More than 325 yards and two touchdowns? More than six deep completions for 235 yards? More than Watson ranking third in the NFL in receiving yards and Golden ranking fourth? More than their pace to finish with more than 3,100 yards?
More than dominating one of the premier cornerbacks in the NFL in Christian Gonzalez? More than routing a defense led by Mike Vrabel? More than being unstoppable when everyone in the stadium knew where Love wanted to throw the ball?
What a scary statement for the rest of the league entering the second half of the season.
Love was magnificent. When the Patriots blitzed, he had answers. When the Patriots had pressure, he made a play. When he had time, he made the Patriots pay.
“Flowing. That’s what it feels like. Feels like you’re just in that flow state and just finding ways to get guys the ball,” Love said. “But, definitely, just feels like you’re flowing. It’s a great feeling, and you just want to keep chasing every play and keep making big plays.
“I think I made some good throws, but I think guys are making some pretty cool catches, as well. So, yeah, we just got to keep you know building on that. Christian and MG, I mean, I looked at their stat line after the game and it was just crazy. It’s crazy to see that, and I think they’re balling right now. So, we just got to keep finding ways to get them the rock.”
The Packers entered Sunday’s game averaging barely 60 rushing yards per game. That put them on pace to have the worst rushing attack in NFL history.
Against a stout Patriots defense, the Packers ran for 129 yards. With Josh Jacobs out with a broken finger and MarShawn Lloyd inactive, coach Matt LaFleur had to let Kaleb Johnson out of the doghouse. He responded with 68 yards on 14 carries. He had 60 yards after contact, by our count.
“I feel like this is a little thing of what I can do when I get comfortable with the system and get familiar with the system,” he said. “Going over plays with [running backs] coach [Ben] Sirmans every day and just building on that and learning what to do on and off the field and just being me, just getting comfortable and confident.”
The Packers should have their backfield for the rest of the season.
In 2024 and 2025, the Packers leaned on Jacobs as the No. 1 runner with Emanuel Wilson providing solid play as the No. 2 and Chris Brooks entering in pass-protecting situations. That should be the plan going into the second half of the season, with Jacobs as the No. 1 back, Johnson as the sidekick and Brooks entering in pass-protecting situations once he’s activated from injured reserve.
And Lloyd? Maybe it’s time to admit defeat on the former third-round pick.
Before the game, Packers defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon called the matchup against New England’s offense a “big-time challenge.” The start of the challenge was quarterback Drake Maye and offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels.
“They’re a Super Bowl-caliber team, and they’re playing that way on offense,” Gannon said on Tuesday. “I think Josh McDaniels does an excellent job. They’re very creative, their scheme is robust, he gets them in the right plays. They got good backs, the O-line’s good, they got skill guys. This is a good crew now.”
The Packers led the Patriots 42-14 late in the third quarter. They forced four turnovers and made life miserable for Maye, last year’s MVP runner-up.
You know all of that. But consider the challenges.
Micah Parsons just returned to practice. The Packers are 11th in points allowed and total defense with their best player having missed all nine games.
The Packers played most of the game with their No. 3 and No. 5 linebackers. Edgerrin Cooper, who had been the team’s best defensive player without Parsons, is out for the season with a torn Achilles and defensive captain Zaire Franklin missed a third game with an injured shin. On Sunday, backup-turned-starter Ty’Ron Hopper played two snaps before exiting with a chest injury.
So, the Packers had to line up with steady veteran Isaiah McDuffie and special-teams ace Nick Niemann. Sure, Niemann gave up a touchdown catch but the Packers shut down one of the top offenses in the league without their All-Pro edge rusher and with a skeleton crew at linebacker.
You’d think an offensive guru like McDaniels and a top quarterback like Maye would be able to take advantage. They couldn’t, though, because Gannon sent blitz after blitz after blitz that McDaniels and Maye couldn’t handle.
“I thought it was pretty solid,” said Xavier McKinney, who had two interceptions. “Obviously, I thought we did a good job of getting the ball. We had a lot of turnovers. I think they gave us some plays that we didn’t really want to give up. They scored 27, so we got some things to get corrected. But I think overall we played a solid game. I do think there’s still a lot of room for improvement.”
That’s a variation of what Love said about there being “more out there,” but it’s the same theme. The defense wrecked the Patriots but there’s room to improve.
“I think JG’s brought a different level of energy to our defense and even to our team, to be honest with you,” McKinney said. “Obviously with the players that we have, everybody’s hungry, everybody is trying to figure out ways where they can be better as individuals, and then collectively that helps the group.”
Added together, if there’s another gear for the offense with the emergence of the running game and there’s room to improve on defense – hello, Micah Parsons – Sunday’s blowout could be the jumping-off point for this team.

title: Snaps, Studs, Duds and Defining Stats From Packers’ Destruction of Patriots
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Are the Green Bay Packers good enough to get to the Super Bowl?
The Packers answered that question in emphatic fashion on Sunday, crushing the defending AFC champion New England Patriots 45-27 on Sunday. Jordan Love made a statement . His receivers caught everything in sight. There was an honest-to-goodness running game. The defense produced four takeaways and the special teams bounced back.
Here is our weekly look at the snap counts, along with some studs and duds.
The Packers played 66 snaps on offense.
Quarterbacks: Jordan Love got to watch the final 9-plus minutes from the sideline. He played 58 snaps, with Tyrod Taylor running out the clock.
Love threw for 372 yards and three touchdowns even while not attempting a pass in the fourth quarter. He was great under pressure, he destroyed the blitz and he made one big-time throw after another. It was a virtuoso performance.
Running Backs: The Packers’ projected running back depth chart was Josh Jacobs, Chris Brooks and MarShawn Lloyd. For most of Sunday’s game, it was Kaleb Johnson and Pierre Strong. With Jacobs suffering a broken finger, Brooks on injured reserve and Lloyd inactive with a knee injury, Strong played 30 snaps, Johnson played 26 and Jacobs was limited to 10.
Johnson had been in the doghouse since fumbling at Tampa Bay. Because of circumstances, he’s probably out of it. Johnson carried the ball 14 times for 68 yards and one touchdown. We credited him with 60 yards after contact and two broken tackles. The Packers, barely averaging 60 rushing yards per game through Week 8, rumbled for 129.
Receivers: Christian Watson and Matthew Golden ran circles around one of the best cornerback tandems in the NFL. Watson played 51 snaps and Golden played 49. They combined to catch 17-of-18 targets for 335 yards with one touchdown apiece.
Savion Williams has become a key piece to the puzzle with 32 snaps. For all his work as a gadget guy, he is far more productive when he plays receiver and does receiver things. His 10-yard touchdown catch was superb work. Bo Melton and J. Michael Sturdivant played 15 snaps apiece. On special teams, Melton played 21 and returned a kickoff to midfield and added two tackles, and Sturdivant played 20.
Tight Ends: Tucker Kraft played 54 snaps. He contributed almost nothing statistically because Love was zeroed in on his receivers. Kraft converted two quarterback sneaks but both were nullified by false starts and then was stuffed when he tried to jump over the pile on the third.
Mark Redman played 24 snaps and had the big block on Kaleb Johnson’s touchdown run. Inactive last week, Jonnu Smith played 16. Drake Dabney was elevated from the practice squad and played six snaps on special teams.
Offensive Line: Right tackle Anthony Belton and center John Williams went the distance, and left tackle Jordan Morgan and right guard Laken Tomlinson played 58.
Left guard Aaron Banks missed some time in the first half and got to watch the end of the game on the sideline. So, he played 46 snaps. Kevin Zeitler finally got some action on offense and played 20 snaps as part of the shuffle following Banks’ injury and then in garbage time.
Morgan was tremendous; he’s really playing well as the blindside protector.
The Packers played 63 snaps on defense.
Defensive Tackles: The Packers’ defensive front will be as fresh as spring daisies for next week’s game against the Vikings. Rookie Chris McClellan played 33 snaps and Karl Brooks played 32, so barely more than half. Devonte Wyatt played 29 snaps, followed by Anthony Campbell with 25 and Jordon Riley with 20.
Brooks is having a really good season, even if the stats haven’t shown it, so it was good for him to have two sacks among his four pressures.
Edges: Just like at defensive tackle, the scoreboard allowed defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon to level out the playing time even more than usual. Brenton Cox led the unit with 34 snaps. He was followed by Dani Dennis-Sutton with 32, Lukas Van Ness with 32 and Barryn Sorrell with 30. Sorrell also logged 25 snaps on special teams.
Cox and Dennis-Sutton shared a sack; Cox for the second consecutive week led the team in pressures with five, according to Next Gen Stats. The others had two apiece.
Linebackers: The Packers came out of training camp with a depth chart of Edgerrin Cooper and Zaire Franklin as the starters and Isaiah McDuffie and Ty’Ron Hopper as the linebackers. Yeah, those were the days. With Cooper on injured reserve and Franklin inactive again with an injured shin, Hopper started but dropped out after two snaps with a chest injury. Even McDuffie was shaken up at the end of the game.
So, the snaps wound up being McDuffie for 60, Nick Niemann for 59, Kristian Welch for three and Hopper for two.
McDuffie led the team with nine tackles, including one sack. Niemann had six tackles. He gave up a touchdown but broke up one pass and had some production as a blitzer.
Cornerbacks: Keisean Nixon and Brandon Cisse’s days were over after 51 snaps. Nixon got beat for a double-move touchdown, the first score he’s allowed this season. Cisse’s pass breakup turned into an interception. According to PFF, he was targeted four times and allowed one catch for 2 yards.
Carrington Valentine played 13 snaps, veteran Benjamin St-Juste – who had played only one snap all season – played 12 and Kamal Hadden played five in the slot. He dropped a pick-six late in the half. St-Juste is a good player; a cornerback-hungry team would be wise to ask the Packers about his availability.
Safeties: Do the Packers’ have the best tandem of safeties in the NFL? Probably. The better question is which of the safeties is better? Evan Williams played 61 snaps. He had one interception and added four pressures, according to PFF. Xavier McKinney played 51 snaps. He had two interceptions, tying him for first in the league with five.
Javon Bullard played 40 snaps in the slot and Kitan Oladapo played 14.
QB Jordan Love: Bombs away.
Jordan Love completed 6 of 8 deep passes (20+ air yards) for 235 yards and a touchdown in Week 9. Love completed six deep passes for the second time this season. No other quarterback in the NFL has done so in any game. #GBvsNE | #GoPackGo pic.twitter.com/lMgscdboLl
WRs Christian Watson and Matthew Golden: They were the dominant forces. On passes thrown 20-plus yards downfield, they combined to catch 6-of-7 for 235 yards. Against premier cornerback Christian Gonzalez, the carnage was 11-of-12 for 192 yards and the two touchdowns, according to Pro Football Focus. With the Monday night game to be played, Watson is third in the league in receiving yards and Golden is fourth.
S Xavier McKinney: McKinney is tied for the NFL lead with five interceptions. Quarterbacks are foolish to throw it in his direction, especially when it’s not thrown at max velocity. He’s just too good to lob one up in his ZIP code.
S Evan Williams: Williams is tied for sixth in the league with three interceptions. He’s got 71 tackles, as well, making him the only player in the league with 60-plus tackles and more than one interception.
DT Karl Brooks: The Packers’ defensive tackles have been playing selfless team defense throughout the season, so the statistical production hasn’t matched their impact. At some point, though, players have to make plays. Brooks had two sacks.
CB Brandon Cisse: The reigning Defensive Rookie of the Month continued his sensational season. He was targeted four times, allowed 2 yards and produced one interception on the deflection that was picked off by Williams.
LG Aaron Banks: Jordan Love got sacked in the first half because Banks botched a stunt. PFF charged him with that sack and three pressures. The Packers need better from their $77 million lineman.
DT Devonte Wyatt: Wyatt signed a three-year, $54.9 million contract extension to keep him in Green Bay through the 2029 season. He shows up twice in the NFL’s statistical gamebook: He started and he played 29 snaps. He had no tackles, no sacks,…

title: Why the Texans Chose to Stand Pat at NFL Trade Deadline
full_text:
The NFL trade deadline has officially come and gone. And over the course of Tuesday's action up until the buzzer, we saw a few deals around the league go down for teams to either buy or sell some talent for the second half of the season.
However, the Houston Texans were not one of those teams.
The Texans seemingly looked around the market to find anything that made sense for them, might've talked to multiple teams in the process, but decided to hold off on adding or subtracting any pieces to their current roster.
The rest of the AFC South, though? They weren't shy to get to dealing . The Jacksonville Jaguars made multiple additions like Jordan Davis and Jessie Bates, while the Tennessee Titans and Indianapolis Colts continued their selling sprees surrounding guys like Amani Hooker and Josh Downs.
So why did the Texans decide to take their conservative approach as opposed to others that might've not been as gun-shy?
Really, it comes down to just where the Texans stand at this particular point in the season, paired with the amount of assets they have on hand to deal.
When taking a step back to look at the Texans' trade deadline situation, it was pretty tough to diagnose the team as true buyers or sellers.
On one hand, the Texans are coming off a resounding win over the LA Chargers this past weekend that injected a bit of hope that this group could make a late-season run.
Their offense was firing on all cylinders, their defense was looking back to their 2025 selves, and one final addition to the roster at the deadline could've gotten Houston one step closer to their ultimate goal.
But the Texans also had reason to hold off on adding a starting-level player to their roster as well.
After all, Houston is still stuck at a 3-5 record with work to do before they're deemed true playoff contenders, meaning a move to "buy now" could only take a couple of weeks, and a couple of losses could turn sour pretty quickly.
On top of that, the Texans have already made a couple of trades to upgrade their roster–– they just didn't happen during the trade deadline.
Houston made a deal heading into Week 6 with the Arizona Cardinals to bring in Marvin Harrison Jr. for a second-round pick and a late-round pick swap, and they also made a trade before Week 1 to add Kayshon Boutte to their receiver room for Jaylen Reed and another late-round pick swap.
The Texans have made moves to get this roster better. They've spent draft capital to make even more upgrades. And really, Houston's roster as currently constructed still has a reasonable amount of life left in their season to consider themselves right within the playoff hunt, even two games back from .500.
So could the Texans have gotten better by making a trade deadline addition to the roster? Sure, every team in the league could have that argument.
But a deadline move just didn't make a ton of sense for the Texans to execute without a truly tantalizing package.
No running backs were on the market that were realistic to acquire and moved the needle in the backfield from where things stood as is, and the same can be said about Houston's other rumored interest in safety.
Without any solid pieces up for grabs, and the lack of urgency from the Texans' side of things to pull the trigger on a deal, it's led to the end result looking like this at the deadline: quiet, without any shakeups, and thus puts a bit more pressure on this current roster to turn things around for a postseason appearance.
Based on their latest win against the Chargers , there's a good amount of optimism in the air that the Texans can make that climb up the standings happen. However, there's a lot more work to do in the weeks ahead for that to become a reality.

title: Which Texans Players Could Get Dealt on Trade Deadline Day
full_text:
The Houston Texans have just a couple of hours to go until they're on the other side of the NFL trade deadline.
﻿ To this point, things have been pretty quiet in H-Town . And that's led to the belief that the Texans could simply let this deadline come and go without making a move to their roster— which is a very real possibility.
But when taking a step back to look at the Texans' roster ahead of the trade deadline, a select few players around the building might make sense as a potential name to ship out for one reason or another.
Whether it be because that player might have value on the trade market if they were shopped, or if they might simply be a better fit in another situation, four players onboard the Texans feel as if they're the most likely names to be on the move, if a trade really is in play before 3 PM CT.
With that in mind, let's take a look at four Texans players that have the most realistic shot of being traded on deadline day:
The Texans' offensive line has taken a bit of a different shape from the state it was expected to be coming out of the offseason.
Back in the summer, the Texans were expected to start free agent signing Wyatt Teller at left guard in hopes that he would be an upgrade for a struggling unit upfront.
But he's only started in two games this season because of an injury to Ed Ingram, and has instead found his role as a bench contributor that might be better suited for a change of scenery at the deadline.
The Texans could find a suitor that has a starting spot in mind for Teller, get minimal draft capital in return for him, but also salvage a bit of their offseason investment that hasn't panned out quite as well as the front office would've hoped.
It's a win-win for the Texans and Teller, if he's looking for a bigger opportunity heading into the second half of the season. And in reality, this feels like it could be the most likely move of all that we see Houston end up making.
A very similar case here for Braden Smith: someone who the Texans signed to a two-year deal earlier in free agency expected him to start on their new-and-improved offensive line, yet hasn't found a consistent role as a starter since beginning the first four weeks of the season on injured reserve.
At most, Smith has filled in as a contributor in the Texans' jumbo looks on offense. But on a line that also has a solid backup swing tackle in Blake Fisher behind their starting duo of Aireontae Ersery and Trent Brown, Smith's presence in this offensive line room becomes a bit redundant without a clearly determined role.
So rather than let Smith sit in the Texans' offensive line room as a backup for the rest of the season, the Texans could strike on a deal for more value than someone like Teller could be worth, reshuffle their tackle room without Smith, and have a better set of draft assets to build with for this offseason.
Could the Texans value Smith more as a depth piece on their offensive line? Might teams be wary about trading significant assets to an injury-prone veteran tackle? Yes and yes. And those two factors might be what hold up a move getting done here. But it's an idea that's worth considering from Houston's lead decision-makers.
It's always fair to question whether or not a quarterback-needy team could be in the market to add Davis Mills; someone who many consider to be one of the more reliable backups in the NFL. And the idea isn't too outlandish to consider here for the Texans .
C.J. Stroud is playing lights-out through eight games of the season. He's going to get a new contract this offseason, and so is Mills, who's currently in the last year under contract and is due to be an unrestricted free agent in 2027.
If the Texans didn't intend on paying Mills another contract, a deadline move would make sense. Houston can cash in on an expiring contract in the form of a draft pick, and send out a backup who's gotten barely any playing time this year anyways.
However, the Texans could still go out and re-sign Mills this summer. And even if they aren't, the front office may simply see more value in Mills as a backup on their roster compared to whatever they could get back in return via trade. And if that's the case, then they might not deal Mills out at all.
This is simply a case of the Texans suffering from an overabundance at a certain position. And in this case, Houston might have one too many tight ends currently on their roster.
And the one name within that group of tight ends that makes sense to ship out would be Cade Stover.
He was just deemed a healthy scratch just last weekend against the LA Chargers, and with the increased involvement of Marlin Klein in the game plan moving forward, it'll be even harder for Stover to make an impact moving forward.
The solution? The Texans could trade away Stover now, get a minimal return for him, and move forward with a slimmer tight end room that opens up more involvement for Klein, as well as Brevin Jordan and Foster Moreau.
