title: One Move Raiders Can't Afford to Get Wrong at Trade Deadline
full_text:
The trade deadline has arrived, and the Las Vegas Raiders have plenty of needs. As the second half of the season approaches, it is clear what the Raiders need and which position groups need the most help. It remains unclear whether the Raiders will make a move ahead of the deadline to fix those issues.
The Raiders have come back to Earth after a 3-0 start to the season. After suffering yet another loss this past Sunday, Las Vegas' front office must decide how to fix its roster as the deadline will soon pass. Las Vegas' first nine games have answered some questions and raised many more.
A productive offseason of roster-building has had a profound impact on the field for the Raiders this season. However, improvements at certain position groups have made the need for improvement elsewhere on the roster that much more apparent.
Las Vegas doesn't just have needs. The Raiders have significant needs.
The Raiders still need a significant talent infusion on their roster. Las Vegas has several position groups on both sides of the ball that could use additional talent. They have several players in starting positions who may not be starting-caliber players on most teams around the league.
If the Raiders were to add a player before the deadline, it would likely be at wide receiver, cornerback, or on their offensive and defensive lines. They are talented enough as is to beat the league's worst teams, which is progress from last season. Still, their needs run deep.
Las Vegas' front office should do its due diligence to see whether it can pull off reasonable trades before the deadline. However, they have no reason to force the issue after the work they've already put in.
After all the moves the Raiders' front office made this offseason to fill out its coaching staff and roster, there are not many moves they can make at the trade deadline. Both trading away players of their own and trading for other players pose risks to the progress the Raiders have made so far.
Aside from Las Vegas receiving an offer they cannot refuse for Maxx Crosby, Kirk Cousins, or Jackson Powers-Johnson, the Raiders should refrain from trading any of their players. They should also refrain from trading away future assets.
Forcing any kind of move would be the biggest move they could make, and it would be wrong. At 4-5, the Raiders are ahead of schedule and would be better served by keeping their draft picks and cap space.
For this season, the wide array of moves the Raiders' front office made this offseason will have to be enough, and rightfully so. Las Vegas' front office hired Klint Kubiak for many reasons. One of those reasons was their belief in Kubiak's ability to develop players.
The progress the Raiders hope to attain over the remainder of the season will not come from more roster additions before the deadline. It will come from Las Vegas' coaching staff working with the roster they were given, which is significantly more than their most recent two coaches had.
The Raiders have lost four of their past five games, making it easy to point to the trade deadline as a time to add talent. However, after the team's Week 9 loss to the San Francisco 49ers, Kubiak pointed to execution as a bigger issue than talent.
“Obviously being able to have the mental toughness on long drives to finish drives out, even if it’s with field goals, defensively start there. Offensively, we had opportunities in that first drive. We  had two of those three opportunities that we missed,” Kubiak said.
“Especially on the -- we get to third and short on the very first third down of the game, we don’t convert. We got a chance to move the chains right there. So, when you’re opening up a game, there’s so many ways that a drive can go. But when you get to third-and-three in the first drive, you expect to convert and maintain possession right there. Now, the second drive was much better, but overall, you look at just the  play count."
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: What the Major Malik Willis Update Means for the Dolphins Offense
full_text:
Turned out Malik Willis' groin injury was much more than a minor issue through which he was playing.
The Miami Dolphins quarterback is going to miss at least the next four games, as he's headed to injured reserve because of what is being described as a "core muscle injury."
The Dolphins are placing QB Malik Willis on injured reserve, sources tell @ringer @netflixsports . Willis has been battling a groin injury that impacted his mobility. An MRI showed it has now developed into a core muscle injury, which requires rest. Not season-ending, but he’ll… pic.twitter.com/UoTDWWVHsl
The Dolphins made the move official late Tuesday afternoon when they announced that Willis would be joining defensive tackle Zach Sieler on injured reserve and that cornerback Reese Taylor was being waived.
Willis was visibly hampered by the injury during the Dolphins' 19-9 loss against the Detroit Lions on Sunday, lacking his normal explosiveness on those few occasions when he scrambled out of the pocket.
After downplaying twice earlier this season injury issues, including after the Week 8 game against the New England Patriots after he was on the injury report during the week, Willis acknowledged his groin felt "tight" against Detroit.
Head coach Jeff Hafley moved his normal press conference from 2:45 p.m. to noon Monday, and then said he didn't have any update on Willis' condition at that time and would be able to share more information Wednesday.
Willis will have to miss at least the next four games, scheduled against the Indianapolis Colts at Lucas Oil Stadium in Week 10, the Buffalo Bills at Highmark Stadium in Week 11, the New York Jets at Hard Rock Stadium in Week 12, and the Denver Broncos at Mile High Stadium in Week 13.
Since the start of the regular season, Willis has dealt with toe, thumb and now this latest issue.
The first time we really noticed him being impacted was that New England game when he had one rushing attempt — a third-and-1 QB sneak at that — after having eight against both the Bengals and New York Jets when he had his best performance of the season.
While Willis denied anything was wrong after the New England game, there was no more hiding it after the Detroit game when he clearly looked hampered while scrambling.
And even one of those scrambles was good enough for a first down, except that Aaron Brewer was flagged for holding.
And, let's be real, Willis being restricted to pocket passing because of a groin injury isn't doing anybody any favors.
Based on the limited sample size we've gotten so far with the Dolphins, it looks like maybe Willis could be a Jalen Hurts type with more arm talent.
But Willis at less than 100 percent and barely able to run — that includes scrambling away from pressure or picking up first downs — just isn't going to work very often. Particularly at this stage with the supporting cast he has.
So this is where we earlier suggested that unless Willis' groin was totally fine as the week of practice begins, Hafley should strongly consider sitting Willis against Indianapolis to make sure he gets right physically so the evaluation can resume properly.
The bottom line is Willis deserves more time before any judgments are made, though it's unrealistic to expect every fan to not want big results yesterday.
But Willis also needs to be at his best physically when he's in the lineup.
With Willis on injured reserve, the Dolphins now will turn to first-year player Kyle McCord, who will be looking at playing in his first NFL game against the Colts on Sunday.
The likelihood is the Dolphins eventually will sign Brady Cook from their practice squad to the active roster to make sure he doesn't get poached and they're left without a backup, though perhaps a veteran could be on the way.
McCord, of course, was acquired in late August in a trade with the Green Bay Packers in exchange for a 2028 sixth-round pick, the same one they got from the Jacksonville Jaguars in exchange for 2025 backup quarterback Quinn Ewers.
McCord was on the Philadelphia Eagles practice squad last year after he failed to make the team as a rookie sixth-round pick, and he then signed with the Packers this offseason.
While word out of Green Bay was that McCord looked good in training camp and the preseason, he didn't impress the Packers enough to convince them to move away from their practice of keeping only two quarterbacks on the 53 and he lost out to veteran Tyrod Taylor. The Packers were intent of re-signing him to the practice squad after waiving him, but figured he wouldn't clear waivers so instead they traded him to the Dolphins.
Because of the timing of the trade, McCord never appeared in the preseason for the Dolphins.
While Willis' work has been uneven so far in his first season as Dolphins quarterback, Hafley often has suggested he's almost like a rookie because of his limited body of work in his first four seasons in the NFL.
With McCord, that's even more accurate because this is a player who has yet to play in an NFL game.
There are good physical traits with which to work, but if there were growing pains with Willis at quarterback, it's probably fair to expect the same with McCord.
But now he's got a four-game mini-audition to show Hafley and the Dolphins coaches what he could offer and what his potential ceiling might look like.

Alain has covered the Miami Dolphins on a full-time basis since 1989 for various publications and media outlets, including Dolphin Digest, The Associated Press and the Dolphins team website. In addition to being a credentialed member of the Miami Dolphins press corps, Alain has covered three Super Bowls (for NFL.com, Football News and the Montreal Gazette), the annual NFL draft, the Senior Bowl, and the NFL Scouting Combine. During his almost 40 years in journalism, which began at the now-defunct Miami News, Alain has covered practically every sport at one time or another, from tennis to golf, baseball, basketball and everything in between. The career also included time as a copy editor, including work on several books, such as "Still Perfect," an inside look at the Miami Dolphins' 1972 perfect season. A native of Montreal, Canada, whose first language is French, Alain grew up a huge hockey fan but soon developed a love for all sports, including NFL football. He has lived in South Florida since the 1980s.

title: Grading the Dolphins on Their Week 9 Performance
full_text:
If hope dealing is illegal, go ahead and mark this report card Exhibit A.
Squint a little and you can see the makings of a good football team in the Miami Dolphins’ 19-9 loss against the Detroit Lions.
Miami is 1-7, and its punter had the longest completion of the day. But Caleb Douglas is starting to look like somebody the Dolphins can build a passing game around, and a defense starting four rookies ended Jared Goff’s 30-game streak with a touchdown pass.
Here’s how each position group graded out.
Malik Willis went 13-for-25 for 128 yards, no touchdowns and an interception. He added 7 yards on two carries and finished with a 50.1 passer rating.
Willis took a shot that Chuck Clark intercepted early in the third, but it wasn’t a particularly misguided decision.
It was third-and-11 with a safety that was shaded to the other side of the field, and Willis had Douglas one-on-one on a corner route. By the time the ball got there, there were two defenders in the picture. Douglas never got enough separation, and Willis left the ball too far inside. Clark had room to cut it off and took it back 34 yards.
Willis is getting better at snapping through his reads. With 11:33 left in the second quarter, Miami ran a play-action from its own 6. As soon as Willis saw the safety and corner bail into Cover 3, his eyes went right to Greg Dulcich in the flat for an 11-yard first down.
The play fakes themselves are abysmal, though. Too often, Willis tucks the ball into his chest before the running back even gets to him. What’s a linebacker or safety supposed to bite on when the back never gets close to the ball?
Once the Lions figured out that bottling up Ollie Gordon II was about all it took to stall Miami’s offense, they started stacking the box. The second-year back went from 5.7 yards per carry before halftime to 1.5 after it. There’s only so much Gordon can do when the lanes are closing before he gets to them.
All in all, 55 yards on 16 carries is a pretty ordinary afternoon, though Gordon did pick up 11 on third-and-6 to keep Miami’s last drive of the first half alive. Kaytron Allen lost a yard on his only carry and got his 46 receiving yards from Bradley Pinion on a fake punt. Carlos Washington Jr. caught one pass for 8 yards.
Miami badly needs production at receiver, and Caleb Douglas is showing the traits you want in a developing No. 1. The Texas Tech product has the size and catch radius, and he can create separation with his routes. He caught six of eight targets for 70 yards Sunday, giving him 296 receiving yards through his first five NFL games, a Dolphins record.
I’ll be Debbie Downer here. His 20-yarder with 3:30 left in the first quarter was a great catch on a poor route. Miami was running a flood concept on second-and-10, which means there is a deep route, an intermediate out for Douglas and a short route underneath. Douglas rounded his break and turned the out into something closer to a corner route. That gave Roger McCreary and Brian Branch a play on a ball that could have been picked. Douglas took it as an opportunity to showcase his athleticism and jumped between them and plucked it out of the air anyway. The separation he created at the top of the route may serve as eye candy, but there aren’t many universes where a coach would call a corner route and a go ball to the same side of the field, which means Douglas likely overextended his out route.
Malik Washington caught two passes for 21 yards, and both moved the chains. Kevin Coleman Jr. had a 16-yard run and would have had a 51-yard catch if a holding penalty hadn’t wiped it out. Chris Bell played 36 offensive snaps and got one target, an incompletion. Douglas and Washington were the only Miami wideouts to catch a pass.
It was a quiet day for Dulcich, who caught two passes for 14 yards. Bobby Slowik dialed up a tight end screen for him in the third quarter, and it went for all of 3 yards.
Will Kacmarek caught one pass for 6 yards, but my favorite play of his came without the ball. He tracked down Detroit linebacker Malcolm Rodriguez in the middle of the field and mauled him to the ground to help clear the way for a 5-yard run. The physicality and willingness to block are already there. He can overshoot his target, though, and that’s where he needs to clean up his footwork and angles. The holding flag that wiped out Coleman’s deep catch was his, too.
Austin Jackson got called for holding with 10 seconds left in the first half, moving Miami from Detroit’s 10 back to the 20. Zane Gonzalez hit the upright from 38 yards on the next snap. Aidan Hutchinson also pressured Willis six times in 16 one-on-one matchups with Jackson, per Next Gen Stats.
Miami got to the 7 after the fake punt in the fourth. Alim McNeill and Derrick Moore sacked Willis on two of the next three snaps, and the Dolphins settled for another field goal. Moore got him again on the next possession. All three sacks came in the fourth quarter, with Miami down 10.
If you told defensive coordinator Sean Duggan that Jahmyr Gibbs would come away with just 74 yards on 20 carries, he would have taken that. He did score the game’s only touchdown on fourth-and-1, but Miami made him earn most of what he got.
Josh Uche ended Detroit’s opening drive with a third-down sack and hit Goff’s throwing arm on the interception. Zeek Biggers got a third-down sack of his own a few plays after Detroit’s fake punt, and Zach Sieler dropped Gibbs for a 3-yard loss in the second quarter.
Then there’s the play where Miles Frazier took Kenneth Grant for a ride. On Gibbs’ 11-yard run in the second quarter, Frazier drove Grant about 10 yards downfield and turned him around so completely that Gibbs ran into him at the first-down marker. Grant got an assist on the tackle, but go watch how he got there.
Jacob Rodriguez continues to show up around the ball. He finished with 10 tackles and a sack, and he got Gibbs in the backfield for a 3-yard loss in the second quarter. Jordyn Brooks led Miami with 12 tackles and dropped Gibbs for a loss of his own on that same drive.
Where I’d like to see Rodriguez speed up is when he has to sort through traffic. There are snaps where you can see the gap open before he commits to it. By the time he gets off the block and fills, the back has already picked up an extra yard or two.
Detroit finished with 181 gross passing yards, and 11 of those came from punter Jack Fox. Amon-Ra St. Brown caught eight passes for 86 yards, and Jameson Williams caught one for 31. Goff hit them for 48 yards on back-to-back snaps right after Miami pulled within three, setting up Gibbs’ touchdown.
Chris Johnson’s interception was the top play from this group. He had the flat in Cover 2, saw the corner route coming over the top and sank into the next window. Uche hit Goff’s arm as he threw, and Johnson was right there to pick it off and take it back 21 yards.
Pinion hit Allen for 46 yards on fourth-and-3 on a fake punt.
That’s cute, but it isn’t his job. He also left the opening kickoff short of the landing zone, giving Detroit the ball at its 40, and hit a 25-yard punt in the second quarter.
Gonzalez made three of four field goals, including a 52-yarder, and scored all nine Miami points.
The Lions converted a fake punt of their own when Fox found Tay Martin for 11 yards on fourth-and-7. Add in the missed 38-yarder before halftime and it was about as up and down a day as this group could have.
Detroit went 3-for-12 on third down and still punted only once. It went 4-for-4 on fourth down, and Miami went 0-for-3 in the red zone. Throw in 11 penalties for 87 yards, and that’s how you lose by 10 on a day your defense only gives up one touchdown.
Tyler M. Carmona is a Miami native whose work has appeared in the Miami Herald and Associated Press. He previously worked as a local television news reporter. title: The Dolphins Should Sit Malik Willis This Week, But Not For the Reason You Think
full_text:
It very well might be that the Miami Dolphins should start Kyle McCord at quarterback in their Week 10 game against the Indianapolis Colts on Sunday.
It's just not for the reason a portion of fans, one that seems to be growing, would suggest.
Like it or not, Malik Willis is the Miami Dolphins' starting quarterback and that's almost assuredly not changing at any point this season.
Just remember the comments from Jeff Hafley to the CBS crew ahead of the Dolphins' Week 7 matchup against the New York Jets when the idea of the fans wanting a change was brought up and Hafley replied with a full backing as well as some astonishment that the idea even would come up.
Fans will be fans, and it's easy to look at Willis' stats and the offense's struggles to decide he's not going to be the answer at quarterback, though that's basically a premature evaluation.
That Willis wouldn't be able to produce big numbers with a supporting cast that anyone would agree is among the worst in the NFL really shouldn't be catching anybody by surprise.
And, no, it's not like you could insert a large number of quarterbacks and suddenly the offense would work, and if you're throwing Josh Allen in as one of those guys, well, let's just understand we're talking about a player who's basically in the top three in the MVP voting every year.
And, yes, if the Dolphins could get a Josh Allen, then Malik Willis could be discarded permanently.
It's just that those guys don't grow on trees and don't come along very often.
The whole idea with Willis was to bring him in at a very reasonable price for a starting quarterback of $45 million guaranteed over the next two years and give him the chance to show he could be the long-term answer quarterback and, if not, the Dolphins can look for that answer in the 2027 draft, in the 2028 or in free agency or the trade market is a high-end veteran becomes available.
It's not an evaluation that needs to be completed right away, maybe not even after the entire 2026 season, certainly not after only eight games.
And that evaluation never was going to be — and never should have been — based strictly on stats and offensive production.
Rather, it's going to come from certain moments, plays, situations and how Willis does with those.
And that evaluation will be completely subjective, with the only opinions that matter being those of GM Jon-Eric Sullivan, head coach Jeff Hafley and the rest of the Dolphins organization.
And, yes, there have been some flashes that suggest Willis could be just fine as the quarterback for a contending team — once the Dolphins beef up the talent around him on offense and some of young players gain more experience.
The numbers will suggest a very poor outing for Willis, with only 128 passing yards and a 50.1 passer rating.
OK, but those numbers have to be evaluated with a 51-yard completion to Kevin Coleman Jr. being nullified by a penalty, Will Kacmarek and Caleb Douglas both dropping passes, one on third down and the other on fourth down.
There also was a completion to Caleb Douglas that didn't count because the Lions were offside, but on that play there was immediate pressure on Willis and he managed to pass around the oncoming blitzer by changing his arm angle to the side and firing a strike.
And then we have to ask ourselves how many quarterbacks actually would make that completion.
Yes, Willis could be more decisive in making decisions to throw passes, but those All-22 reviews make it seems a lot easier than it is.
And the bottom line here is that Willis is operating under duress more often than not because of leaky pass protection.
Another factor to consider in the game against Detroit was that Willis was operating at less than 100 percent, which likely was the case as well against New England.
Remember that Willis showed up on the injury report before the game against the Patriots because of a groin injury and he had one rushing attempt that day — a third-and-1 QB sneak — after having eight against both the Bengals and New York Jets when he had his best performance of the season.
While Willis denied anything was wrong after the New England game, there was no more hiding it after the Detroit game when he clearly looked hampered while scrambling.
And even one of those scrambles was good enough for a first down, except that Aaron Brewer was flagged for holding.
And, let's be real, Willis being restricted to pocket passing because of a groin injury isn't doing anybody any favors.
Based on the limited sample size we've gotten so far with the Dolphins, it looks like maybe Willis could be a Jalen Hurts type with more arm talent.
And this is where we'll remind everyone the Eagles went to the Super Bowl twice with Hurts and won one title. So if Willis gets there, that would be plenty good enough for a starting quarterback.
But Willis at less than 100 percent and barely able to run — that includes scrambling away from pressure or picking up first downs — just isn't going to work very often. Particularly at this stage with the supporting cast he has.
So this is where we would suggest that unless Willis' groin is totally fine as the week of practice begins, Hafley should strongly consider sitting Willis against Indianapolis to make sure he gets right physically so the evaluation can resume properly.
Hafley didn't want to speculate on the severity of Willis' injury Monday, but the nature of groin issues is that typically the only remedy is some time off.
The idea of Kyle McCord starting certainly would please a lot of Dolphins fans, eager to see what he can do and hoping that's the hidden gem the team unearthed with the trade to Green Bay, though we'd caution against expecting too much out of a quarterback who has played exactly zero NFL regular season snaps and is on his third team.
The bottom line is Willis deserves more time before any judgments are made, though it's unrealistic to expect every fan to not want big results yesterday.
But Willis also needs to be at his best physically when he's in the lineup.

title: What to Know About Dolphins DT Zach Sieler's Mysterious Season-Ending Injury
full_text:
There indeed was a major announcement regarding Miami Dolphins defensive tackle Zach Sieler on the day of the NFL trade deadline, but it had nothing to do with him being moved.
Instead, the bombshell report involved a season-ending injury for the team captain.
Sieler ruptured a biceps tendon against the Detroit Lions on Sunday and will undergo season-ending surgery, according to ESPN insider Adam Schefter, citing sources.
Dolphins standout DT Zach Sieler ruptured his biceps and will undergo season-ending surgery, with a 5-6 month recovery expected, per sources. The injury happened on first play Sunday and he played the whole game with it. pic.twitter.com/N1ys0kzlkD
The longest-tenured member of the roster, Sieler had been remarkably durable since joining the Dolphins as a waiver pick-up from the Baltimore Ravens in 2019, missing only two games over the past six seasons — that came in the 2024 season when he was poked in the eye during practice.
To say this news came out of nowhere would be putting it mildly, considering Sieler played 42 snaps in the 19-9 loss against the Lions, only four fewer than he played against New England in Week 8.
There also was no Sieler injury reported in the press box, with the only one reported by the Dolphins being the quad injury to Will Kacmarek after he took a shot after catching a pass near the sideline.
No injury being reported could be explained by Sieler not being tended to on the field or being away from the sideline at any point.
What is notable, however, is that on the very first play from scrimmage against Detroit, a 2-yard run by Jahmyr Gibbs, Sieler was sporting a black contraption around his right upper arm. Sieler was listed on the injury report last week with a shoulder injury and was a limited participant in practice Wednesday and Thursday before being full go Friday.
Against the Lions, Sieler finished with one tackle, good for a 3-yard loss on a running play by Gibbs. While he didn't register a stat on the play, it was his initial pressure on Jared Goff that forced the quarterback out of the pocket and led to the third-down sack by Josh Uche in the first half.
The injury obviously quashed any notion of Sieler being traded before the 4 p.m. ET deadline Tuesday, even though reports indicated earlier the Dolphins had no intention of moving on from him regardless.
Sieler has three more years left on the contract extension he signed in September 2025. He's got a cap number of $20.8 million next year with no guaranteed salary remaining, which would seem to make him a potential candidate for a contract restructure.
That's down the line, though.
The immediate impact is the Dolphins will be left without their best defensive lineman.

title: Examining the Dolphins Connections to the Big Jacksonville Trade
full_text:
In an alternate universe, it could have been the Miami Dolphins who got a 2027 first-round pick and a 2029 second-round selection from the Jacksonville Jaguars on Monday.
Because it could have been the Dolphins who ended up with defensive tackle Jordan Davis in the first round of the 2022 draft.
And that could have happened if not for those 2021 draft trades involving first-round picks where the Dolphins went from third to 12th to sixth in deals with the San Francisco 49ers and then the Philadelphia Eagles.
To remind everyone, the Dolphins got two extra first-round picks for that move from 3 to 12 in what has to be considered one of the greatest value trades they have ever made — considered that in 2013 they did the reverse by going from 12 to 3 and only had to give up a second-round pick to get it done ... that they took Dion Jordan with that third overall pick is a different story altogether.
But instead of staying at 12 and keeping the extra first-round picks in 2022 and 2023, not to mention a third-rounder in 2022, the Dolphins gave up one of their two first-round picks in 2022 to move up to take Jaylen Waddle at number 6.
The pick the Dolphins got from the 49ers actually was sent to the Kansas City Chiefs in the trade that brought Tyreek Hill, but that left Miami without a first-round pick that year.
The Eagles, meanwhile, used the 15th pick in 2022 that they got from the Dolphins to move up to 13th and take Davis, and now they've gotten two premium picks for him.
So essentially, the Dolphins could have stayed at 12 in 2021 and kept their own 2022 first-round pick and in a way landed Davis and have gotten three good years out of him before recouping the draft investment, and then some.
The 12th overall pick in the 2021 draft incidentally was Micah Parsons, and the pick after him was left tackle Rashawn Slater, who would have been selections just as good as taking Waddle, if not better.
The Jaguars obviously were on the lookout for defensive tackle help because they not only traded for Davis, but also for 2017 Dolphins fifth-round pick Davon Godchaux from the New Orleans Saints.
One would think that puts them out of the DT market, which has some significance for the Dolphins because one name mentioned in connection with them at one point was Zach Sieler.
But as the trade deadline got closer and closer, it seemed more likely the Dolphins would not be making many, if any, moves before Tuesday at 4 p.m. ET.
The Dolphins told teams they weren't interested in moving Sieler or center Aaron Brewer, for example, according to SI national writer Albert Breer.
The New York Giants also have been interested in D-tackle help, but again the Dolphins likely aren't moving Sieler.
One last thing on Godchaux, he deserves mention as the one redeeming pick in what is in the running for worst draft class in team history. He was part of a group that included Charles Harris, Raekwon McMillan and Cordrea Tankersley as the top three picks.

title: A Simple (And Logical) Solution to a Clear Dolphins Problem
full_text:
One day after veteran Zane Gonzalez missed a second field goal attempt in as many weeks, Miami Dolphins head coach Jeff Hafley said he and GM Jon-Eric Sullivan hadn't made a decision on their kicker.
We'll make it simple for them: It's time to move on.
The Dolphins will have to make a call one way or another because Gonzalez has exhausted his three practice squad elevations with Miami, meaning he can't kick for the team again in 2026 unless he's signed to the active roster.
And it should be a slam dunk decision, one we're actually surprised hasn't already been made — unless it has been made but Hafley didn't want to reveal it just yet.
It's that much of a non-brainer, at least from where we sit.
Gonzalez's two misses have come in games where the Dolphins gave themselves a chance against quality opponents and they both came at key junctures — a fourth-quarter miss that kept the Dolphins two scores down against the New England Patriots in Week 8 and the miss on the final play of the first half that kept Miami from going into halftime tied 6-6.
As Hafley said after the game and again Monday, the Dolphins have to make those kicks.
Makes on both of those maybe wouldn't have changed the outcome in either game, but it's not like the Dolphins are operating with a big margin for error.
But the biggest reason the Dolphins should move on from Gonzalez is that they should operate with their kickers the same way they have with the rest of the roster, and that's basically treating this season as one big audition for veteran newcomers and a year of development for their draft picks.
Gonzalez has been a solid kicker during his NFL career, but why shouldn't the Dolphins aspire to get better at that position in 2027 and get an early look at somebody with more upside.
The Dolphins already have held tryouts for different kickers this season, and one of them stands out as an intriguing candidate — and it just so happens Hafley and Sullivan are familiar with him.
That would be Lucas Havrisik, who appeared in three games with the Green Bay Packers in 2025 and was 4-for-4 on field goal attempts with a long of 61 yards. Before that, he played nine games for the Rams in 2023 and was 15-for-20.
Or maybe somebody like Tanner Brown, who has never kicked in the NFL but was 25-for-28 for Louisville of the UFL this year with a long of 60 yards.
Brown also was among the kickers who have tried out for Miami this year.
Why not take a shot at one of those unproven young players?
What's the worst that can happen?
The Dolphins have to keep looking for a kicker?
It's not like the one they have now has been overly reliable.
And we could say the same about punter Bradley Pinion, whose 25-yard shank set up a Detroit field goal in the second quarter.
The Dolphins already have brought in punter for tryouts as well, so maybe the time has come to give somebody else a shot.
But the call on Pinion might be tougher because he's already on the 53-man roster. With Gonzalez, it's changing kickers or dumping somebody from the 53 to make room for him.
There's no reason they should do that right now.

title: Miami Dolphins 2026 Week 9 Snap Counts Stories: Secondary Switch, What's Going on With Grant?
full_text:
What stood out regarding play counts in the Miami Dolphins' 19-9 loss against the Detroit on Sunday:
We'll start with the list of inactives, which was highlighted by wide receiver Jalen Tolbert going back to the sidelines and running back Jaylen Wright missing the game with a quad injury.
The only Dolphins player who was active but did not play was backup quarterback Kyle McCord.
Since we've been keeping track every game, the starting lineup was back to seven rookies with fourth-round pick Kyle Louis making his first NFL start. The other six starters were Kadyn Proctor back in action at left guard, Will Kacmarek at tight end, wide receiver Caleb Douglas, linebacker Jacob Rodriguez, cornerback Chris Johnson and safety Michael Taaffe.
-- After Caleb Douglas has the biggest snap count among the wide receivers against New England, this time it was Malik Washington back to having that top spot, though by a small margin (44 to 42).
-- What's notable at wide receiver is Chris Bell having 36 snaps to only 11 for Kevin Coleman Jr., who again was more noticeable with Bell targeted only once for an incompletion where he failed to create separation.
-- Tight end Will Kacmarek, who left the game temporarily after taking a big shot to the side of the knee, played only 20 offensive snaps for a second consecutive game. While there was a contributing factor in this game, we'd still like to see him more after the Dolphins spent a third-round pick on him.
-- We again have a hard time getting Kacmarek being outsnapped by rookie free agent fullback DJ Herman, particularly on a day when the running game didn't have much operating room.
-- As should have been expected, it again was the Ollie Gordon II show at running back, though his snap percentage (72 percent) was smaller than it was against New England. Backups Kaytron Allen (6) and Carlos Washington Jr. (5) combined for 11 snaps.
-- Recent waiver wire pick-up Jared Wayne, who was in the lineup instead of Tolbert, played six offensive snaps and was flagged for two penalties — not exactly a good percentage there.
-- Five players were on the field for all the team's 59 defensive snaps — LB Jordyn Brooks, LB Jacob Rodriguez, S Michael Taaffe, CB Chris Johnson and S Dante Trader. The first four also had 100 percent participation each of the previous two games.
-- Chop Robinson's recent surge was reflected in the face that he got the most snaps on the edge, which hasn't happened this year because that distinction usually goes to Josh Uche. It was Robinson with 39 snaps and Uche to 35, then a major drop for any other edge defender with Rodney McGraw next with 12.
-- While Louis got the start, it should be noted he played only 11 snaps on defense, so categorizing as a starter now would be a stretch.
-- What stood out on the defensive line was the very similar number of snaps between Zach Sieler (42), Zeek Biggers (39) and Jordan Phillips (38), where Sieler usually played far more than his teammates. Given the performance of the defense, this can only be viewed as a positive development.
-- It's not exactly a great sign, however, that 2025 first-round pick Kenneth Grant played only 21 snaps in his fourth game back. This actually was his lowest total since he played 16 snaps against the Bengals in Week 5 in his first game of the season. The Dolphins need more from Grant, period.
-- Another interesting development came at cornerback where JuJu Brents and Jason Marshall Jr. got basically the same work load after Brents had emerged clearly ahead in recent games.
-- Edge Jamree Kromah, who the Dolphins claimed off waivers from the Chicago Bears two weeks ago, made his Miami debut and it consisted of two snaps on defense and four on special teams.
-- Opening-day starter Zayne Anderson was among the seven non-specialists who saw action only on special teams, along with LB Shaka Heyward, LB Jackson Woodard, S Julius Wood, C Andrew Meyer, G Jarrett Kingston and G/T Caedan Wallace.
-- Finally with special teams, rookie Seydou Traore again led the way with 20 snaps, though this time he was tied with Woodard. They were followed with 15 for Louis, Wood and Heyward.

title: Four Losers And Four Winners From Miami's Week 9 Loss
full_text:
Despite an exceptional performance by the defense, the Miami Dolphins were unable to knock off the Detroit Lions, falling by a score of 19-9 as they remain winless at Hard Rock Stadium.
It's no joke what Miami's defense has accomplished since their bye week. This is the first time in the past 30 games that the Lions' quarterback, Jared Goff, has been unable to record a passing touchdown.
Breaking a streak like that doesn't happen by accident. It's just a shame that not only was the offense unable to capitalize on its opportunities, but the special teams also somehow ended up just as ineffective in a game that was this close.
If there needed to be a wake-up call for changes to be made to Miami's special teams, this should be enough justification.
After playing a clean game of football against New England, Bradley Pinion made a pair of mistakes against the Lions — a kickoff that fell short of the landing zone to begin the game, and a punt that went about 25 yards. Not surprisingly, they ended up being catalysts for two field goals. But, hey, at least he can throw a decent football.
Miami didn't believe Riley Patterson was the answer at kicker, so the Dolphins turned back to Zane Gonzalez, who doinked a kick off the upright to close out the first half. It would have tied the game, but clearly asking for consistency at the position has been a bit too much.
And to top it off, allowing Detroit to capitalize on a fake punt to start the second quarter is the icing on the cake.  It seems surreal that, at this point in the season, the Dolphins need to seriously consider a shake-up at both kicker and punter, and their coverage could use some much-needed work as well.
It's another week when Sullivan's picks in the 2026 NFL Draft impressed, and it's making many Miami fans feel like the 2027 draft, which could be a monumental one for the franchise, is in good hands.
Honestly, it's surprising it took Jacob Rodriguez this long to record his first sack, but he did just that in the second quarter, alongside 10 total tackles on the day. Chris Johnson, meanwhile, recorded his first interception of the season, which also happened to be the first pick thrown by Goff in 2026.
That's THREE rookies on this team with an interception (Johnson, Rodriguez, Michael Taaffe). On the other end, Caleb Douglas continues to be as reliable a wide receiver as ever for the offense. Overall, the rookie won big today, which means Sullivan is a winner by proxy.
This might have been the worst collective performance by the offensive line this season. Granted, they faced a pass rush with game-wrecker Aidan Hutchinson. Still, both Jonah Savaiinaea and Austin Jackson looked rough, but it's extra disappointing to see Brewer struggle the way he did.
He looked sharp to start the season, but has been inconsistent as of late, and now there are some fans who are second-guessing the three-year extension. He had trouble standing his ground, being pushed backwards on multiple occasions. On top of that, he was flagged twice for holding — the latter killed the momentum of an otherwise solid drive in the middle of the third quarter.
Detroit wasn't the only team with an effective pass rush. The Dolphins came at Goff with everything they had, resulting in three sacks. Uche was responsible for one of those on Detroit's first drive. The Lions were knocking on the end zone at the 4-yard line, but Uche set them back 6 yards, forcing a field goal attempt instead.
In addition, Uche was able to make contact with Goff's throwing arm, resulting in a wild throw that Johnson capitalized on for the aforementioned interception. This was a pleasant two-game stretch for Uche, with nine tackles, two sacks, and a pass deflection against the Patriots and Lions.
Did the offensive line do Willis any favors? No, not really. But his decision-making, which has been up and (mainly) down this season, was, well, down. There were quite a few general misfires, some overthrows that receivers like Caleb Douglas bailed him out on. But the interception he threw into double coverage might have been one of the worst mistakes he's made on the field so far.
The dual-threat option was nonexistent in this game for Willis, which could be almost entirely due to the nagging groin injury he's been dealing with. If it's this impactful in terms of negating what Willis can do, then maybe Jeff Hafley should consider giving him time to heal and throwing Kyle McCord into the fire in the meantime.
But hey, another nice game for Douglas! Seventy yards off six receptions is nothing to scoff at, and it's not crazy to say he was the sole bright spot of the offense. His 20-yard gain in the first quarter came off a phenomenal snag midair off a pass that was thrown a bit too high.
If it were any other receiver in that situation, it might have been picked off, but Douglas is good enough to make a play like that happen. Believe it or not, this is the first time all season that Douglas was targeted more than Malik Washington — 8 to 3. Unfortunately, it takes more than a rookie wide receiver to carry an entire offense on his back.
Gordon was in a similar situation to Willis — the offensive line didn't help him out in the way they're expected to. So it was a brutal outing for Gordon, with 55 yards on 16 carries. It's not a good thing when the biggest positive is that he kept his cool even through adversity.
What this game really shows is how much De'Von Achane meant to this offense. He could take over a game by himself, as he was physical enough to shake off would-be tacklers in the trenches, even if there weren't comfortable gaps created by the offensive line. Gordon is tough, but he can't do the same thing as consistently.
After a solid performance against Minnesota back on October 4, Biggers was pedestrian against Cincinnati, the New York Jets and New England. However, he was one of many Dolphins in the trenches who teed off on Jared Goff in what should be considered a breakout game for the 23-year-old.
He ended the day with three tackles, a sack, and two QB hits. His sack — the first full sack of his career — came on third down of Detroit's first drive of the second quarter, forcing a Lions punt. It's not a contest, technically, but the 2025 seventh-rounder looked a lot better than the 2025 first-rounder. Just saying.

title: Five Instant Overreactions to the Dolphins-Lions Matchup
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins fought hard, but ultimately lost to the Detroit Lions in a 19-9 bout. There is plenty to analyze in this game from Sunday afternoon, so let's overreact to some of the key developments.
Malik Willis spent much of this game under constant pressure, and while he was able to avoid all but two sacks, he looked almost completely sapped of his athleticism, and his condition appeared to have worsened as the game went along.
Willis has been on the injury report for the last couple weeks with a groin ailment, and it’s pretty clear that it’s impacting his top-end mobility as well as his decision-making. He’s passed up multiple opportunities to run or extend plays, which may be his biggest weapon.
If Willis is banged up enough that it’s changing his calculus inside and outside the pocket, then it’s time to sit him down. It’s less about his performance of late, and more allowing him to get back to a comfortable place so Miami can better evaluate him down the stretch of the season. Plus, an extended look at Kyle McCord could be valuable in deciding whether he’s a long-term answer at backup QB.
One of the lone positives from an abysmal offensive performance is that of Caleb Douglas. The rookie receiver has looked stellar after returning from injury, and made multiple nice plays in this game, the best of which was a full-extension catch where he plucked the ball from the air after a stellar route past the sticks.
Douglas had a fourth-down drop late, but aside from that gaffe, he was easily Miami’s best offensive player. His fluidity and tackle-breaking at  6-4 are both astounding, and he’s risen to the moment as Malik Willis’ No. 1 option. His development is going to be one of the more exciting storylines of Miami’s rebuild, and it wouldn’t be shocking to see him as the centerpiece of an effective Dolphins passing game in the future.
A fun (and successful) fake punt call doesn’t change the fact that the Miami Dolphins’ special teams unit is embarrassing. Missed field goals, kicks short of the landing zone, and shanked punts are all stories that keep repeating themselves. Nothing has been fixed week over week, and we’re at the point where that falls on the coaching staff.
Miami used the last of their practice squad elevations on Zane Gonzalez, and after back-to-back weeks with missed kicks, it would be a massive mistake to bring him back on a regular deal. Furthermore, the social media noise around Chris Tabor’s job security gets deservedly louder and louder, as personnel changes haven’t led to better results. I think a midseason shake-up would be warranted if they decide to go in that direction.
The Miami Dolphins fought hard and remained competitive in a game where they faced the No. 1  offense in the NFL and only put up 228 total yards, and that’s because their defense put up a virtuosic performance.
Miami consistently moved Jared Goff off his spot, sacked him three times in the first half, and forced him to throw an early interception that flipped the field for Miami. Jahmyr Gibbs averaged only 3.7 yards per carry, and Detroit ended the game 3-for-12 on third downs.
Jeff Hafley mixed coverages, threw out all kinds of disguises, and put together some perfectly timed blitzes and stunts. A better offensive performance likely gives this game national recognition as a masterful shutdown of the league’s most effective attack, and it can’t be ignored, regardless of the final result.
With Kadyn Proctor returning from concussion protocol, there was a real opportunity for Miami to flash some of the run-game dominance we’ve seen in recent weeks. However, aside from a few chunk gains, they failed to get anything going.
Ollie Gordon finished with 16 carries for only 55 yards, and Malik Willis was under constant pressure. The only reason the Lions only finished with two sacks is because Willis miraculously avoided several free rushers throughout the game.
The offensive line is a unit defined by its weakest link, and Austin Jackson stuck out in a bad way against Detroit. He was consistently beaten in pass protection, and didn’t do enough in the run game to even it out. Furthermore, Miami’s line has three players in their third year or earlier, and their youth has led to several miscommunications that they’ll need to grow and move on from.
Tyler DeSena is currently a journalism student at the University of Central Florida. Prior to joining Dolphins On SI in 2026, DeSena worked with dolphinstalk.com, and created independent social media content on X, YouTube and TikTok.

title: Miami Dolphins Week 9 Instant Takeaways: Time for New Specialists, Suggestions for Offense
full_text:
That the Miami Dolphins lost against the Detroit Lions to fall to 1-7 in this rebuilding season wasn't a surprise at all, but how it came about? That was a different story.
Be honest, how many figured the uneven Dolphins defense would be able to stymie for most of the game the vaunted Detroit offense and hold it to only one touchdown? No, if the Dolphins were going  to win this game, they would have to outscore the Lions, with the thought that maybe they could do some damage against what statistically is a mediocre Detroit defense.
Well, the defense did its part only to watch the offense come up woefully short.
It was a brutal game all around for the offense, lowlighted by a whole bunch of penalties, a lot of pressure on Malik Willis, a really poor decision by Willis himself that produced a bad interception, other misfires, a couple of dropped passes, the whole sordid affair punctuated by rookie Caleb Douglas dropping a fourth-and-12 pass that should have been good for the first down.
There are so many things to pick apart offensively, though a lot of the fingers will be pointed at Willis because he's the quarterback and, in a best-case scenario, the quarterback of the future for this franchise.
It was difficult to make the case for Willis after this performance, though it must be repeated that he's operating at a major disadvantage with a really poor supporting cast.
It also didn't help that Willis clearly looked hampered by the groin injury that's had him on the injury report the past two weeks. Then again, if Willis can't scramble, it takes away what should be one of the best parts of his game, and if Willis isn't going be operating at full capacity, head coach Jeff Hafley has go to start thinking about using first-year quarterback Kyle McCord until Willis is right physically.
And for those Dolphins fans who keep calling for McCord, we would warn everyone to be careful what they wish for because McCord is going to be hamstrung by the same issues that surround Willis.
One other suggestion on offense is to be more aggressive, particularly near or in the red zone where we really don't need to see run on first and second down when the running game is struggling.
We also would suggest being more bold in a situation like when the Dolphins were down 9-3 in the third quarter and facing a fourth-and-6 from the Detroit 34-yard line. Settling for a 52-yard field goal attempt that still leaves you trailing even if successful isn't the way to go from this vantage point.
-- We do have to give the Dolphins props for a daring move when they had Bradley Pinion throw a pass out of punt formation, which produced their longest play of the game after it was completed to Kaytron Allen. Incidentally, that was the team's first completion by a punter since 2019 when Matt Haack threw a touchdown pass to kicker Jason Sanders in the famous "Mountaineer Shot" play.
-- That was one highlight for the special teams, which otherwise were brutal again. The Dolphins had a Pinion kickoff fall short of the landing zone, Pinion had a 25-yard punt, Zane Gonzalez missed a chip-shot field goal at the end of the first half, a fake punt allowed, and maybe we forgot something. This is a season for evaluation and trying to find hidden gems for 2026 and beyond, and it says Pinion and Gonzalez just aren't it, and it's time for the Dolphins to look for new kicking specialists.
-- The loss, though, was more on the offense than the kicking game.
-- The offensive line remains a work in progress, and this was a rough game against the Detroit pass rush and it wasn't just Aidan Hutchinson who did damage for the Lions. As has been the case most of the season, it was the right side that struggled and that's Jonah Savaiinaea and Austin Jackson. And Aaron Brewer also didn't have a great game, as he's having a hard time following up on his remarkable 2025 season.
-- This is very disappointing because the hope was the offensive line was going to make this offense run, but it's just not happening.
-- The running game again was sluggish, and there's only so much Ollie Gordon II can do without beter blocking up front.
-- That Dolphins pass rush in the first half was nothing short of dominant, easily the best we've seen all season.
-- There were standouts everywhere in that part of the game, particularly Josh Uche, Chop Robinson and Zach Robinson. Shoot, even Zeek Biggers got involved with the pass rush.
-- The pass rush slowed down a bit in the second half, but that had to be expected and nobody should complain about the performance of the defense in the least.
-- Great to see Chris Johnson come up with his first NFL interception the week after he made headlines and highlights for the wrong answer with his missed sack against Drake Maye. That it was an easy pick after Uche hit Jared Goff's arm made no difference. Johnson has been solid as a rookie, much better than his stats might suggest.
-- Really, there was very little not to like about the defensive performance, which had to overcome a pretty bogus DPI call against Jason Marshall Jr. against Amon-Ra St. Brown.
-- The big number here is the Dolphins holding Detroit to 270 yards, by far their lowest total of the season. The previous low was 355 in Week 2 against Buffalo.
-- This unequivocally was a winning performance by the Dolphins defense; it's just too bad the offense couldn't hold up its end of the bargain.

title: 3 Vikings Winners & 3 Losers After Vikings Shake Up QB Room With Kirk Cousins Trade
full_text:
The Vikings waited until the NFL trade deadline, but the team got a deal done that should help their offense. The trade sent a third-round draft pick to the Raiders in exchange for quarterback Kirk Cousins.
Cousins arriving back in Minnesota couldn't happen at a better time. The Vikings are coming off one of the most embarrassing quarterback performances in NFL history, when Carson Wentz had an 8.9 quarterback rating on Monday Night Football against the Buffalo Bills.
This trade should instantly upgrade the Vikings' offense . Bringing in a 15-year veteran quarterback like Cousins, who is familiar with the offense and is currently second in the NFL in passing touchdowns (20), will bring some excitement to the team.
That said, Tuesday's return isn't positive for everyone. Let's take a look at three winners and three losers from the Vikings trading for Cousins
Brian Flores's defense has been legit this season and is the biggest reason the Vikings are 6-2 through their first eight games. All Minnesota needs is a little help from the offense to put some points on the board and look like a dominant team.
On Monday night, Minnesota's defense was on the field for over 42 minutes of the 60-minute game. The offense didn't convert a single third or fourth down all game, putting a ton of pressure on Flores to keep Buffalo from running up the score.
The door is closed for Kyler Murray to prove that his struggles in Arizona were situational. Now, he heads to the bench in Minnesota and will serve as the primary backup for Cousins once he recovers from his hamstring injury.
Will Murray be able to land on his feet once he leaves the Vikings after this season? Or is the former No. 1 overall pick in the 2019 NFL Draft destined to be a backup, even though he has started every NFL game he's played in?
Either way, it sounds like Murray won't get much of a chance to build his case before he hits free agency in March.
Although he hasn't been extremely vocal about his frustration, there is no way superstar wide receiver Justin Jefferson isn't jumping for joy having Cousins back in Minnesota to throw him the football.
From 2020 to 2023, Cousins threw 28 touchdowns to Jefferson, averaging seven TDs per year compared to 5.3 in the last three seasons. The connection between these two players is strong and should translate to the face of the franchise looking more like the player fans know and love.
Although he was already in the doghouse after his abysmal Monday Night Football performance , the coaching staff and front office face a tough decision about Carson Wentz. Since he won't start anymore and won't be the backup, how does he fit in Minnesota?
Having Wentz as the QB3 when he offers no future value would be confusing, especially after Max Brosmer looked better than him against Buffalo. The decision will have to come down to whether to let him go or keep him as a veteran third quarterback option.
The Vikings will finally get an opportunity to see whether Jauan Jennings was a bad fit for the Vikings or if the Minnesota offense was making it impossible for him to be a consistent contributor during his first year with the Purple and Gold. Through six games (two starts), Jennings has only six catches for 54 receiving yards without a touchdown.
Jennings has been a free-agent bust for Minnesota this season, but that could change if he gets on the same page as Cousins. Having him in a competent offense could make a world of difference for a player who looked good during his previous time with the 49ers.
While head coach Kevin O'Connell gets to reunite with Cousins, there is a harsh reality that has to be faced. For a coach often tabbed as a "QB guru" by the media, he will have to admit he failed to evaluate and develop multiple passers.
J.J. McCarthy, Daniel Jones and Sam Darnold were all allowed to leave Minnesota to make room for Murray and Wentz. Neither quarterback he kept has looked capable of commanding an offense this year. Hopefully, a reunion with Cousins will put O'Connell and the offense back on track.
Otherwise, it might be time to reevaluate his future in Purple and Gold.

title: How Kirk Cousins Trade Changes Vikings’ Offense Moving Forward
full_text:
The Vikings finally have their potential savior at quarterback , and it comes in the form of a familiar face.
Kirk Cousins is returning to the Vikings after Minnesota agreed to send one of its 2027 third-round picks to the Las Vegas Raiders. Now, the 6-2 Vikings will be looking for a much-needed boost to their abysmal passing game in the form of the 38-year-old veteran.
The #Vikings have acquired QB Kirk Cousins in a trade with the Raiders. The completion of this trade is pending Cousins passing a physical. 📰: https://t.co/VefqxaBaC4 pic.twitter.com/pbx5QhIvbH
Is this the boost the offense needs? Will Cousins be able to make an immediate impact ?
Let’s break down what the trade means and how it impacts Minnesota’s offense and Super Bowl aspirations.
Cousins provides an immediate, desperately needed boost to a struggling Vikings passing game and, most importantly, familiarity with head coach Kevin O’Connell’s scheme. Vikings QBs have totaled 1,286 passing yards and eight passing touchdowns through eight games, while Cousins has thrown for 2,340 yards and 20 touchdowns through nine.
Cousins also owns the 15th-best passing grade (75.5) on Pro Football Focus this season, whereas Kyler Murray (68.6) and Carson Wentz (36.6) rank 25th and 57th, respectively.
After Monday's embarrassing offensive showing, the Vikings desperately needed to make a move, and new general manager Nolan Teasley did just that. While the third-round price tag may seem high, the Vikings have the added flexibility of an additional third-round pick from the Jonathan Greenard trade with the Eagles. This was simply a no-brainer move.
Now Cousins may make his Vikings re-debut at the site of his last game in purple, Lambeau Field, where a torn Achilles ended his 2023 season.
Redemption. pic.twitter.com/teKTLOfzz1
Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison are likely the happiest people in the locker room, as both have suffered greatly due to the lack of reliable QB play since Sam Darnold’s departure in 2024.
Jefferson averaged 98.9 receiving yards per game in 54 games with Cousins at QB. I’d expect to see the Vikings lean back into the offensive scheme that led Jefferson to the 2022 Offensive Player of the Year Award.
This move signifies that O’Connell and Teasley see a wide-open Super Bowl window for the Vikings thanks to Brian Flores and his stellar defense. The Vikings are averaging the sixth-fewest points per game in the NFL at 18.3, while their defense is allowing only 14.5.
If Cousins and the offense can score 21 or more points against the better teams in the league, the Vikings should be set up well for a deep postseason run.
Luckily, the Vikings retain their first- and second-round selections, so they’ll be able to pursue a rookie quarterback early in the draft if they identify the right QB. If Fernando Mendoza is any indication, Cousins may be one heck of a mentor.

title: What Kirk Cousins Trade Means for Kyler Murray, Carson Wentz and Max Brosmer
full_text:
After watching Carson Wentz put together an ugly performance under the primetime lights on Monday night against the Bills, the Vikings decided that enough was enough and brought back a familiar face to get the offense on track.
On Tuesday, NFL insider Tom Pelissero reported that the Vikings traded a 2027 third-round pick to the Raiders in exchange for veteran quarterback Kirk Cousins.
Blockbuster! The Raiders are trading four-time Pro Bowl QB Kirk Cousins to the Vikings for their 2027 third-round pick, sources tell @ringer @netflixsports . Cousins returns to Minnesota for the playoff push, while Las Vegas turns to No. 1 pick Fernando Mendoza. pic.twitter.com/3SvmtZu6er
In the hours leading up to the deadline, there was speculation that the Vikings could bring Cousins back to the Twin Cities. But now it’s reality, as Minnesota will hopefully have some stability under center.
This season with the Raiders, Cousins is completing 64.1% of his passes for 2,340 passing yards, 20 touchdowns, and eight interceptions. With Cousins in the fold, the question now is what happens to the rest of the QB room, especially since he has a club option for $10 million, per Spotrac.
It’s not impossible to think that Cousins could start for the Purple and Gold not only this season, but also in 2027. But let’s discuss how this trade will impact the other QBs on the roster going forward.
The adage in sports is that your best ability is your availability. For Murray, he’s missed some time due to injury, including Week 9’s contest against the Bills due to a hamstring injury.
The last thing we heard about Murray’s injury is that it’s a grade 2 strain , and he could be out longer than just Monday night. If that’s the case, then it’s a no-brainer to go after Cousins.
When Murray was healthy and on the field, he didn’t exactly light the world on fire under center, completing 64.9% of his passes for 1,022 yards, five touchdowns, and three interceptions. Now, unlike Cousins, Murray has dual-threat ability as an advantage, rushing for 167 yards, but it still hasn’t taken his offense to another level.
In fact, Murray’s yards per pass attempt is sitting at 6.6, which is lower than Cousins' (7.4), and you could make the case that Murray has the better collection of talent around him, but for some reason it hasn’t led to explosive plays and consistency.
With Murray set to be a free agent at the end of this season, it’s likely he’s playing elsewhere in 2027 and not with the Purple and Gold.
Wentz could be the odd man out in Minnesota sooner rather than later, with Cousins coming back to Minneapolis. The Vikings will be projected to have four QBs on their 53-man roster, which is one too many.
The former North Dakota State star did not do himself any favors on Monday night, as he looked like a completely different QB than we saw earlier in the season. The 33-year-old quarterback completed a horrendous 32% of his passes (8-of-25) for 81 yards and two interceptions, which is shocking, given that the Bills’ defense isn’t that great to begin with.
However, Wentz’s latest performance goes in line with what the Vikings have dealt with this entire season at quarterback. The veteran quarterback is also set to become a free agent at the end of this season.
He, like Murray, will likely be playing elsewhere in 2027. But between the two, Murray has a better chance of finding a backup job.
The former undrafted free agent out of the University of Minnesota has been on the active roster since the end of September, but he’s clearly not this team’s backup of the future. Brosmer didn’t even make the 53-man roster out of training camp, as he was waived and re-signed to the taxi squad.
His preseason numbers were nothing to write home about this summer. Brosmer completed 59.3% of his passes for 269 yards and an interception. Minnesota might keep him around as a QB3/practice squad arm with Cousins returning, but his chances of seeing the field are slim to none.

title: Instant Grade: Vikings Land QB Kirk Cousins From the Raiders
full_text:
After hours, days and even weeks of speculation, the Vikings have completed a deal with the Raiders to bring back former quarterback Kirk Cousins to the Land of 10,000 Lakes.
With hours remaining before Tuesday's NFL trade deadline , the Vikings now have their QB1 in a deal that sends Minnesota's 2027 third-round pick to Las Vegas, according to The Ringer' s Tom Pelissero.
It's not every day a starting quarterback gets dealt mid-season, but the Vikings were able to make it happen with Cousins, who will now be tasked with jumpstarting the anemic offense . Let's breakdown this whopper of a trade and hand out a grade.
Sure, the Vikings could've—and clearly should've—signed Cousins this March for pennies on the dollar, but that time has passed, and getting a starting-caliber quarterback who knows the offensive scheme better than the currently rostered quarterbacks is impossible to hate.
The third-round pick stings a bit, but really, the Raiders should've held out for more. All week, the reports out of Las Vegas were that they had no intention of moving Cousins, and yet the desperate Vikings came to them on their hands and knees and were able to swipe him away for a late third. For a team that had no other promising alternatives, the Vikings absolutely came out as winners here.
Of course, Cousins is 38 years old and just a few years removed from an Achilles injury, so the risk of adding him is far from zero, but something had to be done. Kyler Murray was struggling to adapt to head coach Kevin O'Connell's system, Carson Wentz was struggling to relearn the sport, apparently, and Brian Flores's generational defense was going to waste.
Having started nine games for the Raiders, Cousins has completed 64.1% of his passes for 2,340 passing yards while throwing 20 touchdowns to six interceptions. His 77.1 offensive grade ranks 12th-best among 35 qualified QBs this season, per Pro Football Focus .
Surely, there'll be a bit of a readjustment period, but no one in the building is happier than Justin Jefferson, who has just 31 catches for 393 yards halfway through the season. With a new general manager at the helm in Nolan Teasley, it was hard to predict how big the Vikings might go , but he clearly recognizes the urgency of the situation and potentially found the savior

title: Vikings NFL Trade Deadline Tracker: Trades, Rumors, and Latest News

The Vikings have acquired QB Kirk Cousins from the  Raiders in exchange for a 2027 third-rounder , according to NFL insider Tom Pelissero. title: Harmon's Longship Week 9: 4 Vikings Thoughts as Super Bowl Hopes Hang in the Balance at Trade Deadline
full_text:
MINNEAPOLIS, M.N. — I’d say the Vikings offense hit rough seas on Monday night against the Bills, but saying that Carson Wentz steered the ship directly into a cliff would be a more accurate description. After a month and a half of downplaying offensive concerns thanks to an undefeated record, the last two weeks have proven that the Minnesota Vikings’ season desperately needs saving from a peewee-football-level offense.
With the NFL trade deadline approaching on Tuesday at 4 p.m. ET, we’ll soon find out whether general manager Nolan Teasley will try to salvage the wreckage.
Of all the football games I've seen, that was certainly one I will not forget anytime soon. The Vikings’ defense and the crowd at U.S. Bank Stadium came to play. That place was louder than I have ever heard it as the Bills took the field for their first offensive possession. The defense played off the crowd’s energy for most of the night, putting together a truly impressive performance before eventually getting gassed.
Guess that can happen when the opposing offense is able to hold the ball for nearly three quarters of the game.
Carson Wentz's performance on Monday night holds a special place in all-time bad performances from a Vikings QB , and we’ve certainly seen a lot of them. Wentz finished 8-for-25 for a brutal 81 yards and two interceptions. Max Brosmer entered the game late in the fourth and ended with 58 passing yards for reference, albeit against a prevent defense.
Worst total EPA, Vikings QBs since 2024 Wentz vs BUF -28 Brosmer vs. SEA -27.6 Darnold vs. LAR -23 Darnold vs. DET -20 McCarthy vs. ATL -19.9 McCarthy vs. GB -16.9 Brosmer vs. DET -15.2 McCarthy vs. CHI -12.4 Kyler vs. TB -11.8 We have a new champion
O’Connell also ignored his running game almost the entire game in an attempt to help Wentz find a rhythm. Aaron Jones and Jordan Mason ended the day with eleven total carries for 51 yards. Even with Wentz struggling mightily and the defense keeping things close, O’Connell kept going back to the well. The 23-6 final score does not fully tell the tale of just how brutal this offensive performance was.
We can debate all we want about how much blame Kevin O’Connell deserves for the Vikings’ current offensive woes, but one thing is certain: this is his QB room, and he must own it. With no full-time general manager, O’Connell spent this past offseason speaking to the need for a deep and competitive quarterback room.
His solutions? Picking Kyler Murray in free agency, bringing back Carson Wentz, and allowing Max Brosmer to be QB3 after the J.J. McCarthy trade.
pic.twitter.com/6yiyC7t8p7
Simply put, it doesn’t matter if wideouts are getting open or how “close” the offense is if no one in the QB room is capable of throwing an accurate and timely pass. Is O’Connell a poor talent evaluator? Is he causing his QBs to overthink and meltdown under pressure? His only hope now is that Teasley finds him a QB who can run his offense by this afternoon.
This week could not have gone worse for the Vikings in the pursuit of their first division title since 2022. The Packers absolutely dominated the Patriots in a 45-27 showing where both Christian Watson and Matthew Golden put up video-game numbers. Unfortunately, Vikings fans must admit that Jordan Love is, in fact, very good at football. Minnesota will head to Green Bay Sunday on a short-week turnaround.
The Bears and Lions both snuck out close wins against sub-par Florida football teams, but a win is a win in the standings. Caleb Williams continued to flash moments of absolute brilliance against the Bucs before spiraling into a four-interception performance. The Bears would hang on with a 27-24 win. The Lions struggled against a single-win Dolphins team but left Miami witha  19-9 victory.
The Vikings have fallen to third place in the NFC North and the sixth seed in the conference. If the playoffs started today, they would head east to face McCarthy and the New York Giants.
The Packers are currently fourth in the NFC North, but a win against the Vikings on Sunday could change their fortunes quickly. With the Packers hitting their stride and the Vikings' offense doing everything it can to ruin a great season from Brian Flores’ defense, these two squads are heading in dramatically different directions.
This game could look much different if the Vikings are able to make a splash trade acquisition on Tuesday, but Minnesota will have an uphill battle without serious help.

title: 3 Vikings Studs & 2 Duds After Getting Hammered by Bills on MNF in Week 9
full_text:
After a perfect start to the year, the Vikings lost their second game of the season on Monday Night Football. It was a low-scoring affair and the Bills were in control of the game while the Purple and Gold struggled to do anything offensively.
The 23-6 loss was another in a long line of prime-time embarrassments for the Vikings. Under the lights at U.S. Bank Stadium, Minnesota couldn't execute offensively under quarterback Carson Wentz at all, never entering the red zone or converting on third or fourth down with him under center.
Minnesota might still be 6-2 this season, but this game highlighted the major issues this team will face as it continues to play through the challenging schedule. The fact that Minnesota was on offense for 17:28 of the 60:00 says everything that fans need to know about this game.
Yes, Justin Jefferson caught only three passes on the day, though the ball was thrown his way 11 times; however, so many of those passes were either off-target or uncatchable. Still, he finished with 58 receiving yards, the most on the team.
The Vikings are lucky to have a player like Jefferson, who could be extremely vocal about the team's offensive struggles. Instead, he has been professional and chooses his words wisely when talking about his team or speaking with the media.
The fans watching the Vikings at home in prime time didn't hold back from voicing their displeasure over Wentz's play. Watching his passes consistently sail off target was frustrating while watching the defense work so hard. He even threw a backward pass recovered by Buffalo and was credited with a fumble on that play.
Wentz was benched in the fourth quarter but finished eight-for-25, throwing the ball, completing 32% of his passes for 81 yards and two interceptions. His abysmal play resulted in an 8.9 quarterback rating
Carson Wentz had SO MANY open receivers He tried throwing an interception instead 💀 pic.twitter.com/KT77EpHbVC
This should be a wake-up call for the Vikings' front office to see whether the team can get a deal done for a quarterback before the trade deadline.
The Vikings trailed during the entire game, which led to Minnesota running the ball only 11 times with their running backs. That is a shame, since Jordan Mason gained 35 yards on six carries, an average of 5.8 yards per rushing attempt.
Mason helped out as a receiver as well. He caught two of three targets for seven yards despite frustrating quarterback play. When a passer is having as bad a night as Wentz did, having him throw the ball 25 times compared to 11 runs from running backs seems like a terrible idea.
Although he was solid as a return man, Myles Price didn't do much to help the team offensively. He had four passes thrown his way and hauled in one of them for six yards, which was, sadly. enough to be the fifth-most for Minnesota on the night.
He was called for an unnecessary false start penalty in the second quarter that pushed an offense that was already struggling to pick up a first down back five yards. He also bailed out on a fumble during a kickoff return in the first quarter. Thankfully, tight end Ben Yurosek came up with the football to prevent the turnover.
Blake Cashman got banged up during the game, but worked out his shoulder on the sidelines and returned to action. He has been an essential piece of the defense this entire season, and he continued to show his value against Buffalo.
Blake Cashman is not a happy camper as he heads to the blue medical tent. pic.twitter.com/p0y0hlsBf9
There wasn't much that Cashman didn't do in this game. He led the Vikings with 12 tackles, including one for a loss. He also defended two passes against Josh Allen and the Bills, proving he can do whatever defensive coordinator Brian Flores asks of him.
