title: One Trade the 49ers Were Wise to Stay Away From
full_text:
The NFL trade deadline has come and gone, which means the San Francisco 49ers will be content having only made two trades.
It would've been awesome if they pulled the trigger on another defensive lineman, but all in all, they did a fine job with the two trades they executed.
But it's not just about the trades they made. It's also about the trades they didn't make. The one player asset the 49ers have is quarterback Mac Jones .
The Minnesota Vikings checked in with the 49ers for Jones before finalizing a trade with the Las Vegas Raiders for Kirk Cousins. Minnesota desperately needed a quarterback.
The 49ers could've reeled in a nice haul from the Vikings had they drawn out negotiations. However, the 49ers were wise to stay away from trading Jones to Minnesota.
It would've been a poor move to give the Vikings, who are one threat to the 49ers in the NFC, a starting-caliber quarterback. That would've given the Vikings refreshed playoff hopes.
Their vaunted defense will already be a ton for the 49ers to handle. Without a quarterback, it makes defeating them in two weeks and in the playoffs, if they make it, feasible.
The 49ers have a strong path to making the Super Bowl this season. They are, without a doubt, the best team in the NFC.
If they had traded Jones to the Vikings, they would've made their path to the Super Bowl increasingly difficult. Minnesota is arguably the toughest NFC threat to the 49ers because of its defense.
All they needed was competent quarterback play to make them a serious threat. Given that the Vikings gave up a third-round pick for Cousins, that wouldn't have been worth it for the 49ers.
They likely viewed it that way as well, which is why they held a firm and high price for the Vikings for Jones. It's extremely wise of them, because the temptation to trade Jones is there.
Thankfully, they resisted it. Losing Jones hurts them much more than any positive gains from a 2027 third-round pick. Plus, if Brock Purdy ever gets hurt, they are done for.
Jones keeps them alive if Purdy were to ever miss multiple games. He did it last year. The last thing the 49ers wanna do is be their own worst enemy, which trading Jones to the Vikings would've done.
Kudos to them for not making it happen.

title: Grading 49ers NFL Trade Deadline: All Chips are Placed on DeForest Buckner
full_text:
That's a wrap on the 2026 NFL trade deadline.
It ends with the San Francisco 49ers making only two moves. The first was trading a 2027 fourth-round pick to the Indianapolis Colts to reunite with DeForest Buckner on Oct. 27.
The second trade occurred hours before the trade deadline today. Once again, the 49ers made a deal with the Colts. They sent them a 2027 sixth-round pick for veteran Keenan Allen .
One move is a significantly impactful trade, while the other doesn't move the needle that much. Still, both were necessary trades to make. That's why I am giving the 49ers a B grade for their trades.
It starts and ends with Buckner, who is carrying the 49ers' trade deadline grade. All the chips are placed on Buckner since the 49ers didn't add another impactful defensive lineman, which is fine.
Acquiring him was their blockbuster trade, and it's more than enough. Buckner is one of the best defensive tackles in the league. He's great at defending against the run and getting after the quarterback.
But it's more than what he can do on his own. His presence alone will help free everyone on the defensive line, especially with Nick Bosa back.
Not to mention that the 49ers have paired Buckner with Osa Odighizuwa, another top-10 defensive tackle. The 49ers' interior pass rush is set up to be sensational. The secondary will also benefit.
Now, it didn't look that way against the Las Vegas Raiders this past Sunday. The 49ers registered only nine pressures on Kirk Cousins and didn't sack him a single time.
However, Kyle Shanahan was pleased with what he saw from the group. I'm sure better days are ahead for this group. They're way too talented not to create chaos.
The one blemish with the 49ers at the trade deadline is that they didn't make a move for another premier defensive lineman, specifically on the edge. That would've really taken them over the top.
However, no other team acquired a premier pass rusher, which reveals there was no market for one. The only logical one was Khalil Mack, whom the Los Angeles Chargers are foolishly retaining.
The 49ers can't be criticized for not going after another pass rusher when the market has spoken. It was never an option for them, so they can't be blamed for it. It takes two to tango.
It would've been perfect if they did, but that's all it is. A theory. The same goes for wide receiver. Allen doesn't significantly impact them, but he will contribute and strengthen the depth.
The 49ers never had a shot at Garrett Wilson or any other receiver of his caliber. Going after Allen is fine, and Buckner was the perfect acquisition to address their defensive ailments .

title: 3 Most Likely Free Agency Destinations for Brandon Aiyuk After 49ers Cut Him (if they do)
full_text:
The Brandon Aiyuk Saga almost is over for the 49ers.
The trade deadline just passed, and they didn't trade him, but they did acquire Keenan Allen from the Colts for a sixth-round draft pick, which means Aiyuk will not return to the 49ers. Instead, they'll cut him, essentially giving him what he has wanted all along -- the freedom to sign wherever he wants.
NFL Insider Jordan Schultz expects Aiyuk to sign to a team's practice squad when he eventually becomes a free agent, and that should come as no surprise. Aiyuk will have to prove that he can play football and be professional for a few months before any team will offer him a serious contract.
So when will the 49ers release him? And where will he sign once he is released?
The NFL gave the 49ers a two-week roster exemption for Aiyuk because his reinstatement happened so quickly and out of the blue. Once they inevitably cut him, they'll take on massive dead cap hits this year and next, for which they'll have to make accommodations.
The 49ers could release Aiyuk now and end this circus, but that's exactly what he wants them to do. And they don't want to please him. So, don't be surprised if they keep him until the two-week roster exemption expires before releasing him.
But soon enough, Aiyuk will be a free agent. Here are three teams that are most likely to sign him.
This one is a no-brainer. All offseason, Aiyuk was acting as if he already were a member of the Commanders. His best friend from college, Jayden Daniels, is the Commanders' quarterback. Plus, Adam Peters, the Commanders' general manager, had a hand in drafting Aiyuk back when Peters was in the 49ers' front office. Aiyuk has relationships inside that organization. That's why the Commanders would appeal to him, even though they probably won't make the playoffs this season.
Davante Adams is on Injured Reserve with a torn hamstring, and Puka Nacua is expected to be placed on IR after he recently suffered MCL, PCL and turf-toe injuries. So the Rams are desperate. And Aiyuk would be cheap. And he probably would be their No. 1 wide receiver until Nacua and Adams return. And nothing would make Aiyuk happier than to face the 49ers at some point this season. Keep in mind, the 49ers and Rams are scheduled to meet at Levi's Stadium on December 13.
If Aiyuk can't wait until Dec. 13 to face the 49ers, he could sign with the Seahawks, who will face the 49ers at Levi's Stadium on Nov. 29 -- just a few days after his two-week roster exemption with San Francisco ends. The Seahawks need a wide receiver who can take pressure off Jaxon Smith-Njigba, who's carrying the offense by himself. Aiyuk at least has history with Seahawks quarterback Sam Darnold and Seahawks offensive coordinator Brian Fleury, considering all three were on the 49ers together in 2023.
One way or another, it seems delightfully possible that the 49ers will face Aiyuk at some point this season.

title: Grading the 49ers Trade for Colts WR Keenan Allen
full_text:
Reinforcement at the wide receiver position has arrived.
The San Francisco 49ers are trading a 2027 sixth-round pick to the Indianapolis Colts for wide receiver Keenan Allen , per ESPN's Adam Schefter .
After striking out on Jauan Jennings, the 49ers get their veteran receiver in Allen. He's tallied 40 catches on 58 targets for 351 yards and one touchdown this season.
That's not bad for a 34-year-old receiver, which is fitting for the 49ers to acquire him. They already rely on a bunch of players 30 or older with injury histories. Now, they'll look to rely on one more.
Adding Allen doesn't change the trajectory of the 49ers' offense much, if at all. They mainly needed depth with all of the injuries at the position.
Mike Evans will likely be out for several more games with Achilles tendinitis. Deebo Samuel might be back in Week 10 to play the Dallas Cowboys after hurting his hamstring in Week 5.
Demarcus Robinson returned, which was great, and Jordan Watkins has stepped up nicely. Still, another receiver who can contribute was needed.
The 49ers never needed to add a premier wide receiver. They knew that as well, which is why they tried to acquire Jennings from the Minnesota Vikings.
Allen can step in and help the 49ers by tallying a few catches per game, especially for quick passes and short-yardage situations. That is where Allen has thrived this year.
On throws under 10 air yards, Allen has caught 31-of-38 targets for 230 yards and one touchdown, the seventh-most yards among wide receivers, per NFL Pro.
Whenever the 49ers are within 10 yards of the end zone, that is where Allen will be targeted. The same will be true for short-yardage situations when they need a first down.
Allen will be their situational player. That is what they used Evans for. His addition can help shrink that hole a bit, which means Watkins should still receive opportunities.
Allen isn't here to kick him out of the rotation. Rather, he's here to complement Watkins. It's a cool addition for the 49ers while only giving up a sixth-round pick.
But if they were going to trade for a Colts receiver, it should've been for Josh Downs. The price to acquire him must've been too high for them, but he would've impacted the offense more than Allen.
You can't get that excited by this move, but it's nothing to criticize either.

title: What the 49ers' Trade for Keenan Allen Means About Mike Evans
full_text:
The 49ers just acknowledged that Mike Evans might not come back for a while.
They're trading a sixth-round pick to the Indianapolis Colts for veteran wide receiver Keenan Allen, who's a year older than Evans.
If the 49ers were confident that Evans could return from Achilles' tendinitis in the next week or two and stay healthy, you'd think they would have traded for someone other than Allen, because he and Evans are similar. Both are old. Both are slow. Both are big. And both can operate over the middle where Jauan Jennings used to make his money on the 49ers. Keep in mind, the 49ers tried to trade for Jennings, but he preferred to stay in Minnesota. Which means Allen was the 49ers' second choice.
Allen is 34. He's a quality route-runner and a tough possession receiver. And he's experienced, so he probably will contribute right away, as in this Sunday against the Cowboys.
Allen will catch passes for the 49ers. He won't do nothing. But when the playoffs roll around, if Evans misses any time, the 49ers probably will lose. Allen doesn't change that.
The entire offense revolves around Evans' ability to be great. He's the main reason the 49ers beat the Seahawks in Seattle last month, and he's the main reason Brock Purdy was the MVP frontrunner through the first few weeks of the season.
The 49ers need an All-Pro wide receiver to be serious Super Bowl contenders. Someone like prime Evans or prime Brandon Aiyuk. Allen is not an All-Pro talent, and his acquisition indicates that prime Evans may no longer exist and that Aiyuk will be released either today or in two weeks, when his roster exemption expires.
Everyone knows the 49ers desperately need wide receivers. If they had traded for none, the team would have taken major criticism. So they traded a mere sixth-round pick for a graybeard who won't be on the team next year.
If they were serious about insulating themselves from the possibility that Evans will miss playoff games, they would have traded for a legitimate No. 1 receiver in his prime. But the 49ers never have traded a first-round pick for a player in 10 years since Kyle Shanahan and John Lynch joined the franchise.
And why would Shanahan trade a first-round pick? He's not coaching for his job. He has no pressure to win a Super Bowl. The 49ers gave him another extension just a few months ago after losing in the divisional round of the playoffs. He merely has to maintain the status quo.
So he traded for another old player. And if the 49ers fall short, they'll blame injuries.

title: 49ers RB Christian McCaffrey Sets Historic TD Record vs. Raiders
full_text:
The San Francisco 49ers can confidently say they've got the very best out of running back Christian McCaffrey.
McCaffrey has played in San Francisco for four years now and has been extremely influential. His individual honors of winning Offensive Player of the Year and Comeback Player of the Year in 2023 and 2025, respectively, are both campaigns that should go down as some of the best for a running back.
Yet, in 2026, as McCaffrey enters his 30s, an age when running backs typically begin to experience a decline in performance, he continues to produce at an exceptionally high level. Against the Las Vegas Raiders, he made history by setting a record unlike anything seen before.
That achievement saw McCaffrey record his 37th career receiving touchdown, the most by any running back in the Super Bowl era. In doing so, he surpassed the legendary Marshall Faulk to claim the top spot on the all-time list.
It may have been just a 12-yard touchdown, but that isn't the point. The significance was that McCaffrey surpassed another of Faulk's records while also reminding San Francisco of the value he can offer as a receiving threat.
With the 49ers short on options at wide receiver, McCaffrey's ability to make an impact through the air should arguably be utilized even more so right now. The touchdown marked his 19th receiving score in a 49ers uniform and his ninth game for the franchise in which he recorded both a rushing and a receiving touchdown in the same game.
San Francisco has done a solid job of reducing McCaffrey's workload as a runner, and it's an easy cheat code for him to wrap up touchdowns from close range, which seems to be doing the job.
He has almost matched last season's touchdown tally; in fact, he's one away, and averaging 4.5 yards per carry is an improvement from last year. That's hardly surprising because he was used way too much .
His may well be starting to decline in his production, but he's still delivering. And that's the great thing about McCaffrey.
The days of 2022 and 2023 are behind him, but the 49ers are being smart with his usage, which means he's still setting truly historic records.
His usage as both a receiver and a runner makes him such an impressive player, and the 49ers trading for him only adds to the remarkable nature of what McCaffrey brings to the team. He just needs to keep producing and, barring any significant drop-off, there is every chance more records will be set, some of which could prove incredibly difficult to beat.

title: Why 49ers LB Fred Warner Deserves to Win Defensive Player of the Year
full_text:
It's only eight games into the season, but conversations surrounding San Francisco 49ers linebacker Fred Warner and his potential candidacy for Defensive Player of the Year need to start.
It's fair to say that his season-ending injury in Week 6 of 2025 left him hungry to get back on the field and prove himself again. He wasted no time at all as he became the franchise's all-time leading tackler , surpassing Patrick Willis in Week 1.
In fact, just look at the level he's performing at in 2026. So far, it's been all business from Warner : 77 total tackles, 36 solo tackles, 41 assisted tackles, half a sack, five forced fumbles, one fumble recovery and three passes defended. He has also registered 5.5 stuffs and nine stuff yards.
Those stats at the halfway point of the regular season are extremely impressive. He's producing these numbers without carrying an excessive workload, ranking 19th among linebackers in total snap counts. He's the best linebacker in the league for a reason.
Warner's first half of the season serves as a reminder of just how much the 49ers missed when he was sidelined last year. It also makes their run to the playoffs last season even more impressive, considering what they managed without such an influential defensive presence.
This year, his return has highlighted just how important he is to the team, with his leadership and production helping San Francisco to a 7-1 record. Injuries across the defence remain prevalent, but it can be argued that Warner's availability makes him the most important piece of the entire unit.
These are all the reasons to be in the conversations for the Defensive Player of the Year conversations.  An incredible stat line is one contribution, but he alone raises the standard for everyone, too.
There's plenty more football to be played before the DPOY candidates become more obvious, but favourable fixtures ahead and San Francisco's current standing in the NFC suggest the playoffs are on the horizon. One game at a time, though.
Warner has done more than enough to put his name into the DPOY conversation, but the challenge now is to maintain that momentum. There is still room for further improvement, and the opportunity to build on his already impressive numbers is there for the taking.
Given his mentality, attitude and importance to the 49ers, Warner will approach every game with the same mindset: doing everything he can to help his team prevail.

title: Kyle Shanahan Reveals Plans for 49ers' Starting Three Safeties
full_text:
The San Francisco 49ers had a tough decision to make at safety coming out of the bye. They had three players with starting capability and two starting spots to fill. Instead of making a firm decision, the 49ers decided to rotate Malik Mustapha, Marques Sigle, and Ji’Ayir Brown in their Week 9 win over the Las Vegas Raiders.
Head coach Kyle Shanahan admitted that right now he does not have a strong end goal or hope for how things will turn out in the room.
“I don't think we know what the end goal is,” said Shanahan in a conference call on Monday. “We got three good guys that are playing at a very high level. So, you just play that till it plays itself out.”
The 49ers started the season with Ji’Ayir Brown starting next to Marques Sigle. However, as Shanahan noted, that was mostly because third-year starter Malik Mustapha was hurt in the summer leading into the season.
Sigle was playing too well to bench. When Sigle got hurt, Mustapha came back. Now, he is playing too well to bench, according to Shanahan.
“Just like Malik hurt his playing time just because of injuries in training camp,” admitted Shanahan. “Then kind of the same thing happened to Sigle, who was also playing at a real high level before he was hurt. And Tig's been the one who stayed consistent and healthy. So all three of those guys have been going.”
So, according to Shanahan, the team does not plan to bench any of them as of now. They will rotate the group. So, Mustapha plays with Brown, Brown plays with Sigle, and Sigle plays with Mustapha. Shanahan said that if they separate themselves, that is great, but he does not need to see that.
“I think it's been if two separate themselves way over another, then obviously we would keep those guys out there longer,” added Shanahan.  “But we'll just keep doing it week to week, and we'll see what it ends up. But it's a pretty good problem to have.”
Shanahan appears to have no intention of making a firm decision anytime soon. Mustapha led the way with 41 snaps in Week 9. Brown had 31 and Sigle had 22. We will see if they change the rotation in Week 10 when the 49ers take on the Dallas Cowboys.

title: The NFL Just Reinstated Brandon Aiyuk and the 49ers Should Keep Him
full_text:
The Brandon Aiyuk Saga keeps getting more interesting.
Now, the NFL has reinstated him merely one day before the trade deadline, which means he almost certainly will play this season, assuming he still can play at an NFL level.  We haven't seen him on a field in two years.
In addition, the 49ers have given the 49ers a two-week roster exemption for Aiyuk, which means he can be an extra player on their team. But if he's on their roster at 1:00 pacific on Tuesday, then the 49ers will owe him a game check for the week, according to Pro Football Talk's Mike Florio.
I sincerely doubt that the 49ers intend to give Aiyuk any more money just before they trade or release him, considering they've already given him millions just to walk away from the team for a year. Why would they give him a parting gift when they hate him?
I'm guessing the 49ers would like to trade Aiyuk, and they have until tomorrow to do so. And considering his guarantees have been voided, his base salary is $1.2 million this season, and half the year is already over, he is extremely tradeable. A team could send the 49ers a seventh-round pick, pay Aiyuk roughly $500,000 for the rest of the season, and then release him after the season, or keep him if they like him.
It's possible that Aiyuk's agent, Drew Rosenhaus, already has found a team that's willing to trade for Aiyuk, and a tentative deal between that team and the 49ers is in place. That team could be the Kansas City Chiefs, who desperately need a wide receiver.
If the 49ers were to trade for a wide receiver of their own, say George Pickens or Brian Thomas Jr., then by all means, trade Aiyuk. Give him a fresh start elsewhere. Move on.
But if the 49ers don't trade for Pickens or Thomas or some other young potential No. 1 receiver, they should keep Aiyuk. They currently need a wide receiver as desperately as any team in the league. Relying on Mike Evans, Deebo Samuel, Demarcus Robinson and Jordan Watkins is not smart. Because Evans is old and breaking down, and if he misses a playoff game, the 49ers will lose.
Unless they have Aiyuk. We know he has terrific chemistry with Brock Purdy. So why just give him away for next to nothing? Why not keep him until the end of the season, and then cut him?
Let him earm some of those millions the 49ers feel he stole from them.

title: 4 Pivotal Plays That Helped the 49ers Beat the Raiders
full_text:
Defeating the Las Vegas Raiders 38-17 proved to be a little challenging for the San Francisco 49ers , as it got a tad messy in the third quarter.
That is where four pivotal plays that helped them beat the Raiders took place. Without those plays, it would have been a much closer game. Let's dive into what those four pivotal plays for the 49ers were.
JADEN SAID MINE ☝️ 📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/a5Qu8O0ACx
The Raiders opened up the second half with the ball trailing 21-10. They needed to put together a touchdown-scoring drive to get back in the game.
But on the very first play of the third quarter, rookie Jaden Dugger received a gift from Kirk Cousins. I'm not sure if Cousins tried to throw away a pass or was inaccurate, but he threw a layup to Dugger for an interception.
The rookie took it back for a 35-yard touchdown, putting the 49ers up 28-10.  Dugger will never receive an easier pick-six than the one Cousins gifted him. The first one of his career.
Trailing 28-17 at the 5:30 mark in the third quarter, the Raiders started their drive at the 49ers' 40-yard line after stopping them on fourth down.
Right off the bat, Cousins connects with his receiver Tre Tucker for an 18-yard gain. Two plays later, he hits tight end Michael Mayer for what was close to being a touchdown.
However, Upton Stout did his best Fred Warner impression by punching the ball out from Mayer. Warner would recover the fumble in the endzone, causing a touchback.
The Raiders were poised to score on that play, if not one of the next. Stout made an amazing play to deny the Raiders points, which would've made it a four-point game.
Fred Warner STOPS the QB sneak attempt @49ers 📺: FOX/FOX One pic.twitter.com/OuE87DqSfK
After the 49ers extended their lead to 35-17, the Raiders were once again putting together a promising series. They were poised to score six, but at the 12:39 mark of the fourth quarter, they were denied at the one-yard line.
Warner blew up Cousins' sneak, which should've been automatic. He perfectly timed the snap to catapult himself over the offensive line to stop Cousins.
That allowed Dre Greenlaw to push through and tackle Cousins. The play resulted in a loss of two yards, placing the 49ers in a better position to deny a touchdown again.
Two plays after Warner's super hero act, Renardo Green proved yet again that he's leaps and bounds better than he was last season. On 2nd-and-13, Cousins took a corner end zone shot for Tucker.
He thought Tucker was open, but little did he know Green baited him into the throw. As soon as Cousins began his wind up, Green bailed to the receiver and perfectly high-pointed the ball for the pick.
At that point, the game was over. The Raiders needed a touchdown with only 12 minutes left in the game. Green was playing chess, not checkers on that one.

title: Why Didn't the Buccaneers Make a Move at the Trade Deadline?
full_text:
The NFL trade deadline has come and gone, and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers have completely stayed put.
The Bucs did not make any trades, neither selling off a player nor buying from another squad. General manager Jason Licht and head coach Todd Bowles are confident in what they have — at least including the cost of giving up or trading for a player, anyway — as the pair try to win another NFC South title.
That being said, the Bucs are 3-6 and started the season 0-4 — so why stay put at the deadline? To keep it simple, it's a little complicated.
To go more in depth, the Buccaneers were in a sort of trade limbo.
The Bucs were not good enough at the deadline to buy. There are a lot of problems with this team's offense, from the coaching to the talent, and an extra wide receiver or tight end probably wouldn't fix things. That would also require giving up draft capital — a luxury for teams competing, not for teams with a losing record like the Bucs.
At the same time, though, Tampa Bay isn't quite bad enough to sell. The Bucs are still just a half a game out of the NFC South (and will likely be a game back once the Saints and Panthers play), so they're in contention to win the division, as crazy as it seems.
Selling off a player like Vita Vea or Antoine Winfield Jr. may seem appealing for the long term future, but Bowles and Licht need to win now. To do that, they need all the players they can muster, including the team's aging stars on the roster.
There's also the fact that the Bucs rarely trade in season at all. Licht has done it just once, trading for Jets defensive tackle Steve McLendon and giving up a sixth-round pick. Licht highly values draft capital — perhaps more than any other GM in football — and he isn't interested in shuffling around his players while the season is ongoing.
The Bucs stayed put at the deadline. Now, they have to prove that it was a good idea by winning the division and making the playoffs.

title: Buccaneers Bye Week Update: What Are Tampa Bay's Playoff Chances?
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers haven't had the season they wanted.
They started off 0-4, and while they've strung together some wins, they remain just 3-6 heading into their bye week. Normally, that would just about disqualify any team from making the playoffs, but the NFC South is special (derogatory).
As it stands, every team in the NFC South has three wins. The Bucs and the Falcons are 3-6, while the Panthers and the Saints, both of whom have had their bye weeks, are 3-5. The Bucs remain half a game out of NFC South contention, and as the Panthers and Saints play each other, Tampa Bay will likely become one game out of first after Sunday's NFL action.
Despite Tampa Bay's early string of losses and an offense that remains one of the league's worst through the air, the odds are still in their favor to win the division and make the playoffs.
Per The Athletic's playoff simulator , the Bucs still have the best chance to win the NFC South.
The Athletic gives the Bucs a 37% chance to win the NFC South (and a 38% chance to make the playoffs). That's pretty low, but no one else in the division is higher — The Falcons and Panthers both have a 23% chance to make the playoffs, and the Saints have a 16% chance to win the NFC South.
Tampa Bay has largely been kept alive by its weak division, and it likely has the best chance to win that division due to its current division record. The Bucs beat both the Panthers and the Falcons once this year (all while throwing the football just 11 times).
With those two wins already under their belt, they have the best chance to win the division by picking up more of those wins in their next four divisional games — even if they drop other games outside of the NFC South.
The Bucs are on bye while the Panthers and Saints play each other. The Falcons will have a tough task in Week 10 when they host the Kansas City Chiefs at home.

title: Buccaneers Lineman Calls Out Bears’ Jeffery Simmons for Dirty Play
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers dropped their Sunday Night Football game to the Chicago Bears 27-24, and with that, they were unable to take the outright lead in the NFC South.
The story of the game was Tampa Bay's considerable number of turnovers on defense, getting five off the Bears, and considerable ineptitude on offense. The Bucs only scored 10 points off of five turnovers, and quarterback Baker Mayfield even threw a pick-six that saw Chicago add seven points to the board.
One of the biggest challenges the Bucs faced was Bears defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons, who Chicago acquired right before the trade deadline. But when asked about him after the game, Bucs tackle Luke Goedeke said that some aspects of Simmons' tool kit have "no place" in the game.
Goedeke told ESPN writer Kalyn Kahler that he thought Simmons was both holding too much and also launching himself at his head at various points in the game.
“I mean, you’re holding me on one, you came right at my head,” Goedeke said . “I mean, that’s always fun. He’s known for it on pass pro, just holding the tackle so that the DE can run free, so I got that twice. So that’s always a good one. But, yeah, just kind of going back and forth. I mean, respect the guy, but some of the stuff he can really take out of his game. It’s just kind of old, to be honest.”
Goedeke elaborated further, saying that the tactics Simmons used during the matchup have no "place in the game".
"There's no reason to just come out on a TE and just drill a tackle in the side of the head," Goedeke said. "[There's] really not a place in the game for that, to be honest with you."
This wasn't the only grievance that the Bucs had with the Bears. Quarterback Baker Mayfield also told reporters that the Bears were calling out Tampa Bay's snap counts during the matchup, which should have been enforced as a penalty if that claim were true.
Bucs QB Baker Mayfield says he doesn’t know what went into the O-line having five false starts Sunday night, though he says the last one came about because the Bears were “barking out the cadence,” which you can’t do. Acknowledges that it’s tough for the refs to call that one,… pic.twitter.com/cMsobPlg1y
Goedeke also isn't even the first Bucs lineman who has had some beef with Simmons. When the Bucs and the Tennessee Titans held joint practice together in 2025, and during that practice, lineman Cody Mauch got into with Simmons after a rep against him.
It’s getting chippy early between Bucs-Titans 👀 Cody Mauch and Jeffery Simmons getting after it with one another leading to both teams having some words. I’ve missed you football. pic.twitter.com/bVCXe9btHd
Despite all of this, though, the Bucs lost that game against the Bears — and their offense floundered while doing so. Tampa Bay has plenty it needs to figure out over the bye week, and it will certainly need to fix some of its offensive woes when it faces off against the Detroit Lions in Week 11.
The Bucs are 3-6 and half a game out of the NFC South lead. They'll have to string together some wins to take the NFC South, and to do that, the offense simply must be better.

title: Grading Every Buccaneers Position Group After Loss to Bears
full_text:
CHICAGO — Another primetime game for the Bucs in the books — but this time, they couldn’t come away with a win.
The Chicago Bears' offense had some sloppy play throughout, with Caleb Williams having a rough night with four interceptions, but poor execution offensively by the Buccaneers meant that they never could really take advantage.
Let’s take a deep dive into each position group and give our report cards out to each one of them. Some of them are not too bad, but some are not too pretty.
It wasn’t a great game from Baker Mayfield. Two interceptions, some off throws, holding onto the ball too late — it just felt like a mess at times. It didn’t help that some of his playmakers couldn’t catch and execute on their own end, either.
Mayfield admitted after the game that turnovers are something he has to clean up, certainly when one of them went straight for six points for the Bears. This offense has to once again turn it around and, it starts with QB1.
Bucky Irving is playing at phenomenal level right now. He's making guys miss, he's hard to tackle and he fights for every extra yard. He’s been the bright spot of this team and the top weapon offensively for weeks. Kenny Gainwell had a big 44-yard play that helped the Bucs get into the red zone.
With solid blocking up front, I thought both running backs took advantage of the holes when they were there.
This group has been a major letdown going into this season.
Injuries certainly aren’t helping, but when the wideouts are on the field, simple catches and important ones alike are being dropped. Ted Hurst got benched after his drop Sunday night. Tez Johnson had two drops, too, but stayed in the game because of his experience.
This group has to do better mixed in with better play from QB1.
This group isn’t much of a threat in the passing game, and I don’t know if it’ll ever be under Zac Robinson. For the most part, the blocking has been the best part of this unit.
There were some targets to Cade Otton in this game, but Mayfield couldn’t hit him on the throws. Blocking surely helps, but the pass-game threat needs to show life here soon.
This unit did the best they could with how well Chicago’s front seven has been playing as of late, certainly with the addition of Jeffery Simmons.
There were holes for Irving and Gainwell and a good amount time for Mayfield in the pocket. Penalties hurt this grade a tad, but overall, play-wise, not too shabby.
Interior Defensive Line: B
I really liked what I saw from this room along with the pass rush off the edge. They were able to get movement up front and get Williams moving into uncomfortable positions. This certainly helped with the four interceptions on the night in the secondary.
For the most part, this group was finding a groove all throughout the night.
Without having Yaya Diaby in the mix, David Walker, Anthony Nelson and Al-Quadin Muhammad had to step up. Luckily, once again, Rueben Bain Jr. continues to grow. He had a huge play tackling Luther Burden III and causing a fumble, which was recovered by safety Ifeatu Melifonwu.
There were a few plays where things went sideways for Alex Anzalone and Josiah Trotter. I noticed from the press box that Anzalone had to call out Trotter on a missed gap assignment that allowed the Bears to get a first down.
Eye discipline was good, though, with Trotter having a few plays rushing after Williams and not allowing for easy dump-offs. Anzalone grabbed his third interception of the season after having two last week against the Falcons.
It wasn’t a pretty start for the cornerback room, primarily for Zyon McCollum, giving up a touchdown and surrendering wide-open Bears players. He turned around his play by grabbing two interceptions, reaching a career season high of four. McCollum's tackling stood out as well, and he's looked strong in that department all season.
Jacob Parrish tipped a ball off Williams' and helped Anzalone have a takeaway, giving Tampa Bay's offense great field position.
Antoine Winfield Jr. left the game fairly early with an ankle injury after colliding with Calijah Kancey on a tackle. Tykee Smith grabbed an interception, and overall, the unit did fine with the help of the Bucs’ pass rush. Melifonwu picked up a fumble in Bears’ territory, allowing Tampa Bay to tie the game.
Overall, this unit played well.
The kickoff team almost gave up a touchdown, but luckily a holding penalty was called, killing that chance. Kevin Knowles, primarily a gunner on punt teams, had impressive plays throughout the game. He was a fantastic addition right before the season began from Kansas City. Chase McLaughlin is Chase McLaughlin — always a trusted source.

title: Overreactions From Buccaneers' Close Loss to Bears
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers kept it close against the Chicago Bears, but in the end, they weren't able to get a big win in the Windy City.
The Bucs fell to the Bears 27-24 on Sunday Night Football, dropping them to 3-6. It was a game where Tampa Bay's defense dominated once again, netting five turnovers and holding Chicago's offense at bay for most of the game, but the Bucs were unable to get anything going on offense and they couldn't get the win as a result.
As always, we're giving our overreactions to this matchup — here's how we're feeling after Tampa Bay's loss:
The Buccaneers' offense is a mess almost everywhere (we'll talk more about that later). But perhaps the most pressing need the team has is at wide receiver, and that showed itself in a big way on Sunday night.
Tampa Bay's wide receiver corps had numerous drops on the night — rookie Ted Hurst was benched because he had one, and Tez Johnson had two drops across the night. Once again, tight end Cade Otton dominated the target share with eight of them, and outside of a huge bomb to Johnson that saw him net 76 yards on the night, no other Bucs receiver had over 40.
Chris Godwin remains an ineffective part of the offense despite being on a $22 million deal. Emeka Egbuka was drafted by the Bucs in the first round last year, and he has not looked like a WR1.
The Bucs really, really feel the absence of Mike Evans. They need a definitive WR1 on the team, and they need it badly if the passing game is to repair itself in future seasons.
But for right now, though...
The Bucs have had a strong run game with Bucky Irving and Kenny Gainwell, but that cannot carry the entire offense. The Bears proved that.
Offensive coordinator Zac Robinson's passing schemes have struggled all year, and they've continued to flounder when they've actually been needed. The aforementioned wide receiver issue continues to persist, and on top of all that, Tampa Bay's quarterback hasn't played up to standard at all.
Baker Mayfield is making $55 million a year on his extension, but his pressure-to-sack ratio is just under 32% (that's bad) and he threw a backbreaking interception that went for a pick-six, giving the Bears seven points in a game where the defense was holding them at bay. Mayfield has thrown three touchdowns and four interceptions, and his 32.4 QBR is 30th in the NFL.
The Bucs need the passing game to thrive. It doesn't look like there's a way it gets any better this season, and Tampa Bay will continue to lose games as a result.
Despite all that, though? This defense is elite. They generate more turnovers than anyone else in the NFL, they remain stout against the run and the pass, and they have multiple All-Pro-level players on the team this year who are showing out.
That will be enough to win the NFC South. The Carolina Panthers, Atlanta Falcons and New Orleans Saints don't have offenses half as potent as the Bears do, and Tampa Bay should muster enough wins in their next four NFC South matchups to win the division and make the playoffs.
The team isn't good enough to beat good teams and win a playoff game. But they are good enough to win the division and get there.
And if that happens, the Bucs have an interesting question to ask — What happens next?

title: The Good, Bad and Ugly From Buccaneers' 27-24 Loss to Bears
full_text:
Following two consecutive victories for the first time in over a year, the Tampa Bay Buccaneers finally had a little bit of momentum heading into their second primetime game of the 2026 NFL season.
It didn't take long for the Chicago Bears' to squander that momentum, though, as the Bears jumped out to an early 14-0 lead in front of their raucous home crowd at Soldier Field. Despite their offensive struggles in the first half, the Bucs managed to grind their way back into the game thanks to a barrage of splash plays from the defense.
Although the Buccaneers did manage to tie the game with less than three minutes remaining, that was simply too much time to give Ben Johnson's offense, and the Bears won the game by a final score of 27-24.
Let's take a closer look at the good, the bad and the ugly that we saw in this Week 9 matchup between the Buccaneers and Bears .
The rate at which the Buccaneers are turning over their opponents is getting outlandish.
Todd Bowles' defense has generated 13 turnovers over their last three games (yes, you read that correctly). And although producing turnovers at this rate is certainly not sustainable, it sure is fun to watch.
Four of the five Bucs' turnovers on Sunday came via interception, with Tykee Smith providing the first, Zyon McCollum the next two and Alex Anzalone the fourth. The fifth and final turnover came when Rueben Bain Jr. rocked Luther Burden and forced a fumble, which the Bucs recovered deep in Chicago territory.
A defense predicated on consistent pressure and splash plays is how Bowles has always envisioned his defense performing in his dreams, but unfortunately, his worst nightmare appears every time his offense takes the field.
Bucky Irving remains the Buccaneers' most threatening offensive player. Despite a loaded box for much of the game and an entire defensive game plan designed around stopping him, Irving was elusive, relentless and highly productive against a really strong Bears defense.
Irving rushed for 97 yards and two touchdowns to go along with an additional 28 yards through the air on 4 receptions. Even with a non-existent pass game to take the pressure off, Irving refuses to be denied as a ball carrier, and he continues to establish himself as one of the NFL's best all-around running backs.
Mayfield certainly struggled in this football game, but the thumb injury that forced him to miss three games just last month did not appear to limit his ability to throw the football on Sunday.
Baker Mayfield drops it right in the bucket to Tez Johnson 🎯 TBvsCHI on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/XUsnnc2R4S
As encouraging as it was to see Mayfield put some zip on his passes again, his mental processing cost him dearly in this contest.
Mayfield appeared indecisive at times throughout the game and threw two costly interceptions. Unfortunately, this has been the story for Mayfield all season long. And though his injuries have certainly played a role in his poor performance, the vast majority of the issues stem from what's going on between his ears.
Having recently suffered a fractured rib in Week 4 vs. the Packers, which sidelined him for three games, the Bucs were excited to have their star safety, Antoine Winfield Jr., back in the lineup. Unfortunately, Winfield was forced to leave the game on Sunday night after suffering a right ankle injury.
Despite an incredible all-around performance by Bowles' defense, it was a brutal coverage bust on second and long with less than a minute left in the game that allowed Wilson to hit Colston Loveland for a 38-yard gain, ultimately sealing the Bucs' fate.
They forgot about Colston Loveland. pic.twitter.com/mv1rhCXI9a
This headline does not refer to the game of the Buccaneers vs. the Bears, but rather the Buccaneers' offense vs. the Buccaneers' defense.
While Tampa Bay's defense continues to play out of it's mind, the offense simply can't get out of it's own way. It's an incredible contrast between one unit that looks like one of the league's best and the other, which looks like it would have trouble putting up points in the CFL.
What a vicious cycle this game has been. The Bucs’ defense continues to inject life back into this football team while the offense continues to hang them out to dry. Around and around we go.
Although this disheartening dichotomy has plagued the Bucs for most of the season, it was especially evident during Sunday's loss to the Bears, where despite getting five turnovers from the defense, the Buccaneers' offense was only able to generate 10 total points off of those turnovers.

title: Winners and Losers From Buccaneers' Sunday Night Football Loss to Bears
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers defense tried its hardest, but the Bucs offense could not lead the team to a victory on Sunday Night Football.
The Bucs lost their game against the Chicago Bears 27-24 on Sunday, dropping to 3-6. The Bucs' defense managed five turnovers, but the offense got just 10 total points off those turnovers and failed to capitalize on the defense's great game.
Here are our winners and losers for Tampa Bay after this crucial matchup...
It was almost another 100-yard performance for Bucky Irving, but he's a winner tonight for another reason.
Irving ran in a touchdown on Tampa Bay's opening drive of the second half. It was his sixth rushing touchdown of the year, but it was also a touchdown in his hometown of Chicago — this was Irving's first time playing back home, and he gave his family something to remember.
He'll probably never forget scoring a touchdown at Soldier Field, just as he probably dreamed of his whole life growing up. And then after that? He scored again to tie the game with just under three minutes left, cementing this performance as a great one for him.
McCollum had a tough start to his game on Sunday night, getting picked on by Rome Odunze. That didn't last long.
McCollum netted two picks on Caleb Williams across the course of the day. Those turnovers didn't amount to anything (just three points), but that wasn't his fault — he recovered and got the turnovers he need to generate to keep the Bucs in the game.
McCollum has been having an All-Pro year this year, and he kept up the good work on Sunday night. It wasn't enough to win, but that's largely because of the offense and how they handled the game after his turnovers.
Smith was just about everywhere on Sunday night.
He had six total tackles and three solo tackles, and he also had the first interception on the night that kicked off the party. He was one of Tampa Bay's best defensive players, and he really stepped up in the absence of Antoine Winfield Jr. after Winfield went out with an ankle injury.
The Bucs' entire defense balled out, but Smith and McCollum really shined in comparison to the rest.
Bowles' decision-making was costly in this matchup, and it could have cost him the game.
The first questionable decision came on a fourth-and-four at Chicago's four with 14:07 to go in the second. Bowles elected to kick a field goal, but ESPN's analytics model gave the team an extra two percent chance of winning had they gone for it instead of settling for three.
Then, at the end of the half, Bowles elected to kick a field goal instead of trying to score from inside the five with three seconds left. That put Tampa Bay down 17-6 at the half, and the Bucs really could have used those extra points in a tight, tight game against the Bears.
Bowles' defense largely did its job by generating turnovers. But Bowles had to be better with game management, and he wasn't good enough on Sunday.
The last two weeks were easy-going for offensive coordinator Zac Robinson. That wasn't the case on Sunday night, and the offense suffered for it.
Robinson seemed far too comfortable running the ball as a matter of routine as opposed to effectiveness. He put the offense in bad positions early on in the game, and when he had to help facilitate the passing game, he wasn't able to scheme it well enough to help quarterback Baker Mayfield push the ball downfield.
Additionally, the Bucs' offensive line suffered from multiple false starts — that's a problem that the team has been battling all year, and a big part of that is on Robinson, too.
Suddenly, when the Bucs need to throw, Robinson's offense is back to struggling. That's an issue the Bucs are really going to have to face.
It was Baker Mayfield's first game since returning from injury where he really had to throw the football, and it didn't go the way he'd hoped.
Mayfield threw two picks on the night, with one of them going back the other way for a Bears score. The Bucs had four turnovers and, partially due to his efforts, only scored three points off of them.
Mayfield didn't take care of the football, and it was costly. Mayfield has yet to have a great game this year, and that's hurting the offense just as much as Robinson's playcalling has.

title: Buccaneers Could Make Big Step Toward Playoffs With Win vs. Bears
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers and the Chicago Bears are set to face off against each other on Sunday Night Football. It'll be a tough matchup for the Bucs, as the Bears are 6-2 and considered to be Super Bowl contenders at this stage of the season.
The Bucs have an excellent defense, however — the best in the league by numerous advanced metrics — and they've developed a running game that has punished teams in the NFC South, the Carolina Panthers and the Atlanta Falcons, in recent weeks.
It's going to be hard to beat the Bears. But after the New Orleans Saints beat the Cleveland Browns in overtime on Sunday afternoon, the NFC South is in a unique scenario, and the Bucs can take advantage.
The Buccaneers are currently involved in a complete four-way tie for first in the NFC South. Every team in the division has three wins, and the Bucs have yet to play until Sunday night.
At the moment, the Bucs lead the division. They've played one more game than the Panthers, but because the Bucs play late, they've played the same number of games until 8:20 p.m. tonight. The Bucs have the tiebreaker win over the Panthers and have also beaten the Falcons for two NFC South wins, so they're up in front in the four-way tiebreaker.
The good news for the Bucs? If they beat the Bears on Sunday night, they'll move to 4-5 — that would be the best record in the NFC South by itself, and the Bucs would move into sole possession of first place.
If the Bucs don't win, though, the news isn't all too bad. Tampa Bay will be 3-6, and every NFC South team will have the same number of wins. The Panthers and Saints will have one less loss, though, because both have had their bye week already, so the Bucs would remain half a game out of the NFC South lead behind the Panthers.
Tampa Bay has its bye week next week. As a result, the Falcons, Saints and Panthers could take possession of first place while the Bucs take the week off in Week 10.
Tampa Bay plays the Bears in Soldier Field at 8:20 p.m. on Sunday night. A win would be huge, but if the Bucs drop this game to a Super Bowl contender, they're still in shape to fight for the South.

title: Sunday Night Football Injury Update: Will Emeka Egbuka Play for Buccaneers?
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers have one of the biggest challenges of the year ahead of them when they play the Chicago Bears on the road. The Bears are 6-2 and a Super Bowl contender — the Bucs are 3-5 and, despite the record, still very much in the hunt for the NFC South,
The Bucs will want every player they can muster to help beat Chicago. There's one player they won't have for certain, as edge rusher Yaya Diaby sprained his MCL last week against the Atlanta Falcons and was ruled out for this contest.
One other player was ruled questionable, though. Wideout Emeka Egbuka has missed the last two games of the year with a foot injury, and he practiced in full on Thursday and Friday. So will he play for the Bucs on Sunday? Or will their passing offense have to make do without him?
The NFL's Ian Rapoport reported on Sunday that Egbuka is set to play against the Bears on Sunday night.
#Bucs WR Emeka Egbuka (foot) is playing today after being listed as questionable. He missed Wednesday but was a full participant after that.
The move is expected. Egbuka has been recovering from both a concussion and a foot injury these past two weeks — he cleared concussion protocol last week, but his foot injury lingered. Now that he's practiced two days in full, he's definitely set to play against the Bears in a game where the Bucs need him.
Egbuka hasn't been the leading wide receiver the Bucs have perhaps hoped this year, netting 28 receptions for 240 yards and two touchdowns, but the entire passing game has struggled so far for Tampa Bay.
Egbuka will still be a good weapon for Tampa Bay, as they'll need to pass the ball to beat the Bears after throwing just 14 total passes in the last two weeks of play. Quarterback Baker Mayfield should get his first real test at throwing the ball after dislocating his thumb in Week 3 against the Minnesota Vikings.
The Bucs play the Bears in Soldier Field at 8:20 p.m. on Sunday night. When they do, they'll have their first-round pick from 2025 at their disposal.

title: One Major Question Could Define the Bucs' Entire Night Against Bears
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers' defense has stepped it up in recent weeks, particularly along the defensive front. And they will once again need that same presence in Week 9 as they will face one of the premier offenses in the league — the Chicago Bears.
The Bucs' pass rush has ramped it up as of late, exploding for 10 sacks over their past three games after a quiet start to the year. Through eight games, they have 23 sacks this season.
Tampa's resurgence in creating pressure has been a blessing for them, but they will need to continue that when they face the Bears' elite offense led by star quarterback Caleb Williams.
Todd Bowles' defense ranks near the top of the league when it comes to bringing the blitz, sending extra rushers over 40% of the time. The Bucs' front seven will have to create pressure with just four, but bringing an extra guy has proven to work, given how well the secondary has played.
If they are unable to get pressure and get home, it will allow Williams plenty of time to find his open targets in Luther Burden III, Rome Odunze and Colston Loveland. The Bears are a top-three team in the NFL with time to throw (3+ seconds to throw).
Tampa Bay hasn't relied on one star to get home for sacks this year, rather relying on its depth of coordinated packages of Yaya Diaby, Rueben Bain Jr., David Walker, Al-Quadin Muhammad and Anthony Nelson.
Chicago has been vulnerable to sacks on the season when interior gaps collapse, allowing 19 on the season. If the Bucs' interior defensive line of Vita Vea and Calijah Kancey can continue getting push up the middle, it will force Williams off his spot, ultimately disrupting his timing within passing concepts.
With the Bucs' offense being run-dependent, the defense has carried the load of keeping the game close and low-scoring. If the pass rush isn't able to stop the high-flying offense of Chicago, it will force Baker Mayfield to throw the ball.
If Tampa Bay hopes to keep the game close and come away with a statement victory, the pass rush must get home to keep Williams out of his comfort zone.

title: 3 Major Winners, and 2 Losers, From Titans' Defense-Heavy Trade Deadline
full_text:
The trade deadline has officially come and gone for the Tennessee Titans. It was both less eventful than expected and just as impactful as any fan could've hoped it would be.
Defensive studs Jeffery Simmons and Amani Hooker both got moved, while trade suspects Tony Pollard and Calvin Ridley remained in the baby blue and red. It was a defense-heavy deadline with much to talk about for Tennessee moving forward.
Here, we've put together three of the Titans' biggest winners after the cutoff, as well as two losers. Let's dive in to the latter-half outlook for Tennessee after today's shakeups.
According to Jordan Schultz, one of the main reasons Tennessee ending up holding on to Tony Pollard was due to how important he is to Cam Ward's development. As a result of Pollard staying put, Ward is a big winner at the deadline.
Tennessee retaining a piece for the primary reason that he's helpful at Ward's side is a huge sign of confidence in the QB. Ward's Week 8 breakout against the Cincinnati Bengals continues to pay dividends for the progression of his role in the Titans' rebuild.
If you weren't already sure that the Titans continue to believe in Ward as "the guy" moving forward, Pollard being kept should be the period on the end of the sentence.
The scale of Tennessee's rebuild asks (unsurprisingly) for a little more patience from Titans fans. That's like asking for more water from the Grand Canyon.
Jokes aside, the Titans' front office clearly prioritized the new few drafts at the deadline. This is a franchise fully committed to turning the page. With Robert Saleh caught in between a new rebuild and trying to salvage an old one, things look questionable for the current head coach.
It doesn't help that Tennessee traded away arguably Saleh's two best defenders in the process of fast-tracking their rebuild. The defensive specialist has been left to drift without two anchors in his unit, and he may be expected to win sooner than this roster is ready to do so.
Saleh still has plenty of time, but the two trades Tennessee made both make a dent in his armor. The team's 1-7 record obviously doesn't help.
On the flip side from Saleh, general manager Mike Borgonzi is heavily equipped with the assets he needs to continue to hit the mark in the NFL Draft. He doesn't have a flawless record, but WR Carnell Tate and LB Anthony Hill Jr. go down as massive hits.
Now, Borgonzi is set up to capitalize on a vision he had when the Titans hired him in 2025. Mike Herndon pointed out that Borgonzi wanted 12 top-100 picks over a three-year period of time. He's traded this team into a position to accomplish that.
Where those picks end up still matter, and Borgonzi doesn't have infinite slack either. But he goes down as a winner today due to the newly-acquired capital he'll have to build this franchise into a successful one in time.
Naturally, with Pollard sticking around for the rest of his contract year, backup RB Tyjae Spears goes down as a loser today. He came into the 2026 campaign as a clear successor to Pollard's leading role, and has since been outplayed to the point that such a role isn't set for him even when Pollard leaves.
Had Pollard been moved, we could have seen Spears inherit the RB1 spot on a short-term basis with the ability to prove himself afterward. Instead, between the Titans' picks and rookie Nick Singleton behind him, Spears appears to be an afterthought in Brian Daboll's offense.
If he can stay healthy and play well in his limited minutes, Spears may have a chance to reclaim a complimentary role. But with only nine games remaining, he'll go down as a loser at the deadline today.
S Kevin Winston Jr. comes up as our final winner due to the expanded role he'll take on in the secondary with Hooker gone. Winston still has plenty to prove in his second year with the Titans, but he'll get the opportunity to do just that from this point forward.
Winston is recently healthy after missing scattered time with shoulder and quadriceps issues. His ability to play up and stop the run has thus far defined a quiet early tenure in Nashville. The uptick in snaps likely to come for Winston click in with the team's overarching commitment to a younger roster.
Up to now on the season (in six games played) Winston has 51 total tackles and one fumble recovery.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Grading the Titans’ Trade Deadline: 2 Best Defenders Dealt, Calvin Ridley Somehow Stays Put
full_text:
The 2026 NFL trade deadline is officially over, and the Tennessee Titans are one of the prominent teams that sold high on their veteran talent.
Tennessee started by trading All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons and a 2028 fifth-round pick to the Chicago Bears on October 29. In return, the Titans received a 2027 first- and fourth-round pick , and a 2028 first-round selection.
However, that wasn't the final trade made by general manager Mike Borgonzi. On Tuesday, the Titans shipped off safety Amani Hooker and a 2027 fifth-round pick to the Buffalo Bills for a 2027 second-round pick.
Despite running back Tony Pollard and wide receiver Calvin Ridley also being in trade rumors , both ended up staying put, while Simmons and Hooker are elsewhere. With the deadline now in the books, let's grade all of the Titans' major decisions.
Though cutting ties with a franchise legend like Simmons is a tough pill to swallow , Tennessee received a solid return, and if the front office can hit on the draft picks, the trade will end up laying a nice foundation for the future.
Additionally, the deal makes a lot of sense for Simmons, who will now compete for a championship with the Bears. The four-time Pro Bowler may be the missing piece that elevates Chicago into NFC title favorites.
Hooker is tied for the league lead in interceptions with five and is playing the best football of his career. As a result, Tennessee is selling high on the veteran safety, trading him to a premier AFC contender in the Bills.
By acquiring a second-round pick for Hooker, the Titans now have five projected top-100 picks in April's draft, per Tankathon. Tennessee is conducting its rebuild the right way, and paving the path for a bright future.
According to NFL insider Jordan Schultz, the Denver Broncos and New York Giants were interested in trading for Pollard . However, the Titans decided to retain the 29-year-old running back, which is an understandable move.
Pollard is critical to quarterback Cam Ward's development and has been the engine of Brian Daboll's offense this season. Though Pollard will be a free agent in the spring and Tennessee could've added additional 2027 picks for his services, retaining him to keep the offense afloat and help Ward's progression is a logical course of action.
Ridley has been a complete non-factor for the Titans in 2026, tallying just six receptions for 91 yards in seven games so far. The 31-year-old no longer fits into Tennessee's long-term plans, but his veteran experience and past production could have made a trade possible.
But in the end, Ridley is staying put. His recent incident at the Nashville International Airport may have played a part in rival teams losing trade interest, but Tennessee likely would've only gotten a sixth- or seventh-round pick in return for the former 1,000-yard receiver anyway.
We'll see whether Ridley is able to turn it around in the final nine games, but it's still a bit disappointing that the Titans couldn't move on from him before the deadline.

title: Titans Trade Amani Hooker: What Defensive Fire Sale Means for Robert Saleh's Future in Tennessee
full_text:
We've said it time and time again prior to the NFL trade deadline: Expect the unexpected, and nobody gets hurt. The Tennessee Titans moving franchise legend Jeffery Simmons prior to Week 8 should've signaled that nothing was sacred for this 1-7 team in their current state.
Today, the Titans proved that off-the-cuff mindset once more. After reports all week that suggested Tennessee wouldn't move S Amani Hooker, Tom Pelissero delivered the news that the team had done just that. Hooker is a Buffalo Bill, and the Titans are one second-rounder. Tennessee sent a fifth in return.
On the surface, this is the continuation of a defensive fire sale lit by moving Simmons; another sign of the times that Tennessee is ready to hit the rebuild button once again and go full-force with young talent over the next few years of football.
But there's an obvious catch. Robert Saleh is in his first year as head coach, and was meant to not only usher in a better defense, but a better result. The Titans' aforementioned record is evidence that the latter has been a failure up to this point.
With Simmons and Hooker now both gone, what is being said about Saleh's future in Nashville?
Moving off Simmons was one thing, but at the price of two first-round picks (as well as a fourth), it would've been hard to blame Tennessee for turning that offer down. It's a future-changing haul.
Hooker's return is also impressive, but it isn't quite as mind-boggling as what Simmons brought in. On top of that, Hooker - who was drafted by the Titans alongside Simmons in 2019 - was very clearly the team's resident, remaining leader with Simmons gone.
Saleh's own defensive unit is now the team's most listless. DE Jacob Martin, who was brought in this offseason, is about the only nationally-relevant playmaker remaining therein. Question marks are still floating over the heads of CB Alontae Taylor, DL John Franklin-Myers, and others.
That means there's a question mark over Saleh's own head, too. Clearly, the Titans believe in his vision on the sidelines to some degree. But that same front office has already proven their ability to cull out a coach that isn't working. Brian Callahan was fired in less than a season and a half.
Maybe the Titans received two deals that they simply couldn't refuse, and things are progressing as normal for Saleh up to this point. However, two trades within his unit (arguably his two best players), seems to signal that there's some reaching going on over Saleh's head.
He'll undoubtedly have the rest of this season and some of the 2027 campaign to prove himself, but the more trades the Titans make - especially on defense - the clearer it becomes that there's an effort being made to preserve this franchise in the far future.
Another reset in every capacity isn't out of the question, and if any judgement can be gleaned about Saleh from these moves, it's that he's about as safe as Callahan was if Tennessee keeps losing.
