title: LIVE: Titans NFL Trade Deadline Tracker With Trades, Rumors, and Updated News
full_text:
We're now just a little over four hours out from the NFL trade deadline. At this point, we've exhausted our predictive brains and are waiting on the Tennessee Titans to either make a move or stand pat when the 3:00 PM CT cutoff strikes.
As of this morning, our latest update came in the form of a confirmation from Jordan Schultz: Tennessee is not looking to move RB Tony Pollard. He's become almost too crucial to Cam Ward and the offense to be sent packing at the midway point this season.
However, it's worth noting that Albert Breer said it would take "at least a fourth-rounder, and maybe a third" to get Pollard out of Nashville. Breer also admitted that Tennessee "won't give him away," but a different source setting a price there is notable.
If the Colts ultimately refuse to trade Jonathan Taylor, Pollard's value could skyrocket at the buzzer. Past Pollard, the Titans' outlook is mostly up in the air. WR Calvin Ridley still looks like a definite possibility, while S Amani Hooker also appears to be in the currently safe camp with Pollard.
That trio set aside, DE Jermaine Johnson is a name fans should keep an eye on. There has been minimal noise surrounding Johnson, but he's in the final year of his contract and could be argued as an asset worth moving for the Titans to stack more draft capital. LB Cody Barton should be tabbed for similar reasons.
It's straw-grasping from there. We'll keep you looped in as news comes in today, Titans fans. Check back here for the latest.
(12:21 PM) Could Mitch Trubisky be a surprise candidate for the Vikings?
Adam Schefter reported that the Vikings have "begun making calls" earlier today in search of a QB. With Kyler Murray injured and Carson Wentz leading the team to an underwhelming loss in primetime last night, could Mitch Trubisky be a sneaky option?
The Titans have already made it clear that Cam Ward is the guy from here on out; if something were to happen that Ward loses his starting gig next season, it isn't like Trubisky would then step into the starting spotlight for the long haul.
Trubisky is a veteran QB who has been biding time on Tennessee's bench all season. In the midst of today's ongoing dry spell of news, it's worth keeping a possibility like this in the back of our minds. If Minnesota goes shopping, a multi-year signal caller with no current shot at playing is prime trade material.
The Titans could realistically make this happen, even if Trubisky's name has yet to come up.
(12:38 PM) Keenan Allen Trade Potentially Sets Price for Calvin Ridley
Per Adam Schefter and Ian Rapoport, the Colts are sending WR Keenan Allen to the San Francisco 49ers for a sixth-round pick.
For those keeping an eye on Ridley's market, the Titans' ask of a sixth-rounder for Ridley appears to be right on the money, if not a little expensive now given Allen's superior production. With the 49ers off the board for Ridley, the Chiefs and Steelers are two teams to watch closely.
The deadline is about two hours out now. A move like this could light the fuse for more momentum at the WR position, and Ridley now even more centered in that pool of players.
(1:14 PM) Titans Trade S Amani Hooker to Bills for second and fifth-round pick
Per Tom Pelissero, the Titans have traded S Amani Hooker to the Buffalo Bills. Tennessee will reportedly return a second-round pick, and send the Bills a fifth.
Trade! The Titans are sending standout safety Amani Hooker to the Bills, sources tell @ringer @netflixsports . pic.twitter.com/yHu5GwkjcF
We talked about undeniable offers potentially prying players that the Titans didn't want to trade, and Buffalo delivered just that. For a 28-year old defender, a second-round snag would've been hard for Tennessee to turn down.
Although, the move does mark the loss of the NFL's leader in INTs (five) and another one of the Titans' most notable defensive leaders. Robert Saleh's unit takes another serious hit, but the franchise are loading up on draft value for a fast-tracked rebuild.
The Hooker trade ended up being the final move Tennessee would make prior to the deadline. Jordan Schultz reported that both the Broncos and Giants were interested in Pollard, but the Titans held firm to their belief that he's pivotal to Cam Ward's development.
That hold makes sense. Holding Calvin Ridley, on the other hand, is a loss for Tennessee. After being heavily mentioned all week, Ridley didn't get so much as a mention until four minutes prior to the deadline. That was when Albert Breer said he (as well as Pollard) wouldn't be traded.
Looking back, the Titans dealt arguably their two best defenders. The offensive side of the ball went untouched. Tennessee will be three early picks richer heading into the second half of the 2026 season.
Not a promising omen for the final nine games this year, but the Titans will have a better chance than most low-ranking teams to improve quickly in the next few seasons.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: 1 Final Prediction: Forecasting the Landing Spot, and Haul, for Titans' Leading Trade Candidate
full_text:
It's become increasingly obvious that if the Tennessee Titans are going to try to move anyone today, it's pass-catcher Calvin Ridley. Sure, we could see a surprise offer come in for one of Tennessee's numerous pieces of defensive depth, or a team could get desperate and throw something crazy out there for RB Tony Pollard.
But as of right now, Ridley is the only name that keeps coming up as one that the Titans would be open and willing to part with. Now tha t the trade deadline is just a few hours away, news regarding this potential move could pop at any time.
Past the likelihoods and the expectations, though, is a deal that actually has to get done. We circled three suitors as primary candidates to trade for Ridley earlier this week; the Kansas City Chiefs, the Pittsburgh Steelers, and the San Francisco 49ers.
Now that another round of football has been played, I'm making the argument that one of those teams has pulled away. In today's last-second prediction, I have the Kansas City Chiefs sending Tennessee a sixth-round pick to secure Ridley prior to the deadline.
The stars are aligning for this move, and it makes sense for either side.
Rising receiver Xavier Worthy left Kasnas City's Week 9 victory over the New York Jets with a hamstring injury, exasperating the team's need at WR to an even further degree. The Chiefs had just returned leading pass-catcher Rashee Rice after he missed multiple weeks earlier this year.
WR Tyquan Thornton is on IR due to a severe ankle injury he sustained earlier this season; backup options Jeff Caldwell and Jimmy Holiday are also off the board. That leaves Kansas City with little choice but to add to that dwindling room.
Ridley may not have a place in Brian Daboll's offense any longer, but a move west could offer the 31-year old new life. Where the Titans are drafting and signing younger talent for their WR core as a part of an overarching rebuild, the Chiefs are grasping at a (mostly) bygone era of success to try and win another championship.
Their franchise makeup is opposite to Tennessee's. Where the Titans are tearing old pillars down, the Chiefs are gluing and taping them together to try and squeeze another title run or two out of the rubble.
Thus far, it's worked. Kansas City is 6-2. But with the Chiefs openly looking to get stronger at WR, per Zachary Pereles, it's clear they're currently short of the intended mark. The sixth-round asking price for Ridley emerged earlier this week as a sign that Tennessee is ready to move on from him.
Kansas City can certainly afford that tag, and if they strike out on someone like Brian Thomas Jr., taking a flyer on Ridley could be their easiest remaining choice. I think it's more likely than not that we see Ridley moved today, and I'm projecting Kansas City as his eventual destination.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Addition by Subtraction: How Titans’ LB Room is 1 Trade Away From an Upgrade
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans enjoyed a bye in Week 9, but will get back to work in Week 10 against the Jacksonville Jaguars. However, before Sunday's home contest, Tennessee will need to make decisions on the futures of multiple veteran players.
With the Titans sitting at 1-7 and the trade deadline set for Tuesday at 4 p.m. ET, general manager Mike Borgonzi has gotten plenty of calls on the team's veteran pieces who could provide value to contending squads. The common names mentioned in trade discussions have been running back Tony Pollard, safety Amani Hooker, and wide receiver Calvin Ridley.
One player who hasn't been brought up in trade rumors is linebacker Cody Barton, which is surprising. Barton should be one of Tennessee's top trade candidates ahead of the deadline, as moving on from the veteran linebacker makes a ton of sense.
Barton has been a serviceable starter for the Titans this season, tallying 34 tackles and 16 defensive stops with a 62.4 Pro Football Focus grade . As a result, the former Denver Bronco could net Tennessee a solid return on the market, and trading him makes sense given the state of the linebacker room.
Cedric Gray set the Titans franchise record in combined tackles in 2025 with 164. However, Gray has been demoted to a limited rotational role this year, as rookie Anthony Hill Jr. is the starter next to Barton. Though he has endured some of the usual rookie growing pains, Hill has shown promise this year as a potential long-term starter on the Titans' defense. The Texas product has already posted 82 tackles and 24 defensive stops in eight games , but has struggled in coverage.
Regardless, Hill is a defensive piece Tennessee can build around, and it would be wise for the Titans to roll into the future with him and Gray as the starters. Barton's experience is a nice plus, but Gray is more talented, better in pass coverage, and should be the starter.
Barton doesn't offer much upside for the future, and it's strange that head coach Robert Saleh and defensive coordinator Gus Bradley are playing the 29-year-old over the high-potential Gray. As a result, Tennessee should be shopping Barton and looking to send him to a linebacker-needy team to clear the way for Gray to reclaim his starting spot.
We'll see whether Barton is still on the Titans roster after 4 p.m. ET Tuesday. Barton isn't a negative on Saleh's defense, but Gray should be seeing more reps next to Hill.
Dharya Sharma is a sportswriter from Nebraska who has been covering the Tennessee Titans through his website, SharmSports, since 2023. He is also an NFL and NBA writer for The Sporting News and had a previous stop with Sportsnaut. Follow him on X @SharmSports

title: Setting a Price for 5 Titans Trade Candidates Before Tomorrow's Deadline
full_text:
With the trade deadline looming near, many fans are wondering just how active the Titans are going to be. Obviously, they won’t be buyers right now, but this team has plenty of pieces that other teams are surely interested in.
The Ringer’s Tom Pelissero noted that we could see up to 10 trades before Tuesday’s deadline. If that does in fact come to fruition, then it's hardly an exaggeration to say we could be in store for one of the most chaotic trade deadlines in recent history.
During Monday’s press conference, Robert Saleh said that barring unforeseen circumstances, the team they have now will be the one they roll into next Sunday with. Meaning, he’s not expecting any trades between now and the deadline. However, until we get there, speculation will undoubtedly continue to run rampant.
Therefore, I'm going to discuss the Titans’ likeliest trade candidates heading into Tuesday , and what it should take for the team to realistically move on from them if that possibility remains on the table.
This is clearly the most polarizing of all the realistic trade candidates. Some fans believe the Titans should trade him while his value appears to be at its highest, while others believe he’s too important for QB Cam Ward’s development to trade.
I fall under the latter in this situation. Right now, Ward’s only consistent weapons through eight games have been rookie WR Carnell Tate and RB Tony Pollard. Taking half of those away could ultimately be setting Ward up for failure for the rest of the season.
Especially with there being no reliable option behind Pollard at the moment. Not having a consistent ground game will make an already struggling offense completely one-dimensional, which in turn will make defenses hone in on the Titans’ pass catchers, subsequently making Ward’s job way harder than it already is.
The only way you can justify making a move like this is if the return is simply too good to pass up. You can justify trading Pollard for a top-100 pick since that will put you in prime position to get his long-term replacement next Spring without having to sacrifice one of the premium picks you already have.
Getting an extra third-round pick would give the Titans five picks over the first three rounds, three of which are on day two of the draft. If that were the case, it would not shock me one bit if the Titans went ahead and spent one of those picks on someone they believe could be the Titans’ next great running back.
What you won’t be able to justify is potentially sabotaging the most important player on the team solely to get an extra day three pick in return.
The only way the Titans can afford to trade Pollard is if they get something truly valuable in return. Otherwise, this isn’t a move worth making at this particular time, and that's being actively reflected by the team's stubborn attitude toward the move.
Hooker is playing the best ball of his career right now, so it’s easy to see why contending teams are interested in his services. He’s currently tied for the most interceptions in the NFL (five), while also earning an overall grade of 81 (sixth highest) through eight games, per PFF.
Hooker also has an impressive grade against the run (83.9), making him one of the most well-rounded safeties in the league, who also happens to be under contract through the 2028 season.
If the Titans are gonna part ways with someone as valuable and talented as Hooker, the return needs to be substantial. I would try to get a conditional third-round pick that could potentially turn into a second rounder, while ultimately settling for an unconditional third-round pick at absolute worst.
If nobody is willing to meet that price, then the Titans will have no problem keeping Hooker around for the foreseeable future.
Martin has been one of the genuine surprises of the season. When he signed with the Titans back in March, I don’t think even the most optimistic fan could’ve predicted how impactful he would be. Martin has recorded 6.5 sacks in eight games, which is tied with Vikings LB Andrew Van Ginkel for the eighth most in the league.
The veteran pass rusher could be an intriguing addition for a contending team looking to bolster their depth along the edge. With Martin under contract for another year, I would try to get an early day three pick in return.
Getting offered a fifth-round pick is probably more likely, but if I’m moving off my most consistent pass rusher who also happens to be top-10 in sacks, then I think it’s more than fair to want at least a fourth-rounder in return.
With Johnson not under contract beyond this season, I think the only way to get a fourth-round pick out of him would be to throw some conditions on the trade, similarly to what they did with OLB Dre’Mont Jones last season.
Last year, the Titans traded Jones for a conditional fifth-round pick that could turn into a fourth-round selection if the Ravens made the playoffs and Jones records at least two sacks in the regular season. The latter of which he accomplished.
I think something similar for Johnson would be fair, although I don’t see this one happening. The Florida State product has recorded three sacks and five tackles for loss, resulting in an overall grade of 64.2 through eight games, per PFF .
Simply put, moving on from Ridley would be mutually beneficial for everybody involved. Ridley could join a team he’s probably better suited for, while the Titans can get an extra draft pick in return to take another shot at finding a diamond in the rough towards the end of day three.
Ridley has less than 100 yards receiving this season, and it’s clear the Titans favor their young receivers at this point, as they should.
If someone offers the Titans a 2027 or even a 2028 7th-round pick, I think the wise move would be to just take it and move on.
Shaun is a longtime Titans fan who has years of experience in the field. He missed being on the team beat, and is here to change that. He also writes scripts for EA Sports' Madden games, where fans may have heard his work.

title: Final Titans NFL Trade Deadline Big Board: 1 Must-Trade and 4 Outside Possibilities
full_text:
The NFL trade deadline is now just one day and a handful of hours away. Robert Saleh said this morning that the Tennessee Titans are operating as if the roster right now will take the field next Sunday, but we all know it's more complicated than that.
Our last trade big board for the Titans saw seven candidates I believed could be in contention. Now much closer to the deadline, I've whittled that list down and seperated the remaining five candidates into two categories.
Those are the must-trade category, as well as outside possibilities. We'll start with the much shorter former one first.
Calvin Ridley is both the only player that looks especially likely to be moved at this point, and the only one that Tennessee should be trying to trade. You can make a positive case for almost anyone else on this list, but Ridley is essentially a non-factor.
The veteran WR has just six catches on the year, although he's only missed one game. Ridley's inability to find his footing in OC Brian Daboll's offense has resulted in multiple costly drops and a steady decline in opportunities.
As of yesterday, the Titans are still listening to offers on Ridley. A sixth-round pick seems to be the going rate, and there are multiple teams that could sensibly fork over the draft capital to bulk up their postseason chances this year.
Tennessee should seek those teams out and get a deal done by tomorrow at almost any cost.
Now to the guys who will probably stick around... but it's worth visiting the prospect of a trade anyway. Tony Pollard is the elephant in the room, and has all been all season.
It's evident by this point that the Titans aren't looking to trade Pollard. He's become Cam Ward's right-hand man in the backfield, and it seems that Tennessee are intent on keeping him there until his contract expires this offseason.
If the backfield market gets desperate enough, I could see a wild offer convincing Tennessee to go ahead and make the move. A third-round pick, or a package deal, would be hard to turn down.
But the key word there is "convincing." As of right now, Pollard remains an outside possibility because the Titans don't want to trade him. Fans should expect the veteran RB to remain in his leading role barring an unexpected haul.
Jermaine Johnson has been posed as a sort of quiet possibility for Tennessee as we get close to the deadline. There has been little noise surrounding a potential trade with Johnson, but the EDGE certainly fits the bill of someone who could be on the chopping block.
He's in the final year of his rookie contract on a roster ready to turn things over for another reset at any time. Johnson's past connections to Robert Saleh, due to their shared time with the New York Jets, make the opposite argument and provide some staying power.
If Jeffery Simmons hadn't been moved, Johnson would most likely have been a more prominent candidate. As things stand, he's an outside shot with a large role in this defense due to Simmons' absence.
Tennessee is between a rock and a hard place here. It's more probable that he stays, but with fellow d-lineman Jacob Martin heavily outpacing Johnson, the 27-year old rusher is worth mentioning as a potential surprise trade.
Per Jeremy Fowler this morning, the Titans have received calls on S Amani Hooker but don't want to move him. After his three-INT performance against the Cincinnati Bengals in Week 8, Hooker leads the NFL in interceptions with five.
Hooker is 28 years old and under contract with Tennessee through 2028. At this point, he's one of the most valuable assets in Saleh's unit and clearly has gas left in the tank. The kicker, of course, is that he'd arguably bring in the heftiest trade return (save for Pollard) of anyone left on this list.
Like Pollard, the Titans aren't looking to make a move here; it would take a strong offer the likes of which Tennessee hasn't yet seen to drum up any momentum around Hooker. I hesitate to call anyone truly "untouchable" on a 1-7 roster, but Hooker appears to be about as close as you can get with the Titans.
This is as wild a shot in the dark as they come, but our own Isaiah Pinto made an argument for the Titans to move on from Tyjae Spears. Despite there being no noise in this direction, the train of thought is definitely there.
Spears has two total touches in the last three weeks of Titans football. The backup RB's knee issues have kept him at bay this season, but even when he's seen the field (six of eight games), Spears hasn't been able to find a remote groove.
Between the Titans drafting rookie back Nick Singleton last year and probably retaining Pollard the rest of the way, Spears looks like an outlier now and in the future. That isn't even taking into account the possibility that the Titans use a first-round pick on a back in next year's draft.
Spears' age (25) and inexpensive contract could make him a sneakily compelling choice for a team in need of backfield help at the deadline. Given the aforementioned factors, Spears may not be too hard to pry from the Titans' grasp, either.
Not a surefire candidate by any means, but an inarguably sensible one on paper.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Making a Bold Trade Suggestion for Titans if Tony Pollard Won't be Moved: Another RB Goes Instead
full_text:
There are numerous names swirling around the NFL's upcoming trade deadline, with the Titans being one of the biggest expected sellers. The cutoff is at 3 PM CT on November 10.
After trading their franchise best player and multi-time All-Pro DT Jeffery Simmons to the Chicago Bears two weeks ago, many pundits are anticipating Tennessee to seek more draft capital with a 1-7 record. Names like WR Calvin Ridley, RB Tony Pollard, and S Amani Hooker are considered to be the Titans' most notable trade candidates, although the only one with real momentum is Ridley.
In fact, as of now, the Titans have no plans to trade Pollard or Hooker in spite of interest in each. However, there's a young and talented running back that has been oddly benched that a team looking for depth should take a flier on. It's Tyjae Spears.
Entering his fourth NFL season, Spears looked to serve as a viable asset in the Tennessee Titans offense. Many anticipated Spears would take over as starter with Pollard in his age 29 season on an expiring contract.
This is still possible, but recently Pollard has been dominating for the Titans, leaving Spears with back-to-back healthy scratches against the Browns and Bengals. In those two games, Pollard went off. He combined for nearly 300 yards from scrimmage and five touchdowns. The vet has earned the complete trust of OC Brian Daboll.
Unfortunately for Spears, he has slowly seen the field less and less over the course of the season. This year on the whole, Pollard has 296 offensive snaps to Spears' 140, according to Fantasy Pros .
It was only a few weeks ago, in Week 5, when Spears recorded a team-high nine receptions against the Houston Texans, serving as QB Cam Ward's reliable backfield target. Since that game, the former third-round pick has only been given two touches total.
Earlier in the season, Spears proved to have versatility as a pass blocker and a receiving back with 15 receptions for 75 yards and zero drops.
Despite not playing the last two weeks, Spears has more receptions than Pollard, WR Elic Ayomanor, WR Chimere Dike, TE Daniel Bellinger and Ridley, for the team's fourth-most catches. As a runner, Spears has a career average of 4.1 yards per carry with eight touchdowns and only two fumbles. Although his stats may not jump off the page, Spears certainly isn't a one-tool running back.
Currently, the two highly sought-after running backs at the deadline are Saquon Barkley and Jonathan Taylor, who both have contracts through 2028 worth more than $35 million, per Spotrac . Furthermore, Barkley turns 30 in February and Taylor turns 28 in January, and most running backs don't play far into their 30s as a general rule of thumb
Barkley and Taylor may have continuous success in future seasons, but they are two of the top four highest-paid players at their position. Giving up draft capital for stars considered to be entering the latter years of their careers is a gamble.
Meanwhile, Spears is on the last year of his rookie contract, worth roughly $1.4 million this season. His age and inexpensive contract makes Spears an attractive under-the-radar trade candidate looking to add depth to their backfield.
If Tennessee's coaching staff isn't going to play Spears, why keep him?
The Titans have shown a strong liking for Pollard, especially in the last three games, and his recent breakout performances may have won over the organization. Consequently, Spears could find himself in a new uniform next week before Tennessee overhauls their backfield next season.
Isaiah is an award-winning journalist and photojournalist. A graduate from the University of Kentucky, he has previously been published by BloodHorse, KY Insider, and the Kentucky Kernel for multimedia sports coverage. Isaiah is a Tennessee Volunteer at heart bringing his local expertise to Titans coverage.

title: 1 Move the Titans Can't Afford to Get Wrong at the NFL Trade Deadline
full_text:
Two days (a little less now) out from the NFL trade deadline at 3:00 PM CT on November 10, the only real noise-maker remaining for the Tennessee Titans is Calvin Ridley. RB Tony Pollard and S Amani Hooker have basically fallen off the board, leaving the veteran WR as the team's lone likely candidate.
Although, there are a few possibilities that shine through the cracks. A 1-7 squad can't really be held to any standard if the right team comes calling. Take the Jeffery Simmons trade, which nobody saw coming, as the strongest argument to that end.
Now, enter DE Jermaine Johnson. The former New York Jet and Robert Saleh pupil is only in his first year with Tennessee. He was acquired in an offseason trade earlier this year that would set him up to play out the final year of his contract on Nashville.
Naturally, the closer we get to the end of that deal, the bigger the questions are about the Titans' plans with Johnson. He's a tradable player, even if the buzz surrounding that potential move has been limited to completely silent.
But this is a move the Titans would have to approach oh-so carefully.
Trading Tony Pollard would be one thing; the veteran RB is in the final year of his deal, and at 29 years old, really only has utility for the rest of this season. That utility is tied to Cam Ward's growth, though, which makes him a more valuable asset.
Johnson paints a less clear picture. He's only 27 years old, evidenced by him currently being in the fifth year of his rookie deal. His ties to Coach Saleh make his role more interesting, and Johnson's three sacks on the year are good for second on the roster right now.
The DE rides the line between a compelling long-term piece and someone who Tennessee could bear to part with for the right price. Especially because Saleh isn't guaranteed a spot on the sideline forever, someone brought in for his system could appear less compelling if things keep ticking down.
Ridley is a holdover from the Brian Callahan era, and again, he's by far the biggest name on the Titans' trade block. The Titans can't sell Johnson too low, as trading Simmons put even greater pressure on the DE.
But just like anyone else on this roster, if not more so, Johnson shouldn't be a can't-touch player. Perhaps in spite of Saleh's own post-bye aspirations, this is an incomplete Titans team sprinting toward another draft-first reset.
That puts guys like Johnson (and Pollard for that matter) in an awkward spot. It also makes the decision about Johnson at the deadline all the more important.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Commanders News: NFL-Worst on Third Down, Washington Faces the Giants’ Blitz Again | Burgundy Roundup
full_text:
The NFL trade deadline came and went without any moves from the 2-5-1 Washington Commanders . The team apparently had already shifted its focus to its Week 10 opponent, the NFC East-leading New York Giants, who, at 5-2-1, also stood pat at the deadline. With center Lucas Patrick still in concussion protocol, Commanders head coach Dan Quinn confirmed at his presser Tuesday that the team is turning back to Nick Allegretti as the starter . Rookie Matt Gulbin took over for Patrick when he left the Rams game Sunday; Quinn explained after Sunday’s game that Allegretti had been working more at guard, so he went with Gulbin, who had taken the most reps at center. Thursday will mark Allegretti's first start since Week 3 , when he started at right guard. Quinn wants the Commanders to run the ball more, but they keep giving David Blough too few plays to do it. Washington ranks 11th in rushing yards per game and 25th in attempts, while its 31.13% third-down conversion rate is the worst in the NFL . The Commanders converted three of 12 against the Rams and ran only 10 plays in the third quarter. Quinn sees more carries coming from longer drives. Rachaad White and Austin Ekeler won’t get many chances if Washington keeps sending out its punt team after another short series. Quinn said Washington has added extra red-zone repetitions for a second week, so the work started before Sunday’s loss. The Commanders still turned two takeaways in Rams territory into three points and committed three accepted pre-snap penalties. Daniels said he has a say in which plays Blough keeps in the game plan, while acknowledging the first-time coordinator is working through growing pains. They have had those conversations. Thursday is when the offense has to get the details right. Allegretti’s first start back at center comes against a defense that sacked Daniels five times in the October tie. The Giants sent Cover 0 on 10 of his dropbacks late in that game and got three sacks during that stretch. They added seven against Philadelphia on Sunday, three by Arvell Reese. Daniels said Tuesday he needs answers he can check to, including protection adjustments. Allegretti has to get those calls across before the snap, giving Daniels a chance to use them. Washington did not practice Monday and held a walkthrough Tuesday, so both days’ participation listings are estimates. Treylon Burks (foot) improved from a projected nonparticipant Monday to projected limited Tuesday. Terry McLaurin and Dyami Brown remain on IR. Stefon Diggs, Antonio Williams, and Van Jefferson handled the available receiver work against Los Angeles, with Jaden Bradley a possible practice-squad elevation if needed. Tight end Colson Yankoff (knee) and Patrick were estimated nonparticipants for a second day. Chig Okonkwo (hip) and Shy Tuttle (shoulder) improved from projected limited Monday to projected full Tuesday. The Giants held a practice Tuesday, and quarterback J.J. McCarthy (hip) and running back Cam Skattebo (hamstring) were full participants after Monday’s projected limited designations. Abdul Carter (knee/back) and Malik Harrison (groin) stayed limited. Cornerback Colton Hood was added as limited after dislocating a finger at practice on Tuesday.
A month later, Washington has managed only one win since, and will enter the game at 2-5-1 after losing 20-13 to the Rams in Week 9. Commanders head coach Dan Quinn acknowledged the importance of Thursday's game during his presser on Monday: "But what I will say is, like, man, we need this win this week. There’s no doubt." Washington heads to MetLife Stadium this week three games behind the 5-2-1 Giants in the NFC East, where another loss would push Quinn’s team further out of the race.
Drew Rosenhaus on @PatMcAfeeShow : “I think that in all likelihood Brandon (Aiyuk) would probably sign with a team that knows him, somebody that has somehow been affiliated with him either in college or the #49ers . That’s just my guess.” 👋 @Commanders pic.twitter.com/H9VkQCTtDg
Mathematically the Commanders remain alive, but with nine games remaining, any realistic hope the team has for a strong finish likely begins and ends vs. the Giants on Thursday (8:15 p.m. ET, Prime Video). A win and they would be two games back with eight to play and own the tiebreaker -- if that eventually mattered.
Run block and pass block composite ratings So about the Commanders' run game pic.twitter.com/u3335oPcu4
The problem looked at least temporarily fixed when Lucas Patrick stepped into the role against Seattle . Washington had signed Patrick just 11 days before that start. In that game, right guard Sam Cosmi couldn't go, so it made sense to slide Allegretti over. The next week in London, Patrick stayed at center, and Gulbin slid over to right guard. That signaled Patrick had already taken over for the offseason starter, though Quinn initially called the change temporary before naming Patrick the starter the following Friday.
“I’ve worked with some mental health coaches on that just because it’s a tough process — handling some injuries and being out of the lineup,” Allegretti said Tuesday. “For a long time in my career, I kind of just kept all that to myself. So working through that these last couple of years helped me a ton, and I think it’s helped me day to day just to truly enjoy being here, being in the locker room, regardless of what my role is.”
Anthony Davis pranked Jayden Daniels with the help of Jayden’s mom Regina 😂💀 (via @TBSNetwork / @BleacherReport ) pic.twitter.com/QvfNohj8P9

title: Commanders’ Must-Win Giants Rematch Hinges on Replacing Five Players From the Tie
full_text:
The last time the Washington Commanders and New York Giants played, the game ended in a 27-27 tie after both teams missed chances to win in overtime. That day, Stefon Diggs was inactive, and Jer'Zhan (Johnny) Newton was on injured reserve. Terry McLaurin , Dyami Brown, Daron Payne, Jacory "Bill" Croskey-Merritt, and Javon Kinlaw played; all five are now on IR. A month later, Washington has managed only one win since, and will enter the game at 2-5-1 after losing 20-13 to the Rams in Week 9. Commanders head coach Dan Quinn acknowledged the importance of Thursday's game during his presser on Monday: "But what I will say is, like, man, we need this win this week. There’s no doubt." Washington heads to MetLife Stadium this week three games behind the 5-2-1 Giants in the NFC East, where another loss would push Quinn’s team further out of the race.
McLaurin caught four passes for 62 yards in the first meeting, while Brown played 23 offensive snaps. Diggs gives Daniels another proven receiver against New York, but getting him involved has been an issue of its own. He finished with three catches for 51 yards on 38 offensive snaps against the Rams. “So he’s definitely, like, in the front of our thinking. And so we need him, you know,” Quinn said about Diggs Monday. Washington needs that thinking to turn into completions before it’s chasing the game in the final minutes. Van Jefferson has a much bigger part in this offense now, too. He played just three offensive snaps against the Giants, compared with 36 against Los Angeles, where he caught five passes for 58 yards and a touchdown. Antonio Williams’ workload has grown from 42 snaps in the tie to 52 against the Rams. Jefferson should stay involved even if Treylon Burks returns from the foot injury that kept him out Sunday. He gave Blough another weapon to work with. The backfield has changed as well. Croskey-Merritt ran for 82 yards and a touchdown on 11 carries in the first meeting. Rachaad White and Austin Ekeler handled the running-back snaps against the Rams. I’d get both involved early Thursday and make New York account for them as runners and receivers. Blough has to find production there alongside everything he’s asking of the wideouts.
🚨 TOUCHDOWN COMMANDERS 🚨 BILL CROSKEY-MERRITT IS GONE 💨 Washington takes an early 7-0 lead vs. the Giants! pic.twitter.com/RDAz8I7XNg
Daronte Jones has two substantial workloads to replace up front. Payne played 63 of Washington’s 89 defensive snaps in the tie, while Kinlaw played 56. Payne also recorded a sack and a forced fumble. With both players now on IR , Washington will ask a different group to handle the interior work and create some disruption of their own. Newton’s return to the lineup helps, but his first game back also shows how much work falls on the rest of the rotation. He played 20 defensive snaps against the Rams , while Shy Tuttle played 43, Tim Settle 33, and Ricky Barber 15. I’d keep sharing that work, with Newton’s workload based on what he’s ready to handle. Getting him back gives Jones another option; it doesn’t fill both openings on its own. Blough has to get production from a different supporting cast, and Jones has to make this rotation hold up for four quarters. That’s the job Thursday. Quinn’s staff needs useful contributions from the players available now, with little room left for another game that ends in explanations. title: Commanders Daily: Washington Was Short on Receivers. Where Was Stefon Diggs?
full_text:
Heading into the Rams game on Sunday, the Washington Commanders were short on receivers: Terry McLaurin is out for the season, Treylon Burks is out, and Dyami Brown moved to injured reserve. Sounds like a day for Stefon Diggs to shine, right? The problem is Diggs' first catch, a four-yard burner, came with 7:28 left in the third quarter; he wouldn't gain another yard until a five-yarder with 4:41 left in the game. With 52 seconds remaining, they found him again for a 42-yard catch that moved Washington from its own 9 to the Rams' 49 and put the team in position to tie the game. When asked Monday why Diggs only had the one catch entering the final five minutes, Quinn responded by saying, "Yeah. I love his fire, man. Ben, I really do. And the competitive part. So he hit a couple targets earlier, and some that maybe he’s also first in the read to get there. Or for whatever reason, you know, you have to get off that. Or, you know, the read wasn’t there; the coverage took you somewhere else. So he’s definitely, like, in the front of our thinking. And so we need him, you know. And so that’s why he’s in the front of our thinking in those critical spots. So, you know, certainly one towards the end, you know, that gives us a chance to go after it. But, no, he’s always in the front of our thoughts. I love his fire. I love what he brings. And, like most excellent players, like as many opps as you can." Quinn is saying Diggs was the first read on some plays and that coverage pushed Daniels elsewhere on others. That is the politically correct response, but it still doesn't explain why Diggs had only four yards with five minutes left.
"You wish them nothing but the worst" 🤣 Stefon Diggs weighed in on how aware he is of the Commanders place in the NFC East. pic.twitter.com/WqWdICiBQT
After McLaurin’s injury, Quinn said he didn’t expect Diggs’ workload to increase much and pointed to rookie Antonio Williams as a player in line for more opportunities. The snap counts from the Rams game check out: Diggs played 38 of Washington's 62 offensive snaps against Los Angeles, while Williams played 52 and Van Jefferson had 36. Diggs had played 39 of 60 snaps against Philadelphia a week earlier, when Burks and Brown were both available. Even with those two out against Los Angeles, his snap share stayed about the same. Asked whether the two- and three-tight-end packages were why Diggs played less in the first half, Quinn said it wasn’t part of a deliberate design. Diggs missed the first game against New York that ended in a 27-27 tie, meaning Thursday will be his first game against the Giants in the burgundy and gold. The question is: Can Washington connect with Diggs earlier on the opportunities intended for him? His 42-yarder showed what one connection could change, but it arrived with less than a minute left against Los Angeles, a team without its top two cornerbacks .
Stefon Diggs giving the #Commanders life with this 40 yard play pic.twitter.com/U8WGIBxUJt

title: Hughes’ View: The Commanders’ Center Gamble Left Jayden Daniels Exposed
full_text:
The Washington Commanders have hit that point in the season where, at 2-5-1, it's over unless they start winning, and the Giants and Cowboys have a massive fallout. Which could happen, but shouldn't be depended on under normal circumstances. For Washington, they have to ask themselves, how did they get here? Their latest issue on the offensive line stems from the center position: this past weekend, when their starter Lucas Patrick went down with a concussion, they turned to rookie Matt Gulbin. It's ironic because Adam Peters and Dan Quinn spent the offseason trying to convince everyone that Nick Allegretti was that guy and would be the center for 2026. Allegretti has played two snaps since his last start, which came at right guard against the Seattle Seahawks in Week 3. In other words, he's still the same journeyman offensive lineman who came here years ago looking for a chance to start, but better suited as a backup. They tried to sell the fanbase a pumpkin, hoping Cinderella logic would kick in and he'd turn into something more than a dried-up gourd that rots on a warm fall night.
To understand this mistake in motion, you first have to remember that the team's center in 2025, Tyler Biadasz, was abruptly released before free agency, not long before the team struck out on free agent Tyler Linderbaum , who signed with the Raiders. That led the team to Allegretti as the answer, even though he played only 78 NFL snaps at center before 2025 and then started the final two games that season. No reason has ever been given for Biadasz being cut, and Peters dodged rehashing any of it in all of his offseason pressers, but Peters' plan beyond Linderbaum was clearly flawed. After roster cuts, Peters said , "And that's where we went into this offseason feeling that Nick could be our starter, and still do feel that way." Drafting Gulbin in the sixth round may prove to be a great move in the future, but what about protecting your franchise quarterback now? The problem looked at least temporarily fixed when Lucas Patrick stepped into the role against Seattle . Washington had signed Patrick just 11 days before that start. In that game, right guard Sam Cosmi couldn't go, so it made sense to slide Allegretti over. The next week in London, Patrick stayed at center, and Gulbin slid over to right guard. That signaled Patrick had already taken over for the offseason starter, though Quinn initially called the change temporary before naming Patrick the starter the following Friday.
When asked about the situation Sunday after the game , Quinn said the staff has been working Allegretti more at guard now: "In that moment, I would have felt comfortable with Nick as well, but I thought, let’s give the guy who’s got the most reps." Quinn also confirmed Allegretti was healthy. It makes sense that the coach would turn to the player who has practiced the most in the role; the problem is he said this in the preseason: "Nick is one of our smartest players, so that's a position that you rely on." Relied on so much that when the team looks for a replacement weeks later in crunch time with the season on the line, they turn to the sixth-round prospect with very little experience. Gulbin gave up a 12-yard sack to Myles Garrett on third-and-5 at the Rams’ 38, leaving Washington facing fourth-and-17, but who could be mad at a rookie who should have been given more help on that play? The Commanders' protection plan failed when it mattered most Sunday; that's not to say there wasn't effort; it is to say the coaches didn't do their jobs.
Myles Garrett showed Rams fans what they traded for, dominating in his return from injury. 3 SACK, 1 FF vs Commanders. With Garrett back, could the 5-4 Rams make a serious run at winning the NFC? https://t.co/6sIEtDYadN pic.twitter.com/9E0DPtT6qM
Thursday night in New York will tell us whether anybody learned from this. Patrick is in concussion protocol, and Quinn has three days to decide who gets the next snap and what kind of help he’ll have. The Giants are leading the division. They won’t wait while Washington figures it out on the fly. If the rush gets home again because the staff leaves its center on an island, Daniels will be the one paying for decisions he didn’t make. Nine games left sounds hopeful until your quarterback spends the first of them running from the same problem you promised was solved. title: Commanders Report Card: Washington Went Short on Its Last Shot to Tie the Rams
full_text:
File the Washington Commanders' 20-13 loss to the Los Angeles Rams away with the growing annals of painfully close defeats lining their 2-5-1 campaign, right alongside their season-opening outing against the Philadelphia Eagles, their Week 6 excursion against the San Francisco 49ers and that infamous link-up with the New York Giants, a technical tie that found a way to embarrass the fan base more than any 2026 matchup before or since.
The Rams looked exactly as advertised: talented, but never quite in sync. They entered the fourth quarter tied with their Landover hosts thanks to a slew of Commanders-esque holding penalties and miscues, yet still found a way to prevail following more late-game disappointments out of Washington. On which position groups gave it their all, and where criticism will continue to pile:
We expect a lot from Jayden Daniels , someone who's proven talented and clutch enough to drag his team into contention. And while he had highlights, this game still included a few nagging patterns that will continue to make wins tougher to pull off against anyone resembling a contender.
He made his 274 passing yards on a 101.4 passer rating against a Los Angeles defense that needed time to start looking the part, though a few lean quarters in the middle of the game did little to add to the Commanders' early success. He showed up in crunch time with his impressive accuracy and mobile escapability, as usual, reminding fans just how much they'd missed that downfield aggression between the seemingly endless slew of three-and-out punts.
Jayden Daniels & Stefon Diggs connect to move the Commanders close to midfield with 30 seconds to go LARvsWAS on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/SYNnMl9V9Z
That inconsistency has held him back from having his first truly great game of the season, even if he's been above average whenever he's taken the field this fall. The occasional goofs on his part certainly don't help, with one fumble, his first turnover of the season, setting up a Rams field goal before halftime. And on the snap before that disastrous attempted buzzer-beating touchdown, Daniels missed Stefon Diggs downfield after getting lucky on a few dropped potential interceptions.
While Quinn backed the short throw against pressure on the final snap, this streak of gaffes will only continue adding fuel to the fires of those questioning Daniels' situational awareness.
Jacory "Bill" Croskey-Merritt is still on the shelf, leaving a hodgepodge of reserves in Rachaad White and Austin Ekeler to ease Daniels' burden on the ground. They ended up being arguably more effective as dump-off options on a few short passes than they were at navigating dogpiles, finding ways to evade deadly Rams tacklers while failing to back up the coaching staff's insistence on deploying them to start every series.
44 total rushing yards on a combined carry count of 15 still isn't nearly enough to match up against any serious defense, though, and they've been lucky to get nearly as much as they have out of the aging Ekeler a little over a year after he tore his Achilles tendon. Very little between the remaining talent and the blockers creating the holes being dashed through has impressed this season, leaving this piece of the offense to predictably struggle against a team with the Rams' pedigree and depth.
Van Jefferson's doing a lot of heavy lifting in this category, a situation no one could have fathomed he'd slide before the season started. He was one of the final casualties of the preseason cut wave, falling short of the seven-man receiver room that includes the recently injured Terry McLaurin, Jaylin Lane, Treylon Burks and Dyami Brown, as well as Luke McCaffrey, who's since been relegated to the group's full-time return man.
Left without much of anyone to turn to outside of Stefon Diggs and Antonio Williams, who each did enough given their limited targets, the coaching staff somehow struck gold in their last-minute turn to Jefferson. Against a Rams team with whom he'd once won Super Bowl LVI, he stacked a Washington-high 58 yards on five catches, including his first touchdown in the burgundy and gold.
first one of the season for Van Jefferson 🙌 📺 #LARvsWAS FOX pic.twitter.com/7SbDhDOCZy
Chig Okonkwo, similarly, showed up big in this one, coming just one yard short of Jefferson's finish with a handful of his typically athletic moves after the catch. Even if the pass-catching resource pool was depleted this week, the Commanders would be better off leaning more on the downfield attack- at least, if he knows that he's getting enough protection to enjoy the luxury of waiting for his reads to form.
I find it harder than usual to fault Daniels' protective line for this one, as the remaining offensive linemen did stand up for themselves somewhat in the face of a few legendary pass-rushers. Myles Garrett and Aaron Donald repeatedly squared up on the same side of Los Angeles' defense, forcing Washington's hand in choosing which former Defensive Player of the Year winner to double.
Unfortunately for Daniels, and predictably to everyone else, Brandon Coleman was no match for Garrett in his three-sack return to action. Few can hold up to that combination of size and speed, but the fresh round of false starts certainly does wonders for his image in the eyes of the frustrated fan base still pining for usual starter Laremy Tunsil.
Throw in yet another center, rookie Matt Gulbin, to fill in for the hurt Lucas Patrick, and we're left with more questions beyond Garrett's most lopsided matchup partner. How could a front office that was so in on Nick Allegretti as their center through the offseason be this comfortable skipping over him so regularly in parsing through the depth chart? Another dilemma worth investigating amidst the season's nosedive.
Washington Commanders killer Matthew Stafford didn't look like he was having a great time on Northwest Stadium's grass. He threw a pick right at Nick Cross, got bumped into a sack, and required 43 attempts to reach 228 yards; that stat line included a litany of missed connections with his streaking receivers.
K'Lavon Chaisson with a textbook punch out LARvsWAS on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/tu0FRD6Xux
Washington's defensive linemen and backers deserve some credit for at least making it tough on them, and for holding Kyren Williams to 45 yards on 15 carries while more efficient understudy Blake Corum went for 58 on 11, though they did lack some of that same blitzing bite without the Rams' willingness to regularly throw to screens off to the sides of the hashes.
They held their opponents to 3/14 on third downs to give their offense plenty of chances to respond. Still, reigning MVP Stafford is as unafraid to heave down the gut of opposing defenses, a problem that ended up falling on the secondary.
It's hard to pay the back-line defenders too much grace when they didn't even have Davante Adams to occupy their attention, yet they still found a way to allow 150 yards to Puka Nacua. As K'Lavon Chaisson put it after the game, the Rams were “running the same play all day, feeding the same person the ball all day.”
The Commanders could not stop Puka Nacua today. 14 catches for 150 yards and a TD. K'Lavon Chaisson said, "as a defense, you just gotta drop your nuts and figure out how you're going to stop that and not let it happen anymore." pic.twitter.com/vRH5DgbOtz
Ultimately, that admittedly successful playstyle reflects on everyone participating in the productive defense, and no individual defensive back could do much to disrupt Nacua's mission. The team didn't start doubling him on his downhill routes until deep into the outing, too talented to be treated like your average wideout with room to run after his completions.
Cross did his part with a fumble recovery and a pick, and Trey Amos did his part by playing generally good, tight coverage, albeit not as tightly as he played in last week's win over the Eagles. There are pieces…

title: Everything Dan Quinn Said After Commanders’ Loss to Rams
full_text:
The Washington Commanders had two plays from the Rams’ 31 to get into the end zone Sunday. Jayden Daniels threw an incomplete pass to Stefon Diggs with eight seconds left, then went underneath to Chig Okonkwo with three seconds to play. Los Angeles recovered a fumble to seal a 20-13 win . Dan Quinn said Washington checked down to the short throw when the Rams showed pressure. He wanted better execution on the play. Washington fell to 2-5-1 and has a Thursday night rematch against the division-leading New York Giants in Week 10.
Opening statement “All right, let’s get rolling. Frustrating game, and once again, we have not nailed our complementary football, and I’ll keep saying it until we do. We’re halfway through the season, and that all has to click. After stops, don’t think we capitalized. We had two takeaways. I think we only got three points out of it. We had some opportunities for fourth-down stops defensively, to get those stops, to get it flipped the other way. So, all that said, it’s a short week against our division leader on the road, and we got to go and we have to play all three phases together. Seen too much of it where it’s part of it, not the whole thing. And so that’s what we’re going to continue to just practice, and that has to get right. It just has to. Too far along to not have it all working together. All right, let’s get rolling.” The offense got off to a pretty good start but seemed to fall flat. What was missing? “Yeah, I did like the way that we started, too, Nikki. I felt that way. To see us have some runs, have action to go, and I didn’t feel like we were able to sustain that. To get ahead and then here’s a chance even to get a takeaway and go further. But my biggest examples, even the complementary, we had a chance to be on our two-minute to go. We got a takeaway. I think it was maybe a fumble recovery, and then we turned it over again. They get a field goal. Looking back to it, I’ll give them credit, too. I want to watch the tape from a front standpoint, but I liked how we started. But just to not see that sustained, Nikki, that’s the thing that’s especially frustrating.” What went into your decision to challenge the third-quarter play involving Amik Robertson where the ruling was upheld? "After review they thought maybe it was bobbled on the first step. So then that didn't make it into the second step meaning that became the first." "But I think on those ones sometimes like you have to take a shot too. You know when it's a one that you think is reasonable to go when it's clear and obvious many times that gets replay assisted but in that moment I felt like this was one if it's close roll the dice." On the final play, what went into the decision to go with the lateral play instead of taking a shot directly at the end zone? “Yeah. So, there’s two plays that you come in. And so, on the first one, you’re taking a shot to the end zone, just like you described. And sometimes to check for that against a team that does what we call a zero blitz or a max blitz, you want to, ‘OK, here’s the other play where you can’t block them all up.’” “So we got to the second play of what would have been, like, everybody blitzing, check it down and move forward from there. So with eight seconds left, you want two chances at something. And so to not have those, didn’t love our execution at our end.” Lucas Patrick and Amik Robertson went down during the game. Do you have an update on either of them? “The only one I do have is that, with Lucas not coming back, he’s in the concussion protocol. But I’ll give you some updates tomorrow whenever we talk next regarding anyone else. That’s the only one that the medical team hit me on prior to tonight.” A couple of players said they knew what the Rams were going to do on offense, with the inside runs and getting the ball to Puka Nacua. Why was that so hard to stop? “Yeah, yeah, for sure. And I give him credit, too. So the inside style of runs, I guess that’s what they’ve been demonstrating. And I knew that was going to be one of the strengths of their team. I thought both the backs had showed good production doing that. With Nacua, I knew there had also been some on the screen side of things. So it’s not all dropbacks to go. And I think that’s part of what makes him unique is his catch-and-run ability, where it’s not just downfield throws. So on those, you have to be able to roll up and tackle well, John, too. He may get X number of catches for not too far down the field, but knowing that, ‘Hey, man, you got to go get your tackle.’ So having too many yards, that was big for me.”
There are still nine games left. Do you feel like you’re running out of time to turn this around? “Yeah, I think it speaks to the importance of a division leader right away. And so it’s a difficult locker room. We got to turn the page quickly to get to that because we talked earlier, ‘OK, this is where we are,’ but we also know, ‘Man, we have to play at our best.’” How difficult was that spot for Matt Gulbin to come into? How well has he practiced to earn the backup spot, and is Nick Allegretti still an option at center? “In that moment, I would have felt comfortable with Nick as well, but I thought, let’s give the guy who’s got the most reps. That was the decision behind it. It’s difficult, but … this is part of the gig.” Brandon Coleman had a couple of penalties again. In the middle of a game, how do you decide when to put somebody else in if a player is struggling? “Yes. And I want to go back to look. We’ve put a lot of work … what could change to get some of these false starts off. So to have still two remain. I think Sam’s might have been a holding, right, on that one that was prior to the turnover. We’ve made adjustments on how many cadences, what types and that. So I just want to see if it’s a product of too much anticipation against a good rusher. And that’s different to me than a lack of focus. That makes sense, Dave. I’ll give you a better answer once I have a chance to look at him.” Just to be clear on Allegretti, he’s healthy? “Yes. Yeah, yeah. We’ve just been working him more at guard and Matt at center. And, you know, if we have to change, we’ll see what next week looks like as well.” Going back to the last two plays, you mentioned you didn’t like the execution. Was the final play called that way, or was it a check Jayden Daniels made based on what he saw? “Yeah, it has to be one that you get to a second play, and it’s the right adjustment to make it and going. So how long do you wait? You get the full protection and try to throw a Hail Mary, because it’s hard to, on a Hail Mary, get everybody scrambling and buy time when they’re bringing everyone. So that’s the juxtapose of, like, get to a max protection, buy time, or that’s another alternative play. The one before it was really the one I wanted to see more execution when there was maybe eight seconds at that point. There’s just two plays remaining in the game, and you want to give yourself a chance.” Did that call have to do with the Rams keeping three defenders across the goal line on the previous play and expecting to see that again? “I think just more tape history, too, of what could be and what they’ve done.” You were shorthanded at receiver , and it looked like Stefon Diggs played less in the first half while you used a lot of 12 and 13 personnel. Was that part of the plan? “No. No, it wasn’t any further design than another.” Van Jefferson went from the practice squad and having no catches coming in to being one of your leading receivers, especially in the first half. How much of that did you anticipate? “Yeah, I wouldn’t say it was anticipated, Ben, but I would say this is somebody that is a respected player around here. And I can remember after camp having a hard conversation and him coming back on a practice squad when we had a very healthy wide receiver room, knowing it would take a leap of faith to still come, knowing that there were six players already…

title: Commanders Instant Takeaways: Washington’s Offense Let the Rams Off the Hook | Game Pulse
full_text:
The Washington Commanders led 10-6 at halftime Sunday and scored just three points the rest of the way, losing 20-13 to the Los Angeles Rams at Northwest Stadium. The loss dropped Washington to 2-5-1. Both Washington takeaways gave the offense the ball in Rams territory. All the Commanders got out of them was a Drew Stevens field goal. They still got the ball twice in the final six minutes with a chance to tie. The Giants beat Philadelphia 19-11 to move three games ahead of Washington in the NFC East. The Commanders get their rematch Thursday night at MetLife Stadium. Here are my immediate reactions in this week’s Game Pulse. *Game Pulse collects my instant takeaways after each quarter and at the final whistle.
- Washington needed a better answer for Myles Garrett. He finished with three sacks, and the one that hurt most came when he beat rookie center Matt Gulbin and turned third-and-5 at the Rams’ 38 into fourth-and-17. With Lucas Patrick out and a chance to tie the game, I wanted more help for Gulbin in that spot. - I wanted to see Washington double Puka Nacua more. He caught 14 of 19 targets for 150 yards and the go-ahead touchdown. Stafford kept going back to him. At some point, you have to make somebody else beat you.
The Commanders could not stop Puka Nacua today. 14 catches for 150 yards and a TD. K'Lavon Chaisson said, "as a defense, you just gotta drop your nuts and figure out how you're going to stop that and not let it happen anymore." pic.twitter.com/vRH5DgbOtz
- I liked how Washington played the run late. Sonny Styles and Shy Tuttle both made stops behind the line that helped force punts with the Rams trying to run the clock. Styles finished with 13 tackles and Frankie Luvu had 15. That defense gave the offense enough chances to tie it. - Van Jefferson gave Jayden Daniels a reliable option over the middle. He finished with five catches for 58 yards and Washington’s only touchdown, and both of his fourth-quarter catches went for first downs. He also had room on fourth-and-17. I thought Daniels left that one a little short, and Emmanuel Forbes got a hand on it. - I wanted the ball in the end zone on the last snap. Stefon Diggs’ 42-yard catch gave Washington a real chance after it took over at its own 9 with 52 seconds left and no timeouts. With three seconds left from the Rams’ 31, the ball went to Chig Okonkwo short of the goal line, and the Rams recovered a half-hearted attempt at a lateral that ended in a fumble.
End of game sequence was not ideal. WSH got to play he 32 and had two plays left. Neither throw was into end zone. The last play was designed to be short it looks like. Rams brought 5, one on a delay. But looks like routes weren’t vertical. Odd. pic.twitter.com/NLcy5kXil6
- Nick Cross has been Washington’s best defensive back today. He’s had a hand in both takeaways, and he made Stafford pay for trying to force one to Puka Nacua. I liked his work against Tyler Higbee, too. That was a third-down stop Washington had to challenge to get. - Washington went the whole quarter without a first down, even with the ball at the Rams’ 27 after the pick. Brandon Coleman’s false start helped put the offense in third-and-16. Drew Stevens did his job from 41 yards, but I wanted seven with that field position. - Holding the Rams without a conversion on their first nine third downs was good work. What bothered me was how easily they stayed out of third down coming out of halftime. Los Angeles went 69 yards for a touchdown without facing one.
- I’d keep finding ways to get Rachaad White the ball. He turned a short throw into 45 yards to set up Van Jefferson’s touchdown, and he showed what he could do on the ground when John Bates opened a hole on that 14-yard run. With McLaurin out, White can take some of the work off Daniels. - Frankie Luvu has been Washington’s best defender so far. He got to Matthew Stafford for a nine-yard sack, and I liked seeing Jer’Zhan Newton get into the backfield on a run Luvu finished for a loss. That’s the push I wanted to see from Newton in his first game back. - Washington wasted a chance to go up two scores. K’Lavon Chaisson and Nick Cross gave the offense the ball at the Rams’ 40. Sam Cosmi’s hold wiped out a good run, and Myles Garrett forced Daniels’ first turnover of the season . A short field for Washington turned into three points for the Rams.
- That 15-yard throw from Jayden Daniels to Chig Okonkwo was textbook. With McLaurin out, I’d keep giving Daniels that option over the middle. - Both tackles gave me reason to worry. Brandon Coleman got beat on a run that lost four yards, and Josh Conerly Jr. wound up on the ground in pass protection. Daniels got the ball out, but he’s going to need more help against this front. - I liked how Frankie Luvu set the edge against the run. Holding the Rams to a field goal was a good result, but Washington can’t let Stafford stay on the field for 14 plays at a time.
- Myles Garrett is back alongside Aaron Donald, and Byron Young gives Los Angeles another way to get after Jayden Daniels. I’ll be watching how Washington handles first and second down. If the Commanders keep putting themselves in third-and-long, the Rams get to rush on their terms. - Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson are out, which is a break for Washington’s thin receiving group. I want to see Antonio Williams get work early again. If the Rams take away Williams and Stefon Diggs, where does Daniels go with the ball? Chig Okonkwo is one place to look. - Jer’Zhan Newton is back. How much he plays is the first thing I’ll be watching. If Washington can get a push inside with four rushers, Matthew Stafford has less room to step up when Washington’s edge rushers get around the tackles.
The Washington Commanders came into Sunday’s game against the Los Angeles Rams looking to build on their 27-10 win over Philadelphia . The Rams were missing both starting cornerbacks, but with Myles Garrett back, Washington had to give Jayden Daniels enough time to make those absences matter.

title: Commanders’ Depleted Receiving Corps Catches a Break Against Rams
full_text:
The Washington Commanders have only two available wide receivers who have caught a pass for them this season: Stefon Diggs and Antonio Williams. Neither will have to face Trent McDuffie on Sunday. The Rams cornerback is inactive with a back injury, leaving Los Angeles down two starters at the position after Jaylen Watson went on injured reserve Saturday. Jer’Zhan Newton is active for his season debut. The defensive tackle missed Washington’s first seven games with a pectoral injury, practiced fully all week, and was activated from injured reserve Saturday . Here are the Week 9 inactive lists for both teams:
WR Treylon Burks QB Athan Kaliakmanis (emergency third quarterback) CB Fabian Moreau CB Isaac Yiadom G Tanoa Togiai
Treylon Burks was ruled out Friday with a foot injury. Washington placed Dyami Brown on injured reserve Saturday with a calf injury and elevated Jaden Bradley from the practice squad. Bradley is active, giving the Commanders depth at receiver, now that Terry McLaurin is also on injured reserve.
CB Trent McDuffie QB Ty Simpson LS Joe Cardona OLB Darryl Peterson III OL Bill Murray OL Keagan Trost OLB Desjuan Johnson
Los Angeles will have Myles Garrett available for the first time since Week 1. Safety Kam Curl and tight end Colby Parkinson are also active after being listed as questionable Friday. Tight end Terrance Ferguson remains on injured reserve.

title: Commanders vs. Rams Weather Forecast: Wind Could Matter Early
full_text:
Sunday looks like a good afternoon to be at Northwest Stadium. The Washington Commanders host the Los Angeles Rams with sunshine in the forecast and temperatures expected to stay in the low 60s during the game. The wind is worth keeping an eye on early, particularly when either team has a shot at a deep throw or a long field goal. Washington is 2-4-1 coming off its win over Philadelphia. The Rams are 4-4, and kickoff is scheduled for 1 p.m. ET Sunday, Nov. 8, in Landover, Maryland.
The National Weather Service’s hourly forecast for Landover has it at 61 degrees for kickoff, with a west wind around 11 mph and gusts up to 21 mph. Rain chances are listed at 0% through the game window, and sustained winds are expected to ease as the afternoon goes on. Forecast updated Saturday, Nov. 7, at 2:31 p.m. ET. All times are Eastern.
9 a.m. — parking lots open
11 a.m. — stadium gates open
Washington is already working around injuries at receiver , and giving Jayden Daniels time against the Rams’ pass rush is the first concern when it wants to throw deep. If the Commanders get a clean pocket, the gusts are worth accounting for. A ball that stays in the air longer gives the wind more time to move it. Drew Stevens has already hit from 57 yards at Northwest Stadium, but the wind could change what feels like a reasonable attempt early Sunday. A kick into the wind can lose carry, while the same breeze could help from the other end. Warmups should give Stevens and Dan Quinn a better idea of his range in each direction.
The Commanders’ gameday guide lists the RedZone lot opening at 8 a.m., general parking at 9 a.m., Legends Plaza at 10 a.m. and stadium gates at 11 a.m. It could be around 46 degrees when the RedZone lot opens and 52 when the other lots open, with a breeze through the morning. Bring a light jacket if you’re tailgating. By the time you’re in your seat for kickoff, it should be in the low 60s.
